The word "Presbyterian" comes from the New Testament Greek word *presbyteros*, meaning "elder," describing a church government led by elected teaching and ruling elders in local congregations (Acts 14:23; 1 Timothy 5:17) who are accountable to regional presbyteries and a national General Assembly. Regarding the sacraments, the PCA affirms the spiritual presence of Christ in the Lord's Supper and practices both believer's baptism and infant baptism (paedobaptism), viewing baptism as the New Covenant sign that corresponds to Old Testament circumcision for believers and their households (Genesis 17:7; Colossians 2:11–12).

While Christians who hold to believer's baptism or congregational church governance respectfully differ on these secondary matters, faithful believers can recognize the PCA as a gospel-centered branch of the historic church committed to the authority of God's Word. If you are exploring a local PCA church, a helpful next step is to review their summary of beliefs and visit a worship service to observe how Scripture is preached and applied in the life of the congregation.
Where is God now? Where is God when it hurts?

When everything hurts and the pain feels overwhelming, it is deeply understandable to wonder if God is distant or silent. Yet Scripture assures us that God is neither blind to your suffering nor far away. Because of His omnipresence, God is never absent from any part of your life, and He promises to draw especially close to those who are suffering: "The LORD is near to the brokenhearted; He saves the contrite in spirit" (Psalm 34:18). Even King David cried out in anguish, "My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?" (Psalm 22:1), showing us that God welcomes honest, raw lament rather than asking us to pretend everything is fine.

The clearest answer to where God is when it hurts is found in the incarnation and the cross of Jesus Christ. Written to weary believers facing severe hardship and persecution, the letter to the Hebrews reminds us that Jesus is our great High Priest who can "sympathize with our weaknesses" (Hebrews 4:15), using a Greek word (*sympatheo*) that means to suffer alongside or feel with another. God did not remain detached from human agony; the eternal Son took on real human flesh, became "a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief" (Isaiah 53:3), and suffered in our place through His substitutionary atonement. By His death on the cross and His bodily resurrection on the third day, Christ defeated sin and death, securing the promise of a day when He will wipe away every tear (1 Corinthians 15:3–4; Revelation 21:4).

If you do not yet know Him personally, He invites you even in the middle of your pain to turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, so that you may receive forgiveness and a Savior who walks with you through the darkest valley (Psalm 23:4; Romans 5:1).

For today, take one small, concrete step: open your Bible to Psalm 34 or Psalm 22, read it slowly, and speak directly to God in prayer about the exact pain you are carrying right now, holding nothing back. If you are connected to a local church, also consider reaching out to a pastor or a trusted, mature believer so they can walk alongside you and pray with you (James 5:16).

If you feel comfortable sharing, what is causing you this pain right now?
What is the just war theory?

Just war theory is a Christian ethical framework, shaped by early theologians such as Augustine of Hippo and later systematized by Thomas Aquinas, that defines the moral conditions under which a nation may rightly go to war and how armed conflict must be conducted. It seeks to hold together the biblical duty to restrain evil and protect the innocent with the command to love one's neighbor and pursue peace.

Historically, the framework is divided into two parts: *jus ad bellum* (justice in going to war) and *jus in bello* (justice in the conduct of war). Criteria for entering a war include having a just cause (such as defending against unprovoked aggression), being authorized by a legitimate governing authority, acting with right intention (aiming to restore peace rather than seeking vengeance or conquest), exhausting peaceful alternatives as a last resort, and having a reasonable hope of success. Criteria during a war require proportionality, meaning the force used must not exceed the evil being countered, and discrimination, meaning combatants must protect noncombatants and innocent civilians.

Scripturally, this framework rests on the distinction between personal vengeance and the God-ordained role of the civil magistrate. Writing to believers living under the Roman Empire, the Apostle Paul taught that governing authorities are God's servants who carry the sword to restrain and punish wrongdoers (Romans 13:1–4; 1 Peter 2:13–14), even while forbidding individual Christians from taking personal revenge (Romans 12:17–21). Grounded in the truth that every person bears the image of God (Genesis 9:6), just war theory reflects the theological reality of common grace, through which God curbs human wickedness in a fallen world until Christ returns to establish lasting peace (Isaiah 2:4).

Because Scripture does not prescribe a detailed policy manual on modern warfare, faithful Christians hold differing views on the use of force. Many affirm just war principles, while others embrace Christian pacifism based on Jesus' teaching on non-retaliation (Matthew 5:38–39). Both traditions share a deep commitment to honoring the sanctity of life and seeking peace, leaving room for conscience and charity among believers (Matthew 5:9; Romans 14:5). As a practical step, you can use these principles to pray with discernment for national leaders, asking God to grant them restraint, justice, and a genuine pursuit of peace (1 Timothy 2:1–2).
What does it mean that women should have a gentle and quiet spirit (1 Peter 3:4)?

In 1 Peter 3:4, a "gentle and quiet spirit" describes an inner disposition of humble strength and settled peace that trusts in God rather than relying on outward appearance or anxious control. Far from demanding a timid personality or absolute silence, Peter is calling Christian women to cultivate a heart rooted in God's providence that reflects the very character of Christ (Matthew 11:29; 1 Peter 3:4).

In the Greco-Roman world, social status and personal value were heavily displayed through elaborate hairstyles, gold jewelry, and fine clothing, and Christian wives, especially those married to unbelieving husbands, often faced intense relational pressure (1 Peter 3:1–3). Against that backdrop, Peter uses two Greek words to describe this unfading inner beauty: *praus* ("gentle" or "meek"), which refers to strength yielded to God's control rather than weakness, and *hesychios* ("quiet"), which signifies a tranquil, undisturbed heart free from agitation. This meaning is confirmed by the immediate context, where Peter explains that holy women of the past adorned themselves by putting their hope in God and refusing to "give way to fear" (1 Peter 3:5–6). In historic Christian theology, this inward transformation is a fruit of progressive sanctification, as the Holy Spirit matures a believer into Christ's own meekness and steadfast trust in the Father (1 Peter 2:23).

Because this spirit is "of great worth in God's sight," it frees women from the exhausting burden of chasing fleeting cultural standards of beauty or trying to secure their peace through worry (1 Peter 3:4). Practically, a Christian woman can live this out today by pausing when a stressful conversation or insecurity arises, silently entrusting the outcome to God's care, and choosing to speak with calm, respectful honesty rather than sharp words or fearful striving. Such meekness never requires suppressing her God-given gifts, stifling her voice, or tolerating abuse, because a heart anchored in the Lord possesses quiet courage rather than passive weakness.
What does it mean to be free from sin?

To be free from sin means that through Jesus Christ, a believer is liberated from sin's legal guilt and eternal penalty, broken from its ruling tyranny in daily life, and promised final deliverance from its very presence when Christ returns (Romans 8:1; Romans 6:18; 1 John 3:2). It does not mean a Christian becomes instantly incapable of sinning in this life, because Scripture plainly teaches that indwelling sin remains until glory (1 John 1:8).

Writing to believers in first-century Rome, where slavery was an everyday reality, the Apostle Paul uses the vivid language of bondage and liberation to explain this truth (Romans 6:16-18). The Greek word he uses for being "set free" (*eleutheroo*) describes a slave being formally released from a cruel master's ownership so that the master no longer holds legal authority over them (Romans 6:18; Romans 6:22). Because all people have rebelled against a holy God, we are naturally enslaved to sin and stand guilty under His just wrath (Romans 3:23; John 8:34). Yet God sent His Son, who lived a sinless life, died on the cross in our place through penal substitution, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day to purchase our freedom (2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4).

Historic Christian theology summarizes this freedom in three distinct dimensions:

*   **Freedom from the penalty of sin (Justification):** By grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, God pardons our guilt and declares us righteous because Christ paid our debt in full (Ephesians 2:8-9; Romans 5:1). There is no condemnation left for anyone who belongs to Jesus (Romans 8:1).
*   **Freedom from the power of sin (Sanctification):** Sin is no longer the king on the throne of your heart (Romans 6:14). Through progressive sanctification by the Holy Spirit, you are given new desires and the genuine ability to resist temptation and grow in holiness, even though you will still wrestle against old habits until the end of your earthly life (Galatians 5:16-17; Philippians 1:6).
*   **Freedom from the presence of sin (Glorification):** When Jesus Christ returns personally and bodily to judge the living and the dead and renew all things, He will completely remove every trace of sin, sorrow, and temptation forever (1 John 3:2; Revelation 21:4).

Practically, Christian freedom is neither a license to indulge selfish desires nor a crushing burden to achieve perfection by your own willpower (Galatians 5:13). Instead, when temptation knocks today, you no longer have to answer as a helpless slave, and when you do stumble, you can immediately confess your sin to God knowing His forgiveness is secure in Christ (1 John 1:9). A helpful next step this week is to read Romans 6 slowly, pray directly to God thanking Him that sin's mastery is broken, and share your ongoing struggles with a mature believer in a local church for encouragement and prayer (James 5:16).

If you have not yet experienced this freedom, turn from your sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose again to forgive you and give you new life. As you consider what it means to be free from sin, which part of this promise brings you the most hope or raises the biggest question for you right now?
Is God man-made? Did man create the idea of God?

No, God is not man-made. The Bible teaches that the eternal, self-existent God created the universe and made humanity in His own image (Genesis 1:1; Genesis 1:27).

It is completely understandable why many people wonder if the opposite is true. Looking at the sheer variety of conflicting religions throughout history, or noticing how human cultures often project their own desires and fears onto the sky to explain the unknown, it can easily look as though humanity invented the idea of God.

Scripture actually agrees that people frequently manufacture false gods in their own image (Romans 1:22–23), which is why idolatry is addressed throughout the Bible. Yet the true and living God stands in sharp contrast to human invention. While Ancient Near Eastern creation stories typically imagined gods emerging out of preexisting, chaotic matter, the opening line of Genesis deliberately presents God as existing before all things and speaking the cosmos into being out of nothing (Genesis 1:1). Historic Christian theology summarizes this biblical truth with the term aseity, meaning that God is completely self-existent and depends on nothing outside Himself (Psalm 90:2), and imago Dei, meaning that humans bear His image rather than God bearing ours (Genesis 1:27).

Christians also believe that God has not left us to guess about Him in the dark. He makes His eternal power and divine nature clearly known through the created world, which theologians call general revelation (Romans 1:19–20), and He has spoken most clearly through His Word and through His Son, Jesus Christ (Hebrews 1:1–3). Rather than humanity reaching up to invent a deity, the central message of Scripture is that God reached down to rescue us. Because of human sin, we have turned away from our Creator toward self-made idols and stand separated from a holy God (Isaiah 59:2; Romans 3:23). In love, God entered history in the person of Jesus Christ, who lived a sinless life, died on the cross as a substitutionary sacrifice for our sins, and rose bodily from the dead on the third day to reconcile us to God (1 Corinthians 15:3–4; 2 Corinthians 5:21).

If you are exploring whether God is real or invented, a practical step you can take this week is to read through the Gospel of John and ask whether the Jesus you meet there reads like a comforting human myth or the living God confronting our world. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, so that you may receive forgiveness and know the God who made you (John 14:6). What first led you to wonder whether God might be a human invention?
What is the significance of the statement “God is within her; she will not fall” in Psalm 46:5?

The statement “God is within her; she will not fall” in Psalm 46:5 declares that God’s people are completely secure, not because of their own strength, but because the sovereign Lord Himself dwells in their midst. In the immediate context of the psalm, “her” refers to Jerusalem, the city of God and the holy dwelling place of the Most High (Psalm 46:4).

In the ancient Near East, a city’s survival against invading empires depended on massive walls and a reliable water supply, yet Jerusalem had no great river and repeatedly faced overwhelming military threats. Writing against that backdrop, the psalmist uses the same Hebrew word for “fall” (also rendered “be shaken”) that describes mountains slipping into the sea (Psalm 46:2) and earthly kingdoms tottering (Psalm 46:6), drawing a sharp contrast between an unstable world and the unmovable security of Zion.

Theologically, this verse brings together God’s **sovereignty** over creation and nations with His covenantal **immanence**, His personal, active presence among His people as the Lord of Hosts who fights for them (Psalm 46:7). While that promise first comforted Old Testament Israel, the New Testament reveals its fuller reality in Jesus Christ, who is “God with us” (Matthew 1:23) and who now indwells His church by the Holy Spirit as His living temple (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:19–22). Because believers are united to Christ, this truth guarantees the **perseverance of the saints**: though trials may shake us, God’s redeemed people cannot ultimately be overthrown, and this promise will reach its final fulfillment when God dwells directly with His people forever in the New Jerusalem (Revelation 21:3).

When your own circumstances feel as though the earth is giving way, you can steady your heart by reading Psalm 46 aloud in prayer and leaning into the fellowship of a local church, reminding yourself that Christ’s presence within His people is far stronger than any storm.
What does the Bible say about worship?

In the Bible, worship is the reverent, wholehearted response of God's people in which they ascribe supreme worth to the Creator and Redeemer alone. Far more than a weekly musical routine, biblical worship encompasses humble adoration in gathered assembly and faithful obedience in every area of daily life.

In the Old Testament, the primary Hebrew word for worship (*shachah*) means to bow down low before a king, reflecting an Ancient Near Eastern posture of total allegiance to the sovereign Lord who rescued Israel from Egypt (Exodus 20:2–5; Psalm 95:6). In the New Testament, the Greek terms *proskyneo* (to kneel in homage) and *latreuo* (to render sacred, priestly service) carry this meaning forward, joining inward awe with active devotion (Matthew 4:10; Romans 12:1). Together, these biblical portraits anchor the historic Christian understanding of **doxology** (glorifying God) within the **Trinity**: believers worship the Father, through the **atoning** and **mediatorial** work of Jesus Christ, by the enabling of the Holy Spirit (Ephesians 2:18; 1 Timothy 2:5).

Scripture highlights three essential dimensions of true worship:

- **Exclusivity and Reverence:** God alone is holy and worthy of devotion, so Scripture strictly forbids idolatry and calls us to approach Him with reverence and awe (Exodus 20:3–5; Hebrews 12:28–29).
- **In Spirit and in Truth:** Jesus explained that worship is no longer bound to a single earthly sanctuary in Jerusalem or Samaria, because the Father seeks worshipers who honor Him "in spirit and in truth," transformed by His Spirit and grounded in the truth of His Word (John 4:21–24).
- **Whole-Life Sacrifice:** In light of God's saving mercy, believers are urged to offer their bodies as living sacrifices, turning ordinary work, speech, and generosity into a pleasing **sacrifice of praise** (Romans 12:1; 1 Corinthians 10:31; Hebrews 13:15–16).

While faithful Christians express this devotion through varied musical styles or liturgical traditions as matters of Christian liberty, the heart of worship remains delighting in God for who He is and what He has done (Romans 14:5–6; Colossians 3:16). This week, choose one ordinary daily task, such as beginning your workday or preparing a meal, and pause beforehand to thank God directly for Christ's mercy, dedicating that effort to His honor.
What is more important, the death of Christ or His resurrection?

Neither the death of Christ nor His resurrection is more important than the other, because Scripture presents them as two inseparable parts of one saving work. Without the cross, there is no payment for sin, and without the empty tomb, there is no proof that the payment was accepted or that death itself has been defeated.

The Apostle Paul binds them together in Romans 4:25, writing that Jesus "was delivered over to death for our trespasses and was raised to life for our justification." In His death, Christ accomplished penal substitutionary atonement and propitiation. Just as the Old Testament sacrificial system pointed forward to a spotless substitute bearing guilt, Jesus stood in the place of sinners and satisfied God's righteous wrath against sin (Isaiah 53:5–6; 2 Corinthians 5:21). 

In His bodily resurrection, the Father publicly vindicated His Son. Within the first-century Jewish world, resurrection was expected only at the final day of history, so Jesus rising from the grave on the third day declared that His sacrifice was fully sufficient and that God's new creation had already begun. As Paul reminds the church in 1 Corinthians 15:17, "if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile; you are still in your sins."

Together, Christ's sinless life, sacrificial death, burial, and bodily resurrection form the single foundation of the Gospel (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). For your daily walk, this means you can quiet a guilty conscience by looking to the cross where your debt was paid in full, and you can face sorrow or the fear of death with steady hope because your risen Savior lives forever. Because salvation is received by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ, who died and rose again, for forgiveness and new life.

As you reflect on both the cross and the empty tomb, which part of Christ's saving work speaks most deeply to your heart right now?
What is the emerging / emergent church movement?

The emerging church movement (often linked with the "emergent" conversation) was a movement that arose in the late 1990s and early 2000s seeking to adapt Christianity to postmodern culture by rethinking traditional church structures, worship styles, and theological certainty. While some participants simply wanted fresh, authentic ways to reach a changing world, the more prominent "emergent" wing questioned core biblical doctrines, including the authority of Scripture, objective truth, and historic teachings on salvation.

In its early years, the movement reacted against both rigid, detached church traditions and consumer-driven megachurches. Many emerging churches emphasized intimate community, artistic and ancient liturgical practices, conversational preaching, and active care for the poor. Over time, however, the movement fractured between those who held to historic Christian doctrine while updating their methods, and leaders such as Brian McLaren and Rob Bell who deconstructed foundational beliefs about hell, the exclusivity of Christ, and the reliability of the Bible.

From a biblical perspective, there is an important distinction between adapting our cultural methods and altering God's message. Paul became all things to all people so that by all possible means he might save some, yet he never compromised the Gospel itself (1 Corinthians 9:19-23). The Bible presents itself not as shifting human perspectives, but as the breathed-out, infallible Word of God, and Jesus affirmed that God's Word is truth (2 Timothy 3:16; John 17:17). Likewise, the heart of Christianity rests on objective historical realities: Christ's penal substitutionary atonement on the cross, His bodily resurrection, and justification by grace through faith alone (1 Corinthians 15:1-4; Romans 3:23-26; Ephesians 2:8-9). When any movement treats these settled truths as open-ended questions rather than the faith once for all entrusted to the saints, it steps outside biblical Christianity (Jude 1:3).

As you evaluate modern church trends or spiritual conversations today, make it a habit to test every teaching against the plain meaning of Scripture and stay rooted in a local church that preaches the historic Gospel clearly (1 Thessalonians 5:21; Acts 17:11).
What does the Bible say about underage drinking?

The Bible does not specify a legal drinking age, because ancient societies did not regulate alcohol through modern age statutes. However, Scripture speaks clearly to the issue through direct commands to obey governing authorities, honor parents, and walk in wisdom and self-control.

In the ancient Near Eastern and Greco-Roman worlds, wine was an everyday household beverage, often diluted with water, rather than a restricted substance tied to a particular birthday. Within that setting, Scripture presents wine as a gift from God when received with gratitude (Psalm 104:15), while consistently condemning drunkenness as a sin that leads to foolishness and spiritual ruin (Proverbs 20:1; Ephesians 5:18).

While moderate drinking for adults falls under the biblical category of Christian liberty (Romans 14:21; 1 Corinthians 10:31), underage drinking crosses clear moral boundaries established in Scripture:

* **Submission to governing authorities:** God commands believers to submit to civil laws, since governments are established by Him to maintain order and protect human life (Romans 13:1–2; 1 Peter 2:13–14). When a country or state sets a legal drinking age, breaking that law is disobedience to God unless a law forces a believer to violate Scripture.
* **Honoring parents:** Young people living under their parents' care are called to obey and honor their father and mother (Ephesians 6:1–2; Colossians 3:20). Hiding alcohol or sneaking past household rules breaks the trust God calls families to uphold.
* **Pursuing wisdom and self-control:** Scripture repeatedly urges young people to be sober-minded and self-controlled rather than following the crowd into reckless behavior (Titus 2:6; 1 Peter 5:8). In the process of sanctification, the Holy Spirit produces self-control so that believers are mastered by Christ rather than by peer pressure or bodily appetites (Galatians 5:22–23).

If you are navigating this question for yourself or guiding a young person, take a practical step this week by having an honest conversation with your parents, a trusted pastor, or a mature Christian mentor about how to honor God's Word and choose friendships that encourage wisdom rather than temptation.
Will there be a great apostasy / falling away during the end times?

Yes, Scripture teaches that a notable falling away, or rebellion, will occur before the return of Christ (2 Thessalonians 2:3; 1 Timothy 4:1; Matthew 24:10–12). At the same time, faithful Christians hold different views on the exact timing and nature of this event within end-times theology.

In 2 Thessalonians 2:3, the Apostle Paul wrote to a young church in the Greco-Roman city of Thessalonica whose believers were unsettled by rumors that the Day of the Lord had already arrived. To steady them, Paul used the Greek word *apostasia*, meaning a deliberate defection or rebellion, to show that a distinct turning away from the truth must take place first. This **apostasy** does not mean that genuinely born-again Christians can lose their salvation, for Scripture firmly teaches the **perseverance of the saints**, assuring us that God keeps His true people by His power (John 10:28–29; 1 Peter 1:5). Rather, those who fall away reveal that their profession of faith was only outward and that they were never truly united to Christ (1 John 2:19).

While the reality of apostasy is clear, detailed end-times timelines (eschatology) are a non-essential matter where faithful Christians disagree, largely because believers interpret prophetic and apocalyptic language with different emphases. Many Christians (such as premillennialists and many amillennialists) view this falling away as a massive, concentrated departure from the faith near the very end of history, just prior to Christ's return. Other faithful believers (such as partial preterists and some postmillennialists) understand these warnings (Matthew 24:10–12; 2 Thessalonians 2:3) as largely fulfilled during the intense trials and defections leading up to the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70, or as a recurring pattern of false teaching throughout the church age. Because all orthodox Christians stand united on the core truth that Jesus Christ will personally and bodily return to judge the living and the dead (Acts 1:11), we exercise Christian liberty and charity on the finer details of the prophetic calendar, refusing to divide over disputable matters (Romans 14:1–5).

Most importantly, Paul did not reveal these warnings to spark fear or speculation, but to anchor believers in the grace of the Gospel (2 Thessalonians 2:13–15). To guard your heart against drifting, make it a concrete habit this week to read slowly through 2 Thessalonians or 1 John while praying directly to God for discernment, and stay closely connected to a local, Bible-teaching church where fellow believers can encourage you to hold fast to Christ (Hebrews 10:23–25) until He comes again.
Should all pronouns referring to God be capitalized?

No, Scripture does not require you to capitalize pronouns that refer to God, so doing so is a matter of personal preference rather than a biblical command. Because the Bible does not prescribe modern English punctuation or spelling conventions, this is a non-essential issue on which faithful Christians thoughtfully disagree.

Historically, the original biblical languages did not use capitalization the way modern English does. Ancient Hebrew had no distinction between uppercase and lowercase letters, and the earliest New Testament manuscripts were written entirely in Greek capital letters (known as uncials). As a result, the biblical authors did not use capitalization to set divine pronouns apart from ordinary ones.

Today, Christians generally take one of two approaches. Many believers choose to capitalize pronouns such as "He," "Him," and "His" when referring to God as an outward expression of reverence for His holiness (Psalm 99:9), and because it can also help clarify who is being spoken of in a sentence. Other believers keep divine pronouns lowercase, following standard English grammar and the pattern of many classic and modern English Bible translations, recognizing that genuine honor for God comes from the posture of the heart rather than typography (1 Samuel 16:7).

In matters like this, Scripture calls us to practice Christian liberty with charity, neither looking down on those who write differently nor treating a stylistic choice as a test of faithfulness (Romans 14:5–6). Whether you decide to capitalize pronouns for God in your own writing or follow standard grammar, let your focus be on cultivating deep reverence for His name in your heart and doing all things, even in the smallest details of your words, to the glory of God (1 Corinthians 10:31).
What is Kabbalah?

Kabbalah (from a Hebrew word meaning "receiving" or "tradition") is a form of Jewish mysticism that seeks hidden spiritual truths about God and the universe through an esoteric interpretation of the Hebrew Scriptures. Developing prominently among Jewish thinkers in twelfth and thirteenth century Europe through texts such as the *Zohar*, it teaches that God interacts with the world through ten divine emanations (called the *Sefirot*) and assigns symbolic or numerical meanings to Hebrew letters to uncover secret knowledge.

From a biblical perspective grounded in the authority of Scripture, Kabbalah departs significantly from orthodox Christian teaching. While it reflects a human longing to know God, its reliance on secret oral traditions and divine emanations blurs the Creator-creature distinction and treats Scripture as a puzzle for mystics rather than God's clear message to His people. The Bible teaches that God has made His will known through clear special revelation in His written Word, which is sufficient to equip believers for every good work (Deuteronomy 29:29; 2 Timothy 3:16–17). Furthermore, true knowledge of God is not reached by decoding hidden systems, because all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are found in Jesus Christ, in whom the fullness of deity dwells bodily (Colossians 2:3; Colossians 2:8–9; Hebrews 1:1–3).

When you encounter mystical teachings like Kabbalah, test every spiritual claim against the plain meaning of Scripture, trusting God's revealed Word and the person of Christ rather than seeking secret enlightenment elsewhere (Acts 17:11; 1 John 4:1).
Should a Christian be a prepper or in any way involved with doomsday prepping?

Scripture neither commands nor forbids emergency preparedness, so whether a Christian keeps extra supplies is a matter of practical wisdom and Christian liberty rather than a fixed moral rule. What God clearly addresses is the heart behind our preparations, distinguishing faithful stewardship from anxious self-reliance.

Because the Bible gives broad principles of both foresight and radical trust without prescribing a specific pantry size or survival plan, faithful Christians hold different convictions on this issue. On one side, many believers practice modest preparedness as an act of wise stewardship, pointing to biblical examples like Joseph storing grain ahead of a seven-year famine (Genesis 41:46–49) and the proverb commending the prudent person who sees danger ahead and takes cover (Proverbs 22:3). From this perspective, setting aside basic food, water, or medical supplies helps fulfill the responsibility to provide for one's household (1 Timothy 5:8) and equips a believer to care for vulnerable neighbors during storms or supply disruptions. On the other side, many faithful Christians steer clear of "doomsday prepping" out of concern that extreme stockpiling can quietly shift our confidence away from God and toward our own bunkers. They point to Jesus's parable of the rich fool who built bigger barns to secure his future (Luke 12:16–21) and His call not to worry about tomorrow (Matthew 6:25–34), preferring to live simply and invest extra resources directly into immediate ministry and mercy.

In non-essential matters where Scripture does not bind the conscience, believers are called to exercise Christian liberty in love, refusing to judge one another while seeking to honor the Lord in their own convictions (Romans 14:5–8). When Jesus spoke in the Sermon on the Mount to first-century Jewish listeners, many of whom lived with daily economic fragility, He anchored their peace in God's *providence*, meaning God's sovereign, loving care and governance over every detail of His creation (Matthew 6:26–30). In the same way, biblical *eschatology*, the teaching on the end times and Christ's bodily return, calls believers not to panic or retreat from the world, but to live with sober-minded hope and active love until Jesus comes again (1 Thessalonians 5:1–11).

Practically, any emergency readiness you pursue should be shaped by generosity rather than fear, treating extra supplies as a resource to bless your community in a crisis rather than a fortress to shut others out. As a helpful next step, spend time this week praying directly to God while reading Matthew 6:25–34, asking Him to expose any hidden anxiety or misplaced trust in your heart, and talk with a pastor or mature believer in your local church about what balanced, neighbor-loving preparedness looks like for your household.
What is the church?

The church is not a building or a weekly event, but the living community of people whom God has rescued from sin through faith in Jesus Christ and united to Him and to one another. Scripture presents the church both as the universal fellowship of all true believers across time and place, and as local congregations that gather regularly for worship, teaching, and mutual care.

In the New Testament, the Greek word translated as "church" is *ekklesia*, which in the Greco-Roman world referred to an assembly of citizens called out for a specific purpose, and in the Greek Old Testament described Israel gathered solemnly before God. When Jesus promised to build His church (Matthew 16:18), He declared that He is calling out a redeemed people for Himself, whom historic Christian theology describes as both the *invisible church* (all genuine believers known infallibly to God) and the *visible church* (those who profess faith and gather in local congregations).

The Bible uses rich imagery to reveal the church's identity and purpose. It is the body of Christ, with Jesus Himself as the supreme Head (Ephesians 1:22–23; Colossians 1:18), and God's own household, built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets with Christ Jesus as the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:19–22). As a chosen race and royal priesthood, the church exists to proclaim the excellencies of Him who called believers out of darkness into His marvelous light (1 Peter 2:9). Within the local congregation, Christians grow in *sanctification* through the ordinary *means of grace* (the faithful preaching of Scripture, prayer, baptism, and the Lord's Supper) while spurring one another on toward love and good deeds (Acts 2:42; Hebrews 10:24–25).

Because Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25), the Christian life is never meant to be lived in isolation. A vital step for every believer is to commit to a local, Bible-teaching church where you can sit consistently under God's Word, pray with others, and serve alongside fellow Christians.
Does a cashless society have anything to do with the end times?

Scripture does not explicitly mention a "cashless society," though many believers wonder about it because of Revelation 13:16–17, which describes a time when no one can buy or sell without the mark of the beast. How specific end-times prophecies will unfold belongs to the study of eschatology, a non-essential area of Christian theology where faithful believers hold different interpretations because apocalyptic imagery allows for varied interpretive emphasis.

In its first-century Greco-Roman context, the Apostle John wrote the book of Revelation as apocalyptic literature to strengthen churches facing economic and social pressure to participate in emperor worship and pagan trade guilds. While the text portrays real spiritual conflict and real opposition to God's people, Christians understand the timing and mechanics of that economic restriction in different ways.

Many Christians holding a futurist view believe that the rise of digital currencies and centralized payment systems could lay the technological groundwork for a literal, global economic control just before Christ returns. Other faithful believers, including many who hold amillennial or preterist views, understand the ban on buying and selling either as an event tied to first-century Roman persecution or as a recurring symbol throughout church history whenever earthly powers penalize Christians who refuse to compromise their allegiance to Christ.

While Christians may respectfully disagree on these prophetic details, we stand united on the core truth that Jesus Christ will return personally and bodily to judge the living and the dead and renew all things (Acts 1:11; Revelation 21:1–5). Because Scripture does not treat cash or digital transactions as sinful in themselves, believers have Christian liberty to use everyday financial tools with a clear conscience, without judging others or living in fear (Romans 14:5–6). As a practical step, whenever headlines about economic shifts tempt you toward anxiety, read Revelation 4–5 and pray with confidence that the risen Lamb already holds all of history in His hands.
I am a former Catholic. Should I continue to go to Catholic Church so I can reach people for Christ?

It is wonderful that you have a genuine burden to reach Catholic friends and family with the good news of Jesus Christ. Still, as a general rule, it is not wise to continue attending a Catholic church on Sundays as your strategy for evangelism.

First, consider your own spiritual nourishment and biblical calling. God calls every believer to be planted in a local church where the whole counsel of Scripture is faithfully preached, the ordinances are rightly practiced, and godly elders shepherd your soul (Hebrews 10:24–25; Ephesians 4:11–14). To grow in grace, you need steady exposure to the pure Word of God rather than a weekly setting where the authority of Scripture is placed alongside church tradition.

Second, regular attendance can unintentionally blur the very Gospel you want to share. In Galatians 2:16, addressing first-century believers tempted to rely on religious observance for standing with God, Paul insists that a person is justified (declared righteous in God's courtroom) not by works, but through faith in Jesus Christ alone. This is the heart of the biblical doctrine of justification by faith alone, grounded in Christ's penal substitution and finished atonement on the cross (Romans 3:24–26; Ephesians 2:8–9). Because official Roman Catholic teaching views salvation as a process aided by sacraments and merits, and treats the Mass as an ongoing propitiatory sacrifice rather than a remembrance of Christ's sacrifice made "once for all" (Hebrews 10:10–14), participating in Catholic worship regularly sends a confusing signal about where true salvation is found. Attending an occasional family wedding or funeral out of love is quite different from making a Catholic parish your regular Sunday habit (and even at special events, you should refrain from taking the Eucharist out of fidelity to Christ's finished work).

You do not need to sit in the pew at Mass to love and reach Catholic neighbors or loved ones. In fact, faithful witness usually flourishes much better in personal relationships where you can speak openly without liturgical barriers.

Here is a concrete next step you can take this week: commit yourself fully to a local, Bible-teaching church for your own Sunday worship, and then invite a Catholic friend or relative over for a meal or coffee to build a bridge for honest spiritual conversation. When the door opens, you might even offer to read the Gospel of John or the book of Romans together, letting them see in God's own Word the peace that comes through trusting Christ alone (Romans 5:1).

Are there particular friends or family members from your former parish whom you are praying to reach right now?
What does the Bible say about world missions?

From Genesis to Revelation, the Bible teaches that world missions is God's purposeful plan to redeem a people for Himself from every nation through the Gospel of Jesus Christ, and He commands His Church to carry that message to the ends of the earth. Far from being a New Testament afterthought, global mission sits at the very heart of Scripture's unified story of redemption.

In the ancient Near Eastern world, where peoples commonly assumed each nation was ruled by its own local deity, the one true Creator revealed His global purpose by promising Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed through his offspring (Genesis 12:1–3). Israel was set apart as a kingdom of priests to display God's holiness to the surrounding nations (Exodus 19:5–6; Psalm 67:1–3), and the prophets foretold a coming Servant who would become a light for the Gentiles so that God's salvation would reach the ends of the earth (Isaiah 49:6).

That promise finds its fulfillment in Jesus Christ, whose substitutionary death on the cross and bodily resurrection secured atonement for sinners across every culture who trust in Him. Before ascending to heaven, the risen Lord gave the Great Commission, commanding His followers to make disciples of all nations, using the Greek term *ethne* (nations or peoples) to point beyond Israel's borders to every ethnic and cultural group in the Greco-Roman world and beyond (Matthew 28:18–20; Acts 1:8). Because salvation is by grace alone through justification by faith alone in Christ alone, the Church must proclaim Him openly, for there is no other name under heaven by which people can be saved (Acts 4:12; Romans 10:14–15). In historic Christian theology, this missionary task rests on God's sovereign grace and moves toward the promised consummation of history, when a vast multitude from every nation, tribe, people, and tongue will stand before the throne worshipping the Lamb (Revelation 7:9–10).

For believers today, participating in world missions takes concrete shape as you pray faithfully for unreached peoples, give generously through your local church to support vetted missionaries, and speak the Gospel with humility and clarity to neighbors and coworkers who do not yet know Christ.
How should we live our lives in light of our identity in Christ?

Living in light of our identity in Christ means walking in joyful obedience, holiness, and love from a place of secure acceptance rather than trying to earn God's favor. Because believers have been made a new creation, every ordinary moment of life becomes an opportunity to reflect the character of our Savior (2 Corinthians 5:17).

In the New Testament, the Apostle Paul repeatedly uses the phrase "in Christ" when writing to first-century churches surrounded by Greco-Roman idolatry, grounding who believers are before commanding how they should live. This biblical pattern establishes the vital truth of **union with Christ**: through **justification** by faith alone, we are declared righteous and united to Jesus, which becomes the root of our **progressive sanctification** as the Holy Spirit transforms us over time (Romans 6:11; Ephesians 2:8–10). You do not obey in order to become God's child; you obey because, by grace, you already are His child.

Practically, this identity shapes how we fight sin, relate to others, and approach our daily responsibilities. First, it calls us to put off our old sinful habits and put on Christlike character, knowing sin is no longer our master (Romans 6:14; Ephesians 4:22–24). When impatience or bitterness rises in your home or workplace, pause and remind yourself that you belong to Jesus, then choose to speak truthfully and forgive as you have been forgiven (Ephesians 4:32). Second, it leads us to abide closely with God through His appointed means of grace: reading His Word, praying, and gathering faithfully with a local church to encourage and sharpen one another (Colossians 3:16; Hebrews 10:24–25). Third, it turns even mundane tasks into worship, as we seek to honor the Lord in our families, callings, and service to our neighbors (Colossians 3:17; 1 Peter 2:9).

For a concrete step this week, set aside ten minutes each morning to read slowly through Ephesians 1:3–14 or Colossians 3:1–17, noting every truth about who you are in Jesus. Bring those truths directly to God in prayer, thanking Him for His unchanging grace and asking the Holy Spirit to align one specific attitude or relationship with your new life today.
How do I know the Bible is not just mythology?

It is completely understandable to wonder about this. Many people today look at the miracles in Scripture and think they sound similar to ancient Greek or Norse myths, or assume the Bible is simply a collection of moral fables passed down over centuries.

Christians believe, however, that the Bible is fundamentally different from mythology because it is grounded in verifiable history and written by God's *inspiration* (God guiding human authors to record His exact words without error, a truth known as *inerrancy*). The Bible teaches that "All Scripture is God-breathed" (2 Timothy 3:16). While Scripture includes different literary genres such as Hebrew poetry in the Psalms and symbolic prophecy in Revelation, its historical books present real events, real people, and real places.

In the Greco-Roman and Second Temple Jewish world of the New Testament, writers used clear markers to distinguish real history from fables. For example, Luke begins his Gospel by stating that he carefully investigated eyewitness accounts to write an orderly history, and he anchors Jesus' ministry to specific Roman emperors, governors, and Jewish high priests (Luke 1:1–4; Luke 3:1–2). Likewise, the Apostle Peter explicitly rejects the idea that the Christian message is mythical, writing that the apostles "did not follow cleverly devised fables" when declaring Christ's power, because they were "eyewitnesses of His majesty" (2 Peter 1:16). Unlike myths, which take place in a timeless "once upon a time," biblical accounts invite scrutiny in a specific time and geography, much of which has been confirmed by archaeology and outside ancient historians.

At the center of this historical record stands the *incarnation*, death, and bodily *resurrection* of Jesus Christ. The Apostle Paul summarizes the Gospel by noting that Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose on the third day, appearing to over five hundred people at once, most of whom were still alive when Paul wrote and could be questioned directly (1 Corinthians 15:3–6). Because Scripture records real history rather than myth, its central promise is also real: all people have sinned and fallen short of God's holiness, yet God offers forgiveness and eternal life to anyone who turns from sin and trusts in Jesus Christ alone.

As a practical next step, consider reading through the Gospel of Luke over the next week or two, paying close attention to the historical details and eyewitness claims, and ask God directly to show you what is true. What part of the Bible has felt hardest for you to accept as real history?
What does it mean that the Bible is infallible? What is biblical infallibility?

Biblical infallibility means that the Bible is completely trustworthy, incapable of failing, and will never deceive or mislead us in anything it teaches. Closely connected to inerrancy (which teaches that the original manuscripts are free from error in everything they affirm), infallibility emphasizes that Scripture cannot be broken and will never fail to accomplish God's purposes (John 10:35; Isaiah 55:11).

This doctrine rests directly on the character of God and the origin of Scripture. Writing in the first-century Greco-Roman and Jewish world, the Apostle Paul used the Greek word *theopneustos*, meaning "God-breathed," to explain that Scripture originates from God Himself rather than mere human reflection (2 Timothy 3:16). Just as the Old Testament prophets spoke as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit, every part of Scripture comes from God speaking through human authors (2 Peter 1:20–21). Because God cannot lie and His character is wholly faithful, His written Word is completely reliable (Titus 1:2; Psalm 19:7). Historic Christianity summarizes these biblical teachings with terms like verbal plenary inspiration (meaning every word of the whole Bible is inspired by God), infallibility, and inerrancy.

For the Christian, infallibility is not a cold, abstract idea, but a warm and steady anchor for daily life. Because the Word of our God stands forever, you can trust every promise of grace, every moral command, and every hope of eternal life without fear that Scripture will ever prove false (Isaiah 40:8; Psalm 119:160). In practice, believing in an infallible Bible means opening it daily with a humble heart, allowing Scripture to examine and correct your thinking rather than sitting in judgment over what God has spoken.
What does the Bible mean when it says something is unclean?

In the Bible, "unclean" primarily refers to a state of ritual or moral impurity that separates a person or object from God's holy presence and disqualifies them from sacred worship. Throughout Scripture, the term (usually translating the Hebrew word *tame* in the Old Testament and the Greek *akathartos* in the New Testament) encompasses two distinct categories: ceremonial uncleanness and moral defilement.

In the Ancient Near Eastern context of ancient Israel, ceremonial uncleanness was tied to physical conditions associated with decay, bodily discharges, certain animals, or death (Leviticus 11:44–45; Leviticus 15:31). Being ceremonially unclean was not necessarily sinful in itself. Normal, necessary human duties like burying a deceased loved one, experiencing a skin condition, or giving birth rendered an Israelite temporarily unclean, requiring ritual washing and a set waiting period before returning to the tabernacle or temple. These visible boundaries functioned as a daily object lesson, teaching God's covenant people that His absolute holiness cannot dwell casually alongside the mortality and brokenness of a fallen world.

Moral uncleanness, by contrast, is rooted directly in sin, idolatry, and rebellion against God's commands (Isaiah 64:6; Ezekiel 36:25). By the Second Temple period, many Jewish religious leaders treated external rituals and handwashings as the primary measure of righteousness, yet Jesus confronted that misunderstanding by teaching that true defilement comes not from what enters the mouth, but from the sinful thoughts, greed, and pride of the human heart (Mark 7:15–23).

Across the sweep of Scripture, these Old Testament purity laws pointed forward to Jesus Christ, whose substitutionary atonement accomplishes true and lasting cleansing. Because Christ fulfilled the ceremonial law, God declared all foods clean under the New Covenant (Mark 7:19; Acts 10:14–15). While the blood of bulls and goats could only purify the flesh outwardly, the blood of Christ cleanses the conscience from dead works so that sinners can be justified and serve the living God (Hebrews 9:13–14; 1 John 1:7). For Christians today, pursuing holiness and sanctification means turning away from inward sins of the heart, speech, and conduct rather than observing Old Testament dietary or ritual rules, resting daily in the complete cleansing Christ has already secured (2 Corinthians 7:1).
What is the meaning of life?

The ultimate meaning of life is to know, glorify, and enjoy God forever, because He created us in His own image to live in fellowship with Him (Genesis 1:27; Colossians 1:16; 1 Corinthians 10:31). While many people search for lasting purpose in career success, relationships, or personal happiness, Scripture teaches that true fullness of joy is found only in God's presence (Psalm 16:11).

In the Ancient Near Eastern wisdom tradition reflected in Ecclesiastes, King Solomon tested wealth, pleasure, and achievement, only to conclude that life apart from God is a fleeting vapor and that our whole duty is to revere God and obey Him (Ecclesiastes 1:2; Ecclesiastes 12:13). Centuries later, writing to believers in the status-driven Greco-Roman city of Corinth, the Apostle Paul urged them to do everything for God's "glory" (1 Corinthians 10:31), using the Greek word *doxa* to point to the supreme honor and splendor of God's character. Yet because God is completely holy and every human being has sinned, our rebellion separates us from the very Creator we were made to know (Isaiah 59:2; Romans 3:23). We cannot earn our way back to Him through moral effort or good deeds.

Out of pure grace, God Himself restored the path to true life through His Son, Jesus Christ. Jesus, who is truly God and truly man, entered our world in the incarnation, lived the perfect, sinless life we failed to live, and willingly died on the cross in our place (John 1:14; 2 Corinthians 5:21). Through His penal substitution, Christ bore the righteous wrath we deserved for our sin, was buried, and rose bodily from the grave on the third day, conquering death and ascending as exalted Lord (1 Corinthians 15:3–4; Philippians 2:9–11). Because of His finished work, sinners receive justification by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by human works (Ephesians 2:8–9; Romans 5:1).

For those who belong to Christ, even ordinary daily tasks like loving your family, working faithfully, and serving your neighbors become meaningful worship offered to Him (Colossians 3:23–24). You can begin exploring this purpose today by reading a chapter of the Gospel of John and praying honestly to God for understanding. If you are searching for lasting meaning and peace with your Creator, turn from your sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, to receive forgiveness and eternal life.

As you think about what gives life meaning, what has led you to ask this question right now?
How can there be subordination in the Trinity?

Within the Trinity, there is never a subordination of essence, value, or deity, because the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God, co-equal and co-eternal in power and glory (Deuteronomy 6:4; Matthew 28:19; John 10:30). Instead, when Scripture speaks of the Son or the Spirit being sent by or submitting to the Father, it is describing a voluntary, relational ordering in their distinct roles to accomplish creation and redemption, which theologians call the economic Trinity (John 6:38; John 14:26).

To understand this clearly, historic Christianity distinguishes between who God is in His eternal being (the immanent Trinity) and how God acts in history (the economic Trinity). In His eternal essence, the Son possesses complete ontological equality with the Father, as John affirms that the Word was with God and was God (John 1:1; Colossians 2:9). Teaching that the Son is a lesser divine being is an ancient error called subordinationism, which falls outside orthodox Christianity. Rather, the submission we see in the Gospels flows from the Son's loving mission in the incarnation. Writing to believers in the status-conscious Greco-Roman city of Philippi, Paul highlights this humility: though Christ existed in the "form" (Greek *morphe*, pointing to true nature and essence) of God, He emptied Himself by taking the "form" of a servant (Greek *doulos*, meaning a bondservant or slave) and became obedient to death on a cross (Philippians 2:6–8). Because Jesus is one Person with both a full divine nature and a full human nature (the hypostatic union), He genuinely submitted His human will to the Father in order to win our salvation (Matthew 26:39; 1 Corinthians 15:28).

Throughout Scripture, the Father, Son, and Spirit work in perfect harmony: the Father plans and sends, the Son accomplishes redemption, and the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son to apply it to believers (John 15:26; Galatians 4:4–6). While faithful Christians sometimes discuss whether this functional ordering reflects eternal relational patterns within the Godhead or pertains strictly to the work of redemption, all orthodox believers unite in affirming that none of the divine Persons is ever inferior in majesty or divine nature. As Paul reminds the church in Philippians 2:3–5, this truth offers real encouragement for daily life: when you choose to serve others humbly, yield gracefully, and put another person's needs ahead of your own, you are never diminishing your dignity, because you are walking in the very footsteps of the co-equal Son of God.
Why are there so many religions? Do all religions lead to God?

When you look at the vast number of religions around the world, it is completely understandable to feel confused, or to wonder why one faith would claim to be uniquely true. Many thoughtful people view religions as different roads climbing the same mountain, and the idea that only one path leads to God can easily feel narrow or unloving.

To understand why there are so many religions, the Bible points to both how God created us and what happened to our world. Christians believe that God made every human being with an innate awareness of His existence, displaying His eternal power and divine nature through the created world, a truth theologians call general revelation (Romans 1:19–20). Because of humanity's fall into sin, however, our hearts and minds became darkened, leading people to suppress the truth about the one true Creator and replace Him with countless human-made gods and religious systems (Romans 1:21–23). In the first-century Greco-Roman world, the Apostle Paul stepped into Athens, a city overflowing with idols and even an altar dedicated to an unknown god, and explained that God placed humanity on the earth to seek Him, though sin leaves people groping in the dark (Acts 17:22–28).

Because different religions make deeply contradictory claims about who God is and what happens after death, they cannot all lead to the same destination. More importantly, the Bible teaches that all religions do not lead to God because human effort cannot fix our separation from a holy and just Creator (Isaiah 59:2; Romans 3:23). Most world religions operate like ladders we must climb through good deeds, rituals, or spiritual discipline to reach the divine. Christianity is fundamentally different because it announces that God came down to us.

In His great love, God sent His eternal Son, Jesus Christ, who is truly God and truly man, to live the perfectly righteous life we could never live. On the cross, Jesus willingly died in the place of sinners, bearing the just wrath of God against our sin, a saving work known as penal substitution, before He was buried and rose bodily from the grave on the third day as the victorious Lord (1 Corinthians 15:3–4; 2 Corinthians 5:21). Jesus Himself declared, "I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me" (John 14:6). Because He alone conquered sin and death as the one Mediator between God and humanity (1 Timothy 2:5; Acts 4:12), justification (being declared righteous before God) comes by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by our works (Ephesians 2:8–9).

A helpful next step if you are exploring these questions is to read through the Gospel of John, paying close attention to how Jesus spoke with searching people and what He accomplished. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

As you think about Jesus' claim to be the only way to God, what questions or thoughts come to mind for you?
Do Mormons believe in the Trinity?

No, members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (commonly called Mormons) do not believe in the biblical doctrine of the Trinity. Instead, they teach a view called the "Godhead," holding that Heavenly Father, Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit are three separate, distinct divine beings who are united in purpose and will, rather than one God sharing a single divine essence.

Historic Christianity confesses the Trinity: there is one true God who eternally exists in three distinct persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, who share the exact same divine nature. Scripture anchors this in the strict monotheism of the Old Testament, where God declares that there is no other God besides Him, neither formed before Him nor coming after Him (Deuteronomy 6:4; Isaiah 43:10; Isaiah 44:6). In the New Testament, the apostles upheld this single divine nature while recognizing the full deity of the Father, the Son who is the Word made flesh (John 1:1; John 1:14), and the Holy Spirit (Acts 5:3–4), uniting all three in the baptismal command and apostolic blessing (Matthew 28:19; 2 Corinthians 13:14). Early Christians summarized this biblical witness using the Greek term *homoousios* (meaning "of the same substance or essence") to guard the truth that the Father, Son, and Spirit are one God, not three separate gods.

By contrast, Latter-day Saint theology teaches that God the Father has an exalted physical body of flesh and bone, that He progressed to godhood, and that Jesus and the Holy Spirit are separate beings, which amounts to a form of tritheism (three distinct gods). Because the identity of the one true God is an essential foundation of the Christian faith, this teaching places Mormonism outside historic, orthodox Christianity.

We should always treat our Latter-day Saint neighbors with genuine warmth, kindness, and respect, yet true love also requires clarity about who God is as He has revealed Himself in Scripture (1 Peter 3:15; Jude 1:3). If you ever talk about faith with Mormon friends or missionaries, a helpful practical step is to gently ask what they mean when they use familiar words like "God" or "Jesus," and then patiently share from the Bible how the one eternal, unchanging God has made Himself known.
Where is the moral law summarily comprehended?

The moral law is summarily comprehended in the Ten Commandments, which are recorded in Exodus 20:1–17 and repeated in Deuteronomy 5:6–21. Jesus Christ Himself further distilled these ten commands into two great principles: loving God with all our heart, soul, and mind, and loving our neighbor as ourselves (Matthew 22:37–40).

In the historical context of the ancient Near East, God delivered these commands at Mount Sinai using the pattern of a royal covenant between a great King and His redeemed people. Before issuing a single command, the Lord anchored Israel's obedience in His saving grace, reminding them that He had already rescued them from slavery in Egypt (Exodus 20:2). Within this structure, the first four commandments govern our duty to God, while the final six govern our duty to our fellow human beings.

Theologically, this moral law, often called the Decalogue, reflects the unchanging, holy character of God and serves as the permanent rule of righteousness for all humanity. Unlike the temporary ceremonial and civil regulations given specifically to national Israel, the moral law endures across every age. Because no fallen person can keep it perfectly, the law first acts as a mirror that exposes our sin and drives us to Christ, whose perfect obedience and sacrificial death secure our justification before God (Romans 3:20; Galatians 3:24). For those united to Christ through faith, the law is no longer a harsh judge condemning us, but a loving guide for our progressive sanctification as the Holy Spirit empowers us to walk in genuine love (Romans 8:3–4; Romans 13:8–10).

As a practical step this week, read slowly through the Ten Commandments in Exodus 20:1–17, asking God directly to reveal any hidden idols in your heart and to strengthen you to honor Him and serve your neighbors in your daily work and conversations.
What does it mean to be contrite? What is contrition?

To be contrite means to have a deeply humbled, broken, and sorrowful heart over your sin against God. Contrition is that genuine inward grief that turns a person away from pride and self-righteousness toward God's mercy.

In the Old Testament, the Hebrew words translated as "contrite" carry the vivid picture of something crushed or ground down, describing a spirit whose stubborn self-sufficiency has been shattered before a holy God (Psalm 51:17; Isaiah 66:2). Rather than a fleeting regret over getting caught, biblical contrition aligns with what the New Testament calls godly sorrow, which leads to true repentance (2 Corinthians 7:10).

Theologically, contrition is a vital fruit of regeneration and repentance, standing in sharp contrast to worldly remorse. Worldly sorrow merely laments the painful consequences of sin and leads to despair, whereas contrition recognizes the offense of sin against God's holiness and drives the sinner to trust in Christ's penal substitutionary death on the cross for justification and forgiveness (Romans 3:23–25; 1 John 1:9).

Far from turning away those who feel crushed by their guilt, God promises to draw near and revive the humble and contrite in spirit (Psalm 34:18; Isaiah 57:15). Practically, when you become aware of sin in your life, you can practice contrition by honestly confessing that specific sin to God in prayer without making excuses, resting in Christ's grace, and taking a deliberate step to turn away from it.
What does it mean that “at your right hand are pleasures forevermore” (Psalm 16:11)?

In Psalm 16:11, David declares that ultimate, unending joy is found only in God's immediate presence and under His gracious favor. Rather than pointing to fleeting earthly comforts, the promise of "pleasures forevermore" points to the eternal fullness of delight prepared for those who belong to the Lord (Psalm 16:11).

In the ancient world and throughout the Old Testament, a king's "right hand" symbolized the place of highest honor, sovereign power, and secure blessing (Psalm 110:1; Matthew 25:33). Crucially, the New Testament apostles explain that Psalm 16 reaches beyond David's own lifetime, for David died and saw decay, whereas Jesus Christ rose bodily from the grave to enter into eternal joy at the Father's side (Acts 2:25–32; Acts 13:35–37).

This passage connects directly to the historic Christian doctrines of Christ's resurrection, union with Christ, and final glorification. Because Jesus endured the cross "for the joy set before Him" and now sits at the right hand of the throne of God (Hebrews 1:3; Hebrews 12:2), everyone united to Him by grace through faith shares in an imperishable inheritance (1 Peter 1:3–4). Theologians often speak of the pinnacle of this promise as the beatific vision, the blessed reality that God's redeemed people will be completely satisfied when they behold Him face to face in the new creation (1 John 3:2; Revelation 22:3–5). Earthly joys are genuine gifts from our Creator, yet they are only small streams meant to lead our hearts back to the fountain Himself.

As you walk through ordinary routines or heavy seasons, make it a daily practice to thank God for His gifts while deliberately asking Him in prayer to anchor your deepest affections in the risen Christ, who alone is the path of life.
What is divine providence?

Divine providence is God's continual, sovereign, and wise care over all creation, by which He upholds every creature and directs all events toward His appointed ends. Unlike deism, which imagines a distant God who wound up the universe and stepped back, biblical providence teaches that the living God remains intimately involved in every detail of history, from the movement of galaxies to the falling of a single sparrow (Matthew 10:29–30).

Theologians traditionally describe divine providence through two main aspects: preservation and governance. Through preservation, God actively sustains the existence and properties of everything He has made. Scripture declares of Christ that He sustains all things by His powerful word (Hebrews 1:3) and that in Him all things hold together (Colossians 1:17). Through governance, God purposefully directs all things according to His eternal plan, working out everything according to the counsel of His will (Ephesians 1:11).

In the ancient Near Eastern and Greco-Roman worlds, people often viewed history as subject to capricious deities, blind chance, or impersonal fate. Against that backdrop, the biblical authors consistently reveal a personal, holy, and good Creator who reigns over kings, nature, and human choices alike. Historic Christian theology uses the term *concurrence* to summarize how God works through secondary causes (including free human actions and natural laws) without ever becoming the author of sin. We see this clearly in the life of Joseph, who reminded his brothers that what they intended for evil against him, God intended for good to save many lives (Genesis 50:20). Human agents remain morally responsible for their choices, yet God's sovereign wisdom overrules even human wickedness to accomplish redemption, most supremely at the cross of Jesus Christ (Acts 2:23).

Because providence is rooted in the character of a loving and faithful Father, this doctrine brings deep comfort to believers rather than cold fatalism. It assures Christians that God works all things together for the good of those who love Him and are called according to His purpose (Romans 8:28). Practically, when you face an unexpected hardship such as a sudden illness, financial strain, or a broken relationship, you do not have to despair as though your life were at the mercy of blind luck; instead, you can bring your grief honestly to God in prayer and keep walking in faithful obedience, trusting that He is actively using even dark chapters to shape you into the likeness of Christ.
In what ways is the Christian life like the Olympics?

The Bible frequently compares the Christian life to athletic games like the Olympics because both demand rigorous discipline, steadfast endurance, obedience to the rules, and focus on a prize. Unlike Olympians who compete to earn a medal, however, believers run in response to a victory that Jesus Christ has already secured for them.

Writing in a Greco-Roman world where the Olympic and nearby Isthmian Games were celebrated spectacles of intense ten-month training and strict competition, the Apostle Paul and the author of Hebrews used this familiar imagery to describe *progressive sanctification*, which is the lifelong process by which the Holy Spirit shapes believers into the likeness of Christ. Importantly, running this race does not earn *justification* (being declared righteous by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone). Rather, disciplined effort is the grateful fruit of a salvation already given, demonstrating the *perseverance* of those whom God keeps.

Scripture highlights four main ways the Christian life resembles the Olympics:

**1. Disciplined Training and Self-Control**
Olympians structure their diet, sleep, and daily habits so they can perform at their peak. In the same way, believers do not drift into godliness; they exercise spiritual self-control through regular prayer, Scripture intake, and turning away from sinful desires (1 Corinthians 9:24–27).

**2. Endurance and Shedding Hindrances**
The Christian life is a marathon rather than a brief sprint. Just as a runner refuses to carry heavy baggage onto the track, Christians are called to run with endurance by throwing off every unnecessary encumbrance and entangling sin, keeping their eyes fixed on Jesus, who is the author and perfecter of our faith (Hebrews 12:1–2).

**3. Competing According to the Rules**
An athlete who ignores the boundaries of the course is disqualified, regardless of how fast he runs. Faithful Christian living means submitting our conduct and beliefs to the authoritative standard of God's Word rather than inventing our own path (2 Timothy 2:5).

**4. An Imperishable Prize**
While Olympic gold eventually tarnishes and earthly applause fades, believers press forward toward an eternal reward. Unlike earthly games where only one runner takes the top prize, every faithful believer receives the imperishable crown of righteousness from the Lord who loves them (1 Corinthians 9:25; Philippians 3:13–14; 2 Timothy 4:7–8).

As a practical next step, take a few minutes today to identify one distracting habit or lingering sin that slows down your spiritual endurance, and replace it with a steady daily training rhythm of reading a short portion of Scripture and praying before your day gets busy. Sharing that goal with a trusted believer or pastor in your local church will give you the encouragement and accountability you need to keep running well.
What should be the Christian perspective on nudity in art?

Christians should recognize that while lust and sexual exploitation are clearly sinful, the question of non-erotic nudity in fine art is a non-essential matter of wisdom and conscience where faithful believers disagree. Scripture does not issue a blanket prohibition against artistic depictions of the human form, yet it gives clear principles regarding creation, modesty, and purity of heart that require careful discernment.

To think biblically about the human body, we must hold two truths together: the goodness of God's creation and the reality of the Fall. In the beginning, God created men and women in the *imago Dei* (the image of God), declared His creation very good, and placed Adam and Eve in the garden naked and unashamed (Genesis 1:27; Genesis 1:31; Genesis 2:25). When sin entered the world, it brought shame and disordered desires, and God Himself graciously provided coverings for them (Genesis 3:7; Genesis 3:21). Because of our fallen nature, Scripture speaks plainly against lustful looking, sexual immorality, and anything that arouses sinful passion (Matthew 5:28; 1 Thessalonians 4:3–5). Any image, whether labeled "art" or not, that is intended to provoke lust or exploit the human body crosses a settled moral boundary and must be rejected.

Where faithful Christians differ is over classical or non-erotic depictions of the human form, such as historical sculptures or paintings that portray biblical or anatomical scenes without erotic intent. Two main positions exist among Bible-believing Christians:

* **Appreciation within clear boundaries:** Many Christians distinguish between pornography (which seeks to excite lust) and fine art (which seeks to reflect beauty, historical truth, or the craftsmanship of God's creation). Viewing artistic skill as an expression of God's common grace, they believe believers can thoughtfully appreciate certain classical works while guarding their hearts and focusing on what is honorable and pure (Philippians 4:8).
* **Cautious abstinence:** Other faithful Christians choose to avoid artistic nudity altogether. Recognizing the deceitfulness of the human heart, the biblical call to modesty (1 Timothy 2:9), and the command to flee youthful passions (2 Timothy 2:22), they conclude that even well-intentioned nudity can easily become a stumbling block to holiness.

Because Scripture leaves room for differing judgments on non-erotic art, this falls under the principle of Christian liberty. Believers are called not to judge or look down on one another over matters of personal conscience, while taking care never to flaunt their freedom in a way that causes a brother or sister in Christ to stumble (Romans 14:1–4; Romans 14:13; 1 Corinthians 8:9). In all things, our goal is to glorify God in both body and mind (1 Corinthians 10:31).

As a practical step, whenever you encounter nudity in a museum, book, or piece of artwork, pause to examine both the purpose of the work and its effect on your own heart. If an image stirs lustful thoughts or troubles your conscience before God, turn away from it immediately, and consider discussing your boundaries in prayer with God or with a trusted, mature believer in your local church.
Should we allow false teachers into our home?

Christians should not welcome active false teachers into their homes in a way that supports their ministry, gives them a platform, or signals spiritual fellowship with them (2 John 1:10–11). However, this biblical boundary applies specifically to those actively spreading destructive error, not to ordinary unbelievers, neighbors, or friends with whom we may share hospitality and the Gospel.

To understand this command rightly, it helps to look at its original setting. When the Apostle John wrote 2 John 1:7–11, traveling preachers relied on the lodging and provisions of believers, and Christian homes frequently served as the gathering places for local churches. In that first-century Greco-Roman context, welcoming an itinerant teacher into your home and offering a formal greeting (from the Greek *chairein*, conveying a warm wish of success and welcome) functioned as an endorsement of their mission, which is why John warns that doing so makes a believer share in their evil deeds (2 John 1:11). Specifically, John was confronting teachers who denied the incarnation, refusing to confess that Jesus Christ had come in the flesh (2 John 1:7). That error strikes directly at biblical Christology and orthodoxy, turning a mere disagreement into soul-endangering heresy.

At the same time, Scripture calls us to hold truth and love together without confusing a false teacher with a seeking sinner. The Bible instructs believers to turn away from persistent, divisive purveyors of false doctrine (Romans 16:17; Titus 3:10–11), yet Jesus Himself ate with tax collectors and sinners to call them to repentance (Luke 5:30–32), and Paul reminds us that we are not to withdraw completely from unbelievers in the world (1 Corinthians 5:9–10). You can love your neighbors, invite unbelieving friends to dinner, and speak kindly to everyone without inviting a false teacher inside to instruct your household or lending support to a message that denies the deity of Christ or justification by faith alone.

Practically, if someone comes to your door promoting a false gospel, you can kindly and firmly decline to invite them in or accept their materials, while still offering a brief, respectful testimony to who Jesus truly is (1 Peter 3:15). As a concrete next step, take time this week to read 2 John 1:1–11 and talk with your pastor or elders about how your family can practice warm, Christ-honoring hospitality while clearly guarding the apostolic doctrine of the faith.
How is God’s Word a lamp to my feet (Psalm 119:105)?

God’s Word is a lamp to your feet because it gives you clear, trustworthy direction for the very next step you need to take in a dark and confusing world. Rather than revealing every detail of your distant future all at once, Scripture provides the immediate wisdom and moral clarity required to walk faithfully today.
