The Apostle John explains that while no one has ever seen God, the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father's side, "has made Him known" (John 1:18). The Greek verb John uses here (*exegeomai*, from which we get the word "exegesis") carries the sense of explaining, declaring, and bringing something hidden into plain view. Because Jesus Christ is the exact imprint of God's nature, those who looked upon Jesus saw the Father revealed in human form (Hebrews 1:3; John 14:9).

One day, believers who have been made pure in Christ will receive the *beatific vision*, beholding God's face in the renewed creation without fear of judgment (Matthew 5:8; Revelation 22:4). Until that day, we come to know God as He shines His light into our hearts in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). Rather than searching for physical visions, open the Gospels this week in prayer and study the words, compassion, and cross of Jesus to see the true character of God.
Are books such as 90 minutes in Heaven and 23 minutes in Hell biblically based?

Books like *90 Minutes in Heaven* and *23 Minutes in Hell* are not truly biblically based, because they rely on subjective personal experiences rather than the clear teaching of Scripture, and several of their specific claims conflict with what the Bible actually reveals about the afterlife. Even when authors are sincere in recounting what they felt or saw, Christians are called to test every spiritual claim against the written Word of God (1 Thessalonians 5:21; 1 John 4:1).

At the center of this question is the theological principle of the sufficiency of Scripture (grounded in *sola Scriptura*), which affirms that the Bible contains everything God intends for us to know for salvation, godliness, and our hope of eternity (2 Timothy 3:16-17). In the first-century Jewish setting of the Gospels, Jesus told the parable of the rich man and Lazarus to show that people will not be persuaded to repent even if someone returns from the dead, because God has already provided sufficient truth in Moses and the Prophets (Luke 16:29-31). Likewise, when the Apostle Paul reluctantly mentioned his own vision of paradise while countering boastful rivals in Corinth, he noted that he heard inexpressible things that no human is permitted to tell (2 Corinthians 12:1-4). Paul's silence stands in sharp contrast to modern books that offer detailed, marketable tours of the afterlife.

When measured directly against Scripture, both books fall short in important ways:

*   **How they portray hell:** *23 Minutes in Hell* depicts demons acting as torturers who actively torment people in hell. Scripture, however, teaches that Satan and his demons do not rule over hell or serve as its wardens. Instead, the eternal fire was prepared for the devil and his angels, and they themselves will be tormented there forever alongside the unrepentant (Matthew 25:41; Revelation 20:10).
*   **How they portray heaven and death:** While we can be grateful that the author of *90 Minutes in Heaven* survived a devastating accident, his account centers heavily on earthly reunions, music, and sensory impressions while giving little attention to the supreme glory of heaven, which is seeing the Triune God face to face and worshiping the Lamb on the throne (Revelation 4:1-11; Revelation 21:22-23; Revelation 22:3-4). Moreover, the Bible teaches that human beings are appointed to die once and then face judgment, rather than taking temporary visits to the intermediate state to bring back new revelations (Hebrews 9:27).

Because God has spoken with final clarity in His Word, our assurance about eternity must rest on the historical death and bodily resurrection of Jesus Christ, not on anyone's near-death experience (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). Whenever you read a popular book about spiritual experiences or the afterlife, keep an open Bible beside you and ask whether the book anchors you in the written promises of Christ or draws you toward human sensations. For a trustworthy and deeply comforting picture of our eternal hope, spend time this week reading the final two chapters of Revelation (Revelation 21:1-22:21) in your personal devotions and discussing them with fellow believers at your local church.
Why does God not seem to care about the millions of starving children in the world?

Seeing millions of children suffer from starvation is heartbreaking, and it is completely understandable to feel sorrow or wonder how an all-powerful, loving God could allow it. When we look at such devastating suffering, two understandable objections naturally arise: either God is not powerful enough to stop it, or He simply does not care.

The Bible teaches, however, that starvation is not what God originally designed, nor does it reflect indifference on His part. God created a good and abundant world, and scarcity, greed, and suffering entered history through the Fall when humanity rebelled against Him, subjecting all of creation to brokenness (Genesis 3:17–19; Romans 8:20–22). Even in this fallen world, the God of Scripture repeatedly reveals His tender care for the vulnerable. Within the covenant laws given to ancient Israel, standing in sharp contrast to surrounding nations, God commanded His people to leave the edges of their fields unharvested so the poor and fatherless could eat, declaring that He Himself executes justice for the oppressed and gives food to the hungry (Leviticus 19:9–10; Deuteronomy 10:18; Psalm 146:7). That same compassion was visible in first-century Judea when Jesus saw weary crowds, felt deep pity for them, and miraculously fed them (Matthew 14:14–20).

Still, Christians believe we cannot trace every reason why God's providence permits specific tragedies to persist right now, because His wisdom reaches far beyond what we can see (Isaiah 55:8–9). What we can know with certainty is that His delay is not a lack of love. In the incarnation, the eternal Son of God took on human flesh, experienced hunger and sorrow firsthand, and stepped directly into our broken world. At the cross, Jesus bore the judgment for human sin through His penal substitution, died, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day to conquer sin and death (1 Corinthians 15:3–4; 1 Peter 2:24). Because of His resurrection, believers look forward to His personal return and final judgment, when He will wipe away every tear and ensure that no child will ever hunger again (Revelation 7:16–17; Revelation 21:4–5). In the meantime, God calls His people not merely to wrestle with the question of suffering, but to actively feed the hungry and care for the vulnerable in our local communities and beyond (Matthew 25:35–40; James 2:15–17).

Because sin separates every person from a holy God and fractures the world around us, our only lasting hope lies in the Savior who gave Himself to redeem both sinners and creation. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose again for your forgiveness and new life.

As you think about the pain in our world, what makes it hardest for you to reconcile God's goodness with the suffering you see?
What is postmodern therapy, and is it biblical?

Postmodern therapy is a family of counseling approaches, such as Narrative Therapy and Solution-Focused Brief Therapy, rooted in postmodern philosophy, which rejects the existence of objective, absolute truth. Instead of measuring a person's struggles against a fixed moral or created standard, it teaches that reality is socially constructed and treats the client as the ultimate author and expert of their own truth and identity.

At its philosophical foundation, postmodern therapy is not biblical because it replaces the authority of God with human autonomy. Writing into a first-century Greco-Roman world filled with competing philosophies and shifting truth claims, the Apostle Paul reminded Timothy that all Scripture is "God-breathed" (*theopneustos*) and completely equips the believer for every good work (2 Timothy 3:16–17). Historic Christianity summarizes this biblical teaching with the doctrine of *sola Scriptura*, the conviction that the Bible is the inspired, inerrant, and sufficient authority for faith and life. Scripture presents truth not as something we invent, but as something rooted in the unchanging character of God Himself (Psalm 119:160; John 17:17). Furthermore, Jesus did not invite people to construct their own personal meaning, but declared, "I am the way and the truth and the life" (John 14:6).

Postmodern therapy also differs sharply from the Bible in how it understands human brokenness. It generally assumes that our deepest problems stem from oppressive cultural narratives that we can overcome by re-authoring a preferred identity for ourselves. The Bible offers a diagnosis that is more sobering, yet far more hopeful. God made us with immense dignity in the image of God (Genesis 1:27), yet we have all sinned and fallen short of His glory (Romans 3:23), leaving our hearts deceitful and unable to heal themselves (Jeremiah 17:9). Because our deepest problem is moral alienation from a holy God rather than a poorly told story, self-authored truth cannot bring lasting peace. Real transformation comes only through the Gospel: forgiveness through the substitutionary death and bodily resurrection of Jesus Christ, received by grace through faith alone, followed by progressive sanctification as the Holy Spirit renews our minds (Romans 12:2; 2 Corinthians 5:17).

At the same time, believers can exercise thoughtful discernment. Because of God's common grace, a counselor trained in postmodern methods may still practice helpful relational habits, such as listening patiently to your grief or helping you trace how past wounds affect present patterns. Still, listening well is very different from affirming that we are free to define truth for ourselves. If you are considering counseling or evaluating a particular approach, ask the counselor plainly how they view objective truth, human sin, and the authority of Scripture. Above all, share your burdens with faithful pastors or elders in your local church, or seek out a certified biblical counselor (such as through the Association of Certified Biblical Counselors) who will care tenderly for your heart while anchoring your hope in the unchanging truth of Christ.
I am a Christian who is addicted to smoking. How can I quit?

Breaking free from an addiction to smoking is deeply challenging, and feeling trapped in a habit that you want to leave behind can be exhausting and discouraging. Yet as a Christian, you do not fight this battle in your own strength, and your struggle does not place you outside of God's patient care.

In 1 Corinthians 6:12; 1 Corinthians 6:19–20, the Apostle Paul addressed believers in the Greco-Roman city of Corinth who were using a popular cultural slogan ("Everything is permissible for me") to justify indulging their physical appetites. Paul corrected that mindset by reminding them that a Christian must not be mastered by anything, because our bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit, bought at the price of Christ's sacrificial death. 

This truth anchors your fight in the biblical doctrine of progressive sanctification. Because of your union with Christ, there is no condemnation for those who trust in Him (Romans 8:1). You are not trying to quit smoking to earn God's love; rather, because you are already loved and indwelt by the Holy Spirit, God gives you the power to put enslaving habits to death and grow in self-control (Romans 8:13; Galatians 5:22–23). When you stumble or give in to a craving, do not pull away from God in shame. Confess it honestly to Him, resting in His promise to forgive and cleanse you (1 John 1:9).

Because nicotine creates a strong physiological dependency alongside behavioral habits, wise stewardship also involves caring for your physical body. I cannot provide medical advice, so I encourage you to speak with a doctor or qualified healthcare professional about safe medical options to help manage withdrawal symptoms.

Spiritually and practically, here are three concrete steps you can take starting today:

1. **Bring the struggle into the light of your local church.** Addiction thrives in secrecy. Tell a pastor, elder, or trusted mature believer in your congregation what you are fighting, and ask them to pray with you and check in on your progress each week (James 5:16; Galatians 6:2).
2. **Pray directly the moment a craving hits.** You do not need scripted words; speak openly to your Heavenly Father right in the middle of the urge. Ask Him for immediate strength, trusting His promise to give grace in your time of need and a way of escape from temptation (Hebrews 4:16; 1 Corinthians 10:13).
3. **Establish a concrete replacement rhythm.** Remove cigarettes, lighters, and ashtrays from your home and car. Identify the specific moments that trigger the urge to smoke (such as stress at work or a morning routine), and replace that five-minute break with a set alternative, such as stepping outside for a brisk walk while slowly praying through a passage like Psalm 23.

Take heart and stay hopeful. The same Savior who rescued you by His grace will faithfully sustain you one day, and even one craving, at a time, for He who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion until the day of Christ Jesus (Philippians 1:6).
What is mortification of sin / the flesh?

Mortification of sin, or putting to death the deeds of the flesh, is the lifelong, Spirit-empowered practice by which a believer actively weakens, starves, and uproots remaining sinful desires and habits. Scripture commands Christians to put to death the deeds of the body by the Spirit (Romans 8:13) and to put to death earthly practices such as sexual immorality, impurity, lust, evil desires, and greed (Colossians 3:5).

In the Greco-Roman setting of the New Testament, the Apostle Paul chose vivid terms for this work, using the Greek verb *thanatoo* (to put to death) in Romans 8:13 and *nekroo* (to deprive of life or power) in Colossians 3:5. Significantly, Paul addresses these commands to believers who have already died with Christ and been raised to new life in Him (Colossians 3:1–3). Mortification is therefore not an attempt to earn God's favor through external moralism, but the active response of a heart already made alive by grace.

In historic Christian theology, mortification belongs to *progressive sanctification*, which must be carefully distinguished from *justification*. Justification is God's one-time declaration that a sinner is righteous through faith alone in Christ's *penal substitutionary atonement* (Romans 5:1; 2 Corinthians 5:21). Progressive sanctification is the ongoing work of the Holy Spirit conforming believers to the image of Christ as they battle *indwelling sin* (Galatians 5:16–17). While some Christian traditions emphasize a distinct crisis experience of complete victory or passive surrender out of a sincere desire to honor the Spirit's power, Reformed theology holds that God sanctifies His people through active, steady obedience and the ordinary means of grace, namely His Word, prayer, and the fellowship of the local church (Philippians 2:12–13; Acts 2:42).

This battle is hopeful rather than frantic because the condemning guilt of sin has already been removed at the cross (Romans 8:1). We do not fight for acceptance with God; we fight from the acceptance we already possess in Jesus Christ, refusing to make provision for the flesh while nourishing the soul on God's promises (Romans 13:14).

Practically, mortifying sin means cutting off the specific avenues where temptation thrives, such as setting firm boundaries around media, turning away from gossip, or confronting hidden bitterness before it takes root. As a concrete step this week, identify one recurring sin you face, pray directly to God for the Spirit's strength to resist it, and share it with a trusted, mature believer in your local church so they can pray with you and encourage you (James 5:16; Hebrews 3:13) as you walk together in Christlikeness.
Is God’s love reckless?

Literally speaking, God’s love is not reckless, because God is all-wise and sovereign and never acts rashly, carelessly, or without counting the cost. Yet believers sometimes use the word poetically to express how extravagant, relentless, and astonishing His grace appears from a human point of view.

In Scripture, God’s love is anchored in His deliberate, covenantal faithfulness, often expressed by the Old Testament Hebrew word *hesed* (steadfast, loyal love) and revealed supremely in the New Testament through Christ’s self-giving love. In the first-century Jewish context, Jesus’ parable of a shepherd leaving ninety-nine sheep to search for one lost sheep sounded shockingly generous by ordinary human calculation (Luke 15:4–7). Yet that pursuit was never impulsive; the cross was the centerpiece of God’s eternal purpose, as Jesus was delivered up according to "God’s set plan and foreknowledge" (Acts 2:23; Ephesians 1:4–5). These passages ground the historic doctrines of God’s *sovereignty* and *penal substitutionary atonement*, showing that Christ intentionally took the penalty of our sin in our place while we were still His enemies (Romans 5:8; 1 John 4:10).

Calling God’s love "reckless" in a strict literal sense would obscure His *omniscience* and *immutability*, since an all-knowing, unchanging God never takes uncalculated risks or acts out of blind emotion (Isaiah 46:9–10). Instead, His love is fiercely intentional: He knew the exact price of our redemption, the precious blood of His own Son, and freely paid it (1 Peter 1:18–20).

This truth brings tremendous comfort to your daily walk. Because God’s love is a settled, deliberate commitment rather than an erratic impulse, nothing in your past or present can catch Him off guard or cause Him to revoke His grace (Romans 8:38–39). When you feel unworthy or shaken by failure, bring those fears directly to God in prayer and read through Romans 8 slowly, resting in the assurance that the Savior who planned to rescue you from eternity past will faithfully hold you to the end.
Does the Bible teach that there is a gift of celibacy?

Yes, the Bible teaches that celibate singleness is a genuine gift from God given to some believers, just as marriage is a gift given to others (1 Corinthians 7:7). Jesus also affirmed that remaining unmarried for the sake of the kingdom of heaven is a specific calling granted to those able to receive it (Matthew 19:11–12).

In the Greco-Roman city of Corinth, some Christians wondered whether total sexual abstinence was spiritually superior, prompting the Apostle Paul to address both married and single believers directly (1 Corinthians 7:1–9). Writing in Greek, Paul uses the word *charisma* (a gift of grace, the same term used for spiritual gifts) to describe both his own singleness and the married state (1 Corinthians 7:7). Likewise, within a Jewish cultural context where marriage and family were deeply expected, Jesus recognized that God enables certain people to forego marriage for undivided devotion to His kingdom (Matthew 19:12; 1 Corinthians 7:32–35).

Historically, orthodox Christians have understood this gift not as a total absence of human desire or a requirement for lifelong vows, but as God's enabling grace and vocation (calling) to live purely and contentedly in singleness, whether for a season or a lifetime. Neither singleness nor marriage grants higher spiritual status; both are honorable callings in which the Holy Spirit works out our progressive sanctification as we walk faithfully before the Lord (1 Corinthians 7:17; 1 Corinthians 7:35). At the same time, Scripture is realistic about human weakness, so Paul explicitly advises unmarried believers who struggle with self-control and burn with passion to marry rather than fall into sexual sin (1 Corinthians 7:8–9). 

If you are navigating singleness right now, take heart that your present season is neither accidental nor second-class, and look for one practical way this week to use your unencumbered time to serve a family or ministry in your local church while praying for daily contentment and purity.
What did it mean that Satan wanted to be like the Most High in Isaiah 14:14?

In Isaiah 14:14, wanting to be "like the Most High" means striving to usurp God's supreme authority, sovereignty, and rightful worship. It captures the very essence of creaturely pride: rejecting the Creator-creature distinction and claiming the throne that belongs to God alone (Isaiah 14:13–14).

In its immediate literary and Ancient Near Eastern setting, Isaiah 14:4–21 is a prophetic taunt against the arrogant king of Babylon, using poetic imagery of the "morning star" (Hebrew *helel*) boasting that he will climb above the heavens and clouds to rival God (Isaiah 14:12–14). While the passage first addresses a historical earthly tyrant, faithful Christian interpreters have long recognized behind Babylon's boast the spiritual reality of Satan's own pride and rebellion, a pattern reflected in Scripture's warnings against the devil's conceit and downfall (Ezekiel 28:12–17; Luke 10:18; 1 Timothy 3:6).

The Hebrew title "Most High" (*Elyon*) points to God's absolute transcendence and unrivaled rule over heaven and earth (Genesis 14:19; Psalm 97:9). To seek to make oneself like the Most High is not a humble desire to reflect God's moral goodness, which believers are called to do, but a rebellious grab for His independent power and glory (Genesis 3:5; Isaiah 42:8). In theological terms, it is a direct assault on God's *sovereignty* and *aseity* (His self-existence and total independence), and it remains the root of all sin whenever creatures try to sit as lords over their own lives (Romans 1:21–23).

By sharp contrast, Jesus Christ, who truly is equal with God in nature, humbled Himself to the point of death on a cross to rescue proud sinners (Philippians 2:6–8). Because God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble (James 4:6–7; 1 Peter 5:5–6), a practical way to guard against this spirit of self-exaltation today is to begin your morning by consciously surrendering one specific ambition, worry, or decision to God's sovereign will in prayer.
What does the Bible say about the hornet?

In the Bible, the hornet appears in three Old Testament passages as an instrument God promised and used to drive out the Canaanite nations before Israel entered the Promised Land (Exodus 23:28; Deuteronomy 7:20; Joshua 24:12).

Each mention highlights God's direct involvement in securing Israel's inheritance. In Exodus 23:28, the LORD promises to send the hornet ahead of His people to clear away the Hivites, Canaanites, and Hittites gradually so the land would not become desolate. Later, in Deuteronomy 7:20, Moses encourages Israel not to fear the surrounding nations, assuring them that God would send the hornet against even the survivors who went into hiding. Finally, in Joshua 24:12, Joshua looks back at the conquest and affirms that God fulfilled His word, driving out the two Amorite kings not by Israel's sword or bow, but by the hornet sent before them.

The Hebrew word translated "hornet" (*tsir'ah*) refers to a stinging insect such as a hornet or wasp. Because the term appears only in these three contexts, Bible scholars debate whether God sent literal swarms of insects to panic the Canaanites or used the word figuratively to describe overwhelming divine terror (some also note the hornet was a royal emblem of Egypt, whose earlier military campaigns weakened Canaan before Israel arrived). Regardless of the exact means, the biblical text presents this as a real, historical act of God's deliverance on behalf of His covenant people.

Theologically, these passages display the sovereignty and providence of God, demonstrating that the Creator commands every part of creation and history to fulfill His promises and ensure that salvation belongs to Him alone. In our daily lives, this reminds us to trade anxious self-reliance for steady trust in the Lord, committing our work, fears, and battles to Him in prayer rather than depending solely on our own strength.
What were the key events in the life of Jesus Christ?

The key events in the earthly life of Jesus Christ include His miraculous virgin birth, His baptism and temptation, His public ministry of teaching and miracles, His sacrificial death on the cross, His bodily resurrection on the third day, and His ascension into heaven. Together, these real historical events form the heart of the Christian faith and reveal God's plan to rescue sinners.

Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born to the virgin Mary in Bethlehem during the reign of Caesar Augustus (Matthew 1:18–25; Luke 2:1–7). In this incarnation, the eternal Son of God took on a true human nature while remaining fully God, a truth historic Christianity summarizes as the hypostatic union (John 1:14; Colossians 2:9).

Around age thirty, Jesus was baptized by John the Baptist in the Jordan River and immediately overcame the devil's temptations in the wilderness (Matthew 3:13–17; Matthew 4:1–11). Stepping into the world of Second Temple Judaism under Roman rule, where faithful Israelites longed for God's promised Messiah, Jesus spent roughly three years preaching the kingdom of God, calling twelve apostles, performing miracles, and living in complete, sinless obedience to God's law (Mark 1:14–15; Hebrews 4:15).

The climax of His earthly life took place in Jerusalem during the Passover festival, where He was falsely accused, tried before Pontius Pilate, and crucified (Luke 23:1–49). His death was not a mere tragedy, but an act of penal substitutionary atonement, in which the sinless Christ willingly bore the wrath of God in the place of guilty sinners, was buried, and rose bodily from the grave on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Luke 24:36–43). Forty days after His resurrection, He ascended into heaven, where He reigns until He returns personally to judge the living and the dead and renew all things (Acts 1:9–11).

Because Jesus truly lived, died, and rose again, sinners can receive justification, being declared righteous before a holy God by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone (Romans 3:24–26). If you would like to trace these events for yourself, consider setting aside fifteen minutes a day this week to read through the Gospel of Mark, asking God to show you who Jesus is and to lead you to trust in Him for forgiveness and new life.
Do Christians need a day of rest?

Yes, Christians need a regular rhythm of rest because God built limits into human nature and modeled rest at creation for our good, even though faithful believers hold different views on whether a specific 24-hour day remains legally binding. Setting aside regular time to stop working, worship with the church, and delight in God refreshes both body and soul.

In the Old Testament, the Hebrew word *shabbat* simply means "to cease" or "to stop," pointing back to God resting on the seventh day as a creation ordinance (Genesis 2:2–3) before it was given to Israel in the Mosaic Law (Exodus 20:8–11). After Jesus rose from the dead, the early church in the Greco-Roman world began gathering on the first day of the week, called the Lord's Day, to break bread and hear Scripture taught (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2; Revelation 1:10). 

Because the New Testament emphasizes both the value of rest and our fulfillment in Christ, faithful Christians disagree on how the Fourth Commandment applies today, making strict Sabbath observance a non-essential matter where believers should practice Christian liberty and charity (Romans 14:5–6). 

One historic Christian view holds that the Sabbath is a perpetual moral law that continues in the Christian Lord's Day (Sunday), calling believers to lay aside ordinary labor and recreation to devote the whole day to public worship, mercy, and rest. Another faithful view teaches that the Mosaic Sabbath was a shadow pointing to Jesus Christ, who secures our true rest through justification and union with Him (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 4:9–10). Those who hold this second view do not see a single 24-hour day as strictly binding, yet they still treasure regular rest and prioritize gathering on Sunday for worship and sanctification, remembering Jesus' words that the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath (Mark 2:27).

Whichever view you hold, refusing to rest quietly denies our creaturely limits and tempts us to trust our own productivity rather than God's providence. As a practical step this week, look at your calendar and protect Sunday (or a dedicated weekly day if your work requires it) by finishing chores and errands ahead of time, committing to gather with your local church (Hebrews 10:25), and reserving unhurried hours for Scripture, prayer, and physical renewal. Above all, let your weekly rest remind you that your standing with God never depends on endless striving, for Jesus calls all who are weary and burdened to find deep rest for their souls in Him (Matthew 11:28–30).
How can I be a good Christian?

Being a faithful Christian does not begin with trying harder to be a morally good person, because no one can earn acceptance with God through human effort (Ephesians 2:8–9; Titus 3:5). Rather, the Christian life starts with receiving salvation as a free gift through faith in Jesus Christ, and then growing in joyful obedience by the power of the Holy Spirit (Romans 5:1; Galatians 5:16).

The foundation of everything is the Gospel. God is perfectly holy and just, and every human being has sinned and stands separated from Him (Isaiah 6:3; Romans 3:23). Because we cannot save ourselves, God sent His eternal Son, Jesus Christ, who took on true humanity, lived a completely sinless life, died on the cross in the place of sinners to bear God's wrath, was buried, rose bodily from the dead on the third day, and now reigns as exalted Lord (John 1:14; 1 Corinthians 15:3–4; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Philippians 2:9–11). In the letters of the New Testament, the Greek word translated as "justify" draws on ancient courtroom language meaning to declare someone righteous before a judge. Through Christ's finished work, sinners receive *justification* (a right standing before God) by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, rather than by good works (Romans 3:28; Galatians 2:16). If you have not yet placed your trust in Him, turn from your sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

Once you belong to Christ, becoming a maturing believer is a lifelong process called *sanctification*, in which the Holy Spirit steadily transforms your heart and conduct to reflect Jesus (2 Corinthians 3:18; Philippians 2:12–13). Good works do not earn your salvation, yet they naturally flow out of a grateful heart that has already been redeemed (Ephesians 2:10). God nurtures this growth through simple, steady habits of grace: reading and meditating on the Bible, speaking directly to God in prayer, and committing yourself to a faithful local church where you can worship, learn, and care for fellow believers (Acts 2:42; Hebrews 10:24–25).

As a practical step this week, set aside fifteen minutes each morning to read one chapter of the Gospel of John and pray directly to God, asking Him to help you know Christ more deeply and walk in His ways. Where are you right now in your relationship with Jesus, and what led you to ask about following Him today?
What does the Bible say about lawsuits / suing?

Scripture strongly discourages Christians from taking one another to secular courts over personal or financial disputes, calling believers instead to pursue reconciliation and even suffer loss for the sake of Christ's name (1 Corinthians 6:1–8). At the same time, the Bible affirms civil government as God's appointed servant for justice, meaning the legal system is not inherently sinful when used for protection from harm, criminal accountability, or unavoidable legal matters (Romans 13:1–4).

In the Greco-Roman world of first-century Corinth, public lawsuits were frequently used by the wealthy and well-connected to pursue status, financial gain, and humiliation over rivals. Addressing this cultural habit within the church, the Apostle Paul rebuked believers for dragging fellow Christians before unbelieving judges, reminding them that saints united to Christ will one day judge the world and even angels (1 Corinthians 6:1–3). Jesus had already established a clear pattern for resolving offenses between believers: go privately to the person who sinned against you, bring one or two witnesses if needed, and bring the matter to the church if reconciliation fails (Matthew 18:15–17). Paul pressed this further, asking why believers would not rather be wronged or defrauded than bring shame upon the Gospel before a watching world (1 Corinthians 6:7). In theological terms, these commands protect the church's corporate sanctification and witness, teaching us to entrust justice to God's providence rather than seeking personal vengeance (Romans 12:19).

However, Scripture does not prohibit every use of the courts. God established the civil magistrate to restrain evil and uphold public order (Romans 13:1–4; 1 Peter 2:13–14), and Paul himself appealed to his legal rights as a Roman citizen to seek protection from injustice (Acts 25:10–12). Consequently, Christians should never use passages about avoiding lawsuits to cover up crimes, abuse, or harm against the vulnerable; reporting criminal wrongdoing to civil authorities is both biblical and loving. 

In non-criminal matters involving unbelievers, insurance claims, or unrepentant individuals who refuse church accountability, faithful Christians sometimes hold different views on when legal action is appropriate. In these areas of Christian liberty, believers must examine their hearts for greed or bitterness, seek to settle matters quickly when possible, and strive to live at peace with everyone as far as it depends on them (Matthew 5:25; Romans 12:18).

Please note that I cannot provide legal advice, so if you are facing a specific dispute, you should consult a qualified attorney. As a practical step, before pursuing any legal action, bring the situation before God in prayer, pursue direct and peaceful reconciliation if it is safe to do so, and seek wise counsel from your local church elders or pastors so that your actions honor Christ.
What is kingdom now teaching?

Kingdom Now theology is a modern teaching, often associated with certain charismatic and dominionist movements, which claims that Satan stole dominion over the earth from humanity at the Fall and that the church must reclaim spiritual, cultural, and political control over earthly institutions before Jesus Christ can return.

While Christians rightly long to see Christ honored in every sphere of life, Kingdom Now teaching departs from Scripture in several important areas:

* **Divine Sovereignty:** This teaching often assumes God lost authority over the world when Adam sinned and must wait for believers to win it back for Him. Scripture, however, affirms **divine sovereignty** from beginning to end. God never surrendered His throne to Satan; the earth belongs to the Lord, and He works out everything according to the counsel of His will (Psalm 24:1; Daniel 4:34–35; Ephesians 1:11).
* **Over-Realized Eschatology:** In the New Testament, the Greek word translated "kingdom" (*basileia*) refers primarily to God's royal reign rather than just a physical territory. Jesus inaugurated His saving reign through His life, death, and resurrection (Mark 1:15; Colossians 1:13), and He already holds all authority in heaven and on earth (Matthew 28:18). Yet Scripture presents an "already, not yet" tension. Jesus plainly stated that His kingdom is not of this world (John 18:36), and the final destruction of every enemy and the renewal of creation await His personal, bodily return (1 Corinthians 15:24–28; Revelation 21:1–5). Placing the burden on the church to conquer earthly systems before Jesus can return is a form of **over-realized eschatology**, expecting right now what God has promised only at the end of the age. (This also differs from historic postmillennialism, an orthodox view held by some faithful Christians who anticipate widespread Gospel growth through the ordinary preaching of the Word rather than claiming God lost control or that believers must seize political power to unlock Christ's return.)
* **Apostolic Authority:** Proponents of Kingdom Now theology frequently teach that God has restored modern-day apostles and prophets to lead this global takeover. By contrast, the New Testament teaches that the church is built on the completed foundation of the biblical apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus Himself as the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20).

Because Jesus already reigns at the Father's right hand, believers do not carry the burden of conquering society so that Christ is permitted to return. Instead, Scripture encourages us to walk faithfully in God's grace, share the Gospel, serve our neighbors in our daily callings, and wait with steady hope for the appearing of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ (Titus 2:11–14), trusting Him alone to bring His kingdom to full perfection when He comes again.
What is The Infinite Way?

The Infinite Way is a modern mystical teaching and spiritual movement founded by Joel S. Goldsmith in the mid-twentieth century, drawing heavily from Christian Science and the New Thought tradition. It teaches that God is an infinite, impersonal consciousness and that sin, sickness, and evil are illusions overcome through silent meditation and realizing one's inner spiritual oneness with the divine.

Although The Infinite Way uses biblical vocabulary and quotes Scripture, its core teachings stand outside historic, orthodox Christianity. First, the Bible reveals a personal, holy God who created the universe distinct from Himself, and it treats human sin not as a mental illusion, but as real moral rebellion against our Maker that brings genuine guilt and separation from Him (Genesis 1:1; Isaiah 59:2; Romans 3:23). Second, rather than viewing "the Christ" as a universal awareness anyone can awaken within themselves, Scripture teaches the incarnation: Jesus of Nazareth is the unique, eternal Son of God who took on real human flesh, truly God and truly man (John 1:14; Colossians 2:9).

Because sin is real and God is just, human beings cannot meditate their way into peace with God. Salvation is secured through penal substitution, in which Christ willingly bore the righteous judgment for our sins on the cross and rose bodily from the dead on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4; 2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 Peter 2:24). Consequently, sinners are reconciled to God not through inner self-realization, but through justification by grace alone, received through faith alone in Jesus Christ alone (Romans 5:1; Ephesians 2:8–9).

In contrast to any mystical system, Jesus declared, "I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me" (John 14:6). If you are exploring The Infinite Way because you long for spiritual peace, healing, or closeness to God, I gently encourage you to turn from sin and trust in the risen Lord Jesus Christ, who freely gives forgiveness and eternal life. A practical step you can take today is to open a Bible and read the Gospel of John, asking God directly in prayer to show you who Jesus truly is and what He has done for you.
Does God have favorites?

No, God does not have favorites in the way human beings do, because Scripture plainly teaches that God shows no favoritism or partiality (Romans 2:11; Acts 10:34–35). He never prefers one person over another because of wealth, ethnicity, social status, intelligence, or outward appearance.

In the Bible, the words translated as "partiality" or "favoritism" come from an ancient legal idiom meaning "to receive" or "lift up the face" (Deuteronomy 10:17; James 2:1–4). In the ancient world, this pictured a judge looking favorably on someone because of their social standing, connections, or a bribe rather than the truth. By contrast, God's absolute **impartiality** means that His justice is completely fair and His standard is identical for everyone, whether rich or poor, powerful or obscure (Galatians 3:28).

Sometimes people wonder about this when they read that God chose Israel in the Old Testament or that Jesus had a particularly close circle of friends among His disciples. Yet Scripture explains that God did not choose Israel because they were greater or more deserving than other nations, but solely out of His own love and faithfulness (Deuteronomy 7:7–8). In theology, this is called **sovereign grace**. Unlike human favoritism, God's rescuing love is never sparked by human merit or superiority; it is free mercy shown to undeserving sinners out of His own goodness (Ephesians 1:4–5). Even Jesus' close friendships during His earthly ministry never limited His mission, which was to lay down His life to redeem people from every tribe, tongue, and nation (Revelation 5:9).

Because God does not play favorites, no one is too impressive to need His forgiveness, and no one is too broken to receive it. Through **justification** by faith alone, anyone who turns from sin and trusts in Jesus Christ, who died on the cross for sinners and rose bodily from the dead, is welcomed equally as a beloved child of God (Romans 10:12–13; John 1:12). In your daily life, this truth frees you from trying to earn God's affection by comparing yourself to others, and it calls you to treat every person you meet today, regardless of background or status, with the same dignity and fairness that God shows (James 2:8–9).
How can I live a holy life?

Living a holy life begins not with trying harder to earn God's favor, but with resting in Jesus Christ, who died for our sins and rose again so that we might be reconciled to God and made new (Romans 5:1; 2 Corinthians 5:17). If you are trusting in Christ by faith alone, God has already declared you righteous, and from that secure foundation He calls and empowers you to grow in practical godliness (1 Corinthians 1:30; Titus 2:11–12).

In Scripture, the Hebrew word *qadosh* and the Greek word *hagios* (translated "holy") carry the core meaning of being set apart for God's sacred purpose, reflecting His own pure and righteous character (1 Peter 1:15–16). Historic Christian theology summarizes this lifelong growth as **progressive sanctification**, distinguishing it from **justification** (God's one-time legal declaration that a sinner is forgiven and righteous in Christ). Justification gives you a right standing with God, while progressive sanctification is the ongoing work of the Holy Spirit conforming your desires, thoughts, and actions to the image of Christ (Philippians 1:6; 2 Corinthians 3:18).

God has given His people ordinary, steady means of grace through which He cultivates this holiness:

* **Immerse yourself in Scripture.** Jesus prayed that the Father would sanctify His followers by the truth of God's Word (John 17:17). Reading and meditating on Scripture daily trains your mind to recognize God's voice and guards your heart against temptation (Psalm 119:11).
* **Depend on the Holy Spirit in prayer.** Holiness is the fruit of the Spirit, not mere human willpower (Galatians 5:16; Galatians 5:22–23). Come honestly before God in prayer, confessing sin quickly and asking Him for grace and strength right in your moment of need (1 John 1:9; Hebrews 4:16).
* **Actively put off sin and put on righteousness.** Because you belong to Christ, Scripture calls you to deliberately turn away from sinful habits and cultivate love, humility, and patience in their place (Colossians 3:5–10; Ephesians 4:22–24).
* **Walk closely with a local church.** God never intended you to pursue holiness in isolation. Gathering regularly for worship, biblical preaching, and mutual encouragement with fellow believers protects your heart and stirs you toward obedience (Hebrews 10:24–25).

As a concrete next step this week, set aside fifteen minutes each morning to read through Romans 6 or Ephesians 4, then pray directly to God about one specific attitude or habit you need His Spirit to reshape today. Alongside that, consider reaching out to a pastor or mature Christian friend in your local church to ask them to pray for you and check in on your growth (James 5:16).

Is there a particular area of your life or a recurring struggle where pursuing holiness feels especially difficult right now?
What is the sinner's prayer?

The "sinner's prayer" is a modern Christian term for a personal prayer of repentance and faith in which someone acknowledges their sin before God and trusts in Jesus Christ for salvation. While the Bible never prescribes a specific script or formula to recite, it consistently teaches that God welcomes every person who turns to Him in humble faith.

In the first-century Jewish world of Jesus' ministry, many religious leaders prided themselves on their own moral performance, yet Jesus commended a despised tax collector who stood at a distance, beat his chest, and pleaded for God to have mercy on him as a sinner (Luke 18:13). Likewise, the Apostle Paul wrote that whoever confesses Jesus as Lord and believes in their heart that God raised Him from the dead will be saved (Romans 10:9–13). These passages anchor the biblical doctrine of justification by grace alone through faith alone: we are not made right with God by reciting magic words or earning merit, but by resting in Christ's perfect life, His substitutionary death on the cross for our sins, and His bodily resurrection (Ephesians 2:8–9; 1 Corinthians 15:3–4).

Because repeating a set of words without genuine repentance can create a false sense of security, Scripture calls us to look to Christ Himself rather than relying on a past ritual (2 Corinthians 13:5). If you want to speak to God about your salvation, you do not need a scripted prayer; simply pray directly to Him in your own words, honestly confessing your sin and thanking Him for the mercy found in Jesus.

If you have never done so, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose again for you, for forgiveness and new life. Are you asking out of curiosity about Christian practices, or are you thinking through what it means to know God personally?
How can a Christian avoid being a doormat for other people?

It is a common mistake to confuse Christian humility with being a doormat, yet Scripture never calls you to surrender your dignity or enable mistreatment. True biblical meekness, captured by the Greek word *prautes* in Matthew 5:5, does not mean weakness or spinelessness, but strength held under the gentle control of God.

First, understand what Jesus meant when He commanded believers to "turn the other cheek" in Matthew 5:39. In that first-century Jewish and Greco-Roman context, a slap on the cheek was a stinging personal insult rather than a license for ongoing harm. Jesus was forbidding personal vengeance and petty retaliation, not forbidding wise boundaries, self-protection, or lawful accountability, just as Paul later appealed to his legal rights as a Roman citizen when mistreated (Acts 22:25).

Second, examine your motives by distinguishing genuine love from the fear of man. Letting people walk all over you is often not an act of Christlike sacrifice, but people-pleasing rooted in a desire to avoid conflict or win approval (Proverbs 29:25; Galatians 1:10). As the Holy Spirit works in your sanctification, growing you into Christ's likeness, He frees you from needing everyone's approval so that you can love others truthfully (Ephesians 4:15). Real love seeks another person's spiritual good, which means refusing to enable their laziness, manipulation, or sin. Scripture draws a helpful line between bearing one another's crushing burdens and letting each person carry their own daily responsibilities (Galatians 6:2; Galatians 6:5).

Third, practice faithful stewardship by following Jesus's own example of setting boundaries. Though He came to lay down His life, Jesus regularly stepped away from demanding crowds to pray and remain faithful to the Father's mission (Mark 1:35–38; Luke 5:16). When a request violates your God-given responsibilities to your family, work, or health, practice giving a calm, gracious "no" without offering frantic excuses or apologizing for having limits.

For a concrete next step this week, identify one recurring situation where you tend to say "yes" out of guilt or fear, and ask a mature believer or elder in your local church to help you think through a clear, kind boundary for that relationship. As you prepare, pray directly to the Lord using Proverbs 29:25 and Psalm 118:6, asking Him to replace your fear of people's reactions with quiet confidence in His care.
What does it mean that the workers are few (Matthew 9:37)?

In Matthew 9:37, Jesus means that there are far more spiritually needy people ready to hear the Gospel than there are faithful believers actively laboring to bring them the truth of God's kingdom. Using the picture of a ripe crop waiting to be gathered, He is calling His disciples to recognize the urgency of evangelism and the shortage of committed messengers.

In the immediate context, Jesus has been preaching and healing throughout Galilee, and He is moved with deep compassion for the crowds because they are "harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd" (Matthew 9:35–36). In first-century Galilee, many ordinary people were weighed down by heavy religious traditions and neglected by Israel's spiritual leaders, echoing Old Testament warnings about unfaithful shepherds (Numbers 27:17; Ezekiel 34:5–6). In Greek, the word translated "workers" (*ergatai*) refers to field laborers engaged in demanding, hands-on harvest work, emphasizing that advancing the Gospel requires diligent, sacrificial service rather than passive sympathy.

This passage also displays the harmony between the sovereignty of God and human responsibility. Immediately after pointing out the shortage of laborers, Jesus commands His followers to pray, "Ask the Lord of the harvest, therefore, to send out workers into His harvest" (Matthew 9:38). God Himself is the sovereign Lord over the harvest who regenerates hearts and gathers His people, yet He works through appointed means of grace, specifically the faithful prayers of His church and the proclamation of His Word (Romans 10:14–15). In fact, Jesus begins answering that very prayer in the next chapter by commissioning the twelve apostles to go out and preach (Matthew 10:1–8).

For Christians today, this truth should move us from mere concern about a broken world to purposeful action. Begin by praying regularly that God would raise up faithful pastors, missionaries, and bold witnesses in your local church, and look for one natural opportunity this week to share the hope of Christ with a neighbor, friend, or coworker.
What was the purpose of the Levitical Law?

The Levitical Law was given by God through Moses to instruct Israel in holiness, sacrificial worship, and daily life as His covenant people, while revealing human sinfulness and pointing forward to Jesus Christ. Given at Mount Sinai shortly after Israel's deliverance from Egypt, these statutes governed life around the tabernacle so that a sinful nation could dwell safely in the presence of a holy God (Exodus 25:8; Leviticus 11:44-45).

Scripture highlights three primary purposes for this Law:

First, it displayed the character of God and exposed human sin. God declared to Israel, "Be holy because I, the LORD your God, am holy" (Leviticus 19:2). By setting forth a spotless standard, the Law made clear that humanity falls short and that no sinner can achieve justification before God through works of the law (Romans 3:20; Galatians 3:10-11).

Second, it taught the necessity of substitutionary atonement. The sacrificial rituals demonstrated that sin carries the penalty of death and that life is in the blood given on the altar to make atonement (Leviticus 17:11). However, the blood of bulls and goats could never permanently remove guilt (Hebrews 10:4). Instead, the ceremonial system served as a shadow of the good things to come (Hebrews 10:1), pointing ahead to the penal substitution of Jesus Christ, who offered Himself once for all on the cross (Hebrews 10:10-14).

Third, it set Israel apart until the coming of the Messiah. By regulating diet, festivals, and worship, the Law distinguished Israel from the surrounding nations as a kingdom of priests (Exodus 19:5-6). As the Apostle Paul explains, the Law acted as a guardian to lead us to Christ, so that we might be justified by faith (Galatians 3:24-25).

Because Christ has fulfilled the Law through His sinless life, sacrificial death, and resurrection, believers today no longer keep the ceremonial sacrifices. Instead, when you read the Old Testament books of the Law, you can pause to thank God for Christ's finished work and ask Him in prayer to cultivate practical, Spirit-led holiness in your everyday life (1 Peter 1:15-16).
What does the Bible say about confession of sin to a priest?

The Bible does not teach that Christians must confess their sins to a human priest in order to be forgiven by God. Instead, Scripture teaches that believers confess their sins directly to God through Jesus Christ, our one Mediator and Great High Priest (1 Timothy 2:5; Hebrews 4:14–16).

In the Old Testament, Israel relied on Levitical priests to offer animal sacrifices and represent the people before God's holy presence (Leviticus 4:20; Leviticus 16:30). Under the New Covenant, however, those earthly priests and sacrifices were fulfilled in Jesus Christ, whose once-for-all death opened direct access to God's throne of grace (Hebrews 7:23–27; Hebrews 10:19–22). Because of Christ's penal substitution on the cross and our justification by faith alone, Scripture affirms the priesthood of all believers, meaning every Christian can approach God personally without needing an earthly intermediary (1 Peter 2:9; Romans 5:1). As the Apostle John promises, "If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness" (1 John 1:9).

While the New Testament never establishes a separate priestly office to hear private confessions, it does encourage horizontal confession among Christians. Believers are instructed to confess their sins to one another so they can pray for each other and experience spiritual healing (James 5:16), and to seek reconciliation directly with anyone they have wronged (Matthew 5:23–24). Some church traditions point to Jesus telling His apostles that whosever sins they forgive are forgiven (John 20:23). Yet when read alongside the rest of Scripture, this describes the church's ministerial authority to declare God's terms of pardon through the Gospel, not a power given to human priests to grant absolution on their own authority (Mark 2:7; Acts 10:43).

In daily life, this means that whenever sin weighs on your conscience, you can go straight to your Heavenly Father in prayer, trusting completely in Christ's finished work for full forgiveness, and also invite a trusted pastor or mature believer to pray with you and walk alongside you in accountability.
Should Christians go to nightclubs? Is clubbing a sin?

Scripture does not explicitly name nightclubs, so whether a Christian may ever step inside one is a matter of wisdom and Christian liberty rather than a universal command. However, the Bible clearly condemns as sin the behaviors that often define club culture, such as drunkenness, sexual immorality, lust, and wild carousing (Galatians 5:19–21; Ephesians 5:18).

In the Greco-Roman world of the New Testament, the apostles warned believers to leave behind *komos* (translated as carousing or revelry), which referred to unrestrained, drunken nocturnal partying marked by sensual indulgence (Romans 13:13; 1 Peter 4:3). While enjoying music or dancing is not inherently sinful, God's moral law is unchanging: lustful looking, feeding the desires of the flesh, and losing self-control through alcohol are always sin (Matthew 5:28; Romans 13:14; 1 Corinthians 6:18). Because believers are called to progressive sanctification, meaning we are being set apart by the Holy Spirit to reflect Christ's holiness in every area of life, we must never treat environments that cater to sin lightly (1 Thessalonians 4:3–7).

Because Scripture does not issue a direct rule against entering a music or dance venue itself, faithful Christians who love the Lord sometimes arrive at different conclusions on how to apply wisdom here (Romans 14:1–13). Many Christians choose to avoid nightclubs altogether because the atmosphere is frequently designed to stir up temptation, compromise a clear witness, and dull spiritual alertness (1 Thessalonians 5:22; 2 Timothy 2:22). Other Christians exercise cautious Christian liberty, choosing occasionally to attend a venue (for instance, with godly friends for a specific celebration or to enjoy music) while strictly abstaining from drunkenness, lust, and immodesty, and staying mindful not to cause a fellow believer to stumble (Romans 14:13–21; 1 Corinthians 10:23–33). Neither group should fall into legalism by treating personal convictions as universal commands, nor into license by using freedom as a cover for sin (Galatians 5:13).

When deciding for yourself, do not merely ask whether walking through the door is permitted, but ask three honest questions: Can I remain completely sober and pure in thought in that setting, will my presence honor Christ and guard my witness, and can I go with a completely clear conscience before God (1 Corinthians 10:31; Romans 14:23)? As a practical next step, pray directly to God for honest discernment regarding your motives, and speak openly with a mature believer or an elder in your local church who knows your temptations and can help you establish wise boundaries.
Does the statue outside the United Nations have any connection to the beast of the end times?

No, there is no biblical or factual connection between that sculpture and the beast described in end-times prophecy. The piece, a brightly painted Mexican folk-art sculpture (an *alebrije* combining a jaguar and eagle wings) temporarily displayed outside the United Nations as a gift from Oaxaca, Mexico, merely bears a passing visual resemblance to the imagery found in Daniel and Revelation.

In biblical apocalyptic literature, composite animals are not predictions about modern art installations, but symbolic portraits of human empires, oppressive rulers, and spiritual rebellion against God (Daniel 7:3-7; Daniel 7:17; Revelation 13:1-4). Writing within a Jewish and Second Temple prophetic tradition, the Apostle John describes a beast resembling a leopard, a bear, and a lion, deliberately echoing Daniel's earlier visions of successive world kingdoms empowered by spiritual evil (Daniel 7:4-6; Revelation 13:2). In both books, the focus is on political and spiritual powers that exalt themselves against the Lord, not on a literal statue.

How these vivid prophecies map onto history and the end times belongs to the area of **eschatology** (the study of the last things), a non-essential matter in which faithful, Bible-believing Christians respectfully disagree. Because apocalyptic language uses rich symbolism rather than a modern calendar, Christians hold different interpretive emphases: for example, futurists generally understand the beast of Revelation 13 as a coming global ruler and political-religious system just before Christ's return, whereas idealists view the beast as a recurring symbol of ungodly empire throughout the church age, and partial preterists see it as primarily fulfilled in first-century Rome. In matters of non-essential interpretation like this, Scripture calls us to humility, Christian liberty, and unity, urging us to "pursue what leads to peace and to mutual edification" rather than getting entangled in speculation (Romans 14:19).

What remains unshakably clear and essential for every believer is the sovereignty of God and the certainty of our Lord's return. Jesus Christ will return personally and bodily to judge the living and the dead, overthrow every rebellious power, and renew all things (Acts 1:11; Revelation 19:11-16; Revelation 21:5). Instead of letting internet rumors about sculptures stir up anxiety, anchor your confidence in the plain teaching of God's Word (1 Thessalonians 5:4-11). A helpful next step this week is to set aside social media speculation, read through a chapter of 1 Thessalonians each day to see how the apostles actually prepared believers for Christ's return, and talk over any lingering questions with a pastor or trusted mature Christian in your local church.
What is the sign of Jonah?

The sign of Jonah is Jesus' promise that, just as the prophet Jonah spent three days and three nights inside a great fish before being delivered, Jesus Himself would be buried in the earth and rise bodily from the dead on the third day (Matthew 12:38–40; Luke 11:29–30). It stands as God's ultimate authenticating miracle proving that Jesus is the promised Messiah and Lord.

In the first-century Jewish world, religious leaders expected a prophet to validate his authority with unmistakable wonders, which led the scribes and Pharisees to demand a sign from Jesus on their own terms (Matthew 12:38). Jesus refused to indulge their unbelief and instead pointed back to the historical account of Jonah as a divine foreshadowing, a biblical typology, of His own death and resurrection (Jonah 1:17; Matthew 12:39–40). In standard Jewish time reckoning, the phrase "three days and three nights" refers to any part of three consecutive calendar days, matching Jesus' burial on Friday afternoon and His resurrection on Sunday morning.

Jesus also highlighted the second half of Jonah's ministry: the pagan people of Nineveh repented when Jonah preached, yet many in Jesus' own generation refused to listen even though "One greater than Jonah is here" (Matthew 12:41; Luke 11:32). Together, these truths point directly to the heart of the Gospel, showing that Christ's penal substitutionary death on the cross, His burial, and His victorious resurrection secure justification and forgiveness for sinners (Romans 4:25; 1 Corinthians 15:3–4). Rather than waiting for more evidence on human terms, the sign of Jonah calls us to humble ourselves today, turn from our sin in repentance, and place our trust in the risen Christ.
What does it mean to walk worthy?

To "walk worthy" in Scripture means living a daily life that aligns with and reflects the high calling and grace God has given to believers in Jesus Christ (Ephesians 4:1; 1 Thessalonians 2:12). It is never about trying to earn God's favor through moral effort, but about living in a way that corresponds to the salvation already freely received.

In the New Testament, the Greek word for "walk" (*peripateo*) reflects a familiar Jewish and Greco-Roman idiom for a person's daily conduct, while the word translated "worthy" comes from a term (*axios*) that pictured bringing two sides of a weighing scale into balance. When the Apostle Paul urges Christians to "walk in a manner worthy of the calling you have received" (Ephesians 4:1), he is calling believers to let their everyday character match the immense weight of Christ's saving mercy.

Here it helps to remember the vital biblical distinction between *justification* and *sanctification*. Through justification, sinners are declared completely righteous before God by grace alone through faith alone in Christ, based on His finished death and resurrection. Progressive sanctification then follows as the lifelong work of the Holy Spirit, who grows believers in holiness through the ordinary means of grace, such as Scripture, prayer, and Christian fellowship. Because a believer's standing with God is already secure through union with Christ, walking worthy is the grateful fruit of salvation, never the price of it.

Scripture shows that this worthy walk looks remarkably grounded in ordinary life. It appears in the way we relate to others with humility, gentleness, patience, and loving forbearance to keep the unity of the church (Ephesians 4:2–3). It also means bearing fruit in good works, growing in the knowledge of God, and standing firm in the gospel under pressure (Colossians 1:10; Philippians 1:27). In concrete terms, walking worthy looks like speaking truthfully and kindly to a spouse or coworker, refusing to hold onto bitterness when wronged, and faithfully serving in your local church.

As a simple next step this week, read Ephesians 4:1–3 each morning and pray directly to God, asking Him to reveal one specific relationship or habit where you can practice Christlike patience and humility today.
What is a divine appointment?

A divine appointment is an ordinary or unexpected encounter between people that God sovereignly orchestrates to accomplish His specific spiritual purposes, such as sharing the Gospel, offering encouragement, or meeting a pressing need. Although the exact phrase does not appear in Scripture, the concept is rooted in the biblical doctrine of **providence**, which teaches that God actively governs and directs all creation, down to the smallest details of daily life (Proverbs 16:9; Matthew 10:29–30).

Scripture shows that what looks like mere coincidence from a human perspective is often the quiet, purposeful hand of God at work. Under the Old Testament law of gleaning, which allowed the poor to gather leftover grain during harvest, the widow Ruth went out simply to find food and "happened" to step into the field of Boaz, a meeting God used to rescue her family and preserve the lineage of the Messiah (Ruth 2:3; Ruth 4:13–17). In the New Testament, along a desert trade route between Jerusalem and Gaza, the Holy Spirit directed Philip to cross paths with an Ethiopian court official who was reading the prophet Isaiah in his chariot, turning a roadside encounter into an opportunity to proclaim Christ and baptize a new believer (Acts 8:26–38). In every generation, God prepares the timing, the circumstances, and the hearts involved so His people can walk in the good works He has prepared in advance (Ephesians 2:10).

Recognizing God's providence transforms routine moments like a commute, a workplace conversation, or an errand into opportunities for faithful service. Tomorrow morning before you begin your day, ask the Lord in prayer to keep you attentive to the people right in front of you and ready to offer practical kindness, gentle encouragement, or a clear word about Jesus when the door opens.
What is the Qur’an?

The Qur’an is the central religious text of Islam, believed by Muslims to be the literal, final word of God (Allah) revealed to the prophet Muhammad through the angel Gabriel over roughly twenty-three years in the seventh century. Written in Arabic and arranged into 114 chapters called surahs, it serves as the supreme authority for Islamic belief, worship, and daily life.

While Christians honor our Muslim neighbors as fellow image-bearers of God (Genesis 1:27), historic Christianity does not recognize the Qur’an as divine revelation because its message contradicts the core truths of the Bible. Christians hold that the sixty-six books of the Old and New Testaments are God’s complete, inspired, and infallible special revelation, pointing from start to finish to the person and work of Jesus Christ (Hebrews 1:1–2; 2 Timothy 3:16). In contrast, the Qur’an explicitly rejects the Trinity, the deity of Christ, and the reality of His substitutionary death on the cross and bodily resurrection, all of which are essential to the Gospel (John 1:1–14; 1 Corinthians 15:3–4). Understanding these differences equips believers to speak with Muslim friends in a spirit of gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15), holding firmly to Jesus as the one mediator between God and humanity (1 Timothy 2:5). In practice, this means listening patiently to what our neighbors actually believe while prayerfully looking for opportunities to share the grace of Christ's cross.
What would have happened “if the Lord had not been on our side” (Psalm 124:2)?

According to the psalmist, if the Lord had not been on Israel's side when enemies attacked, the people would have been "swallowed us alive" in the heat of their foes' burning anger and completely overwhelmed as if swept away by a raging flood (Psalm 124:3–5). Without God's intervention, Israel would have been devoured like helpless prey in a predator's teeth and left permanently trapped like a bird in a hunter's snare (Psalm 124:6–7).

Composed by David and later sung by Jewish pilgrims traveling up to Jerusalem as a Song of Ascents, this psalm reflects the vulnerable reality of a small nation surrounded by hostile Ancient Near Eastern powers. In that literary and historical context, sudden flash floods and wild beasts symbolized chaos and unstoppable destruction from which human strength could not deliver. By concluding that "our help is in the name of the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth" (Psalm 124:8), the psalmist grounds Israel's survival in God's sovereign providence, His purposeful and almighty care over all creation to preserve His people. For believers today, this physical rescue also foreshadows our ultimate redemption in Jesus Christ, who tore open the snare of sin, death, and Satan's power through His death and bodily resurrection (Colossians 1:13–14; Hebrews 2:14–15).

Because the same Creator still keeps His people, this psalm calls us away from anxious self-reliance toward humble gratitude. When you face heavy pressure or opposition this week, take five minutes to recall specific times the Lord has brought you through past difficulties, and thank Him directly in prayer as your present help.
What did Jesus mean when He said it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to get into heaven?

Jesus used vivid hyperbole to teach that entering God's kingdom is utterly impossible through human wealth, effort, or moral achievement, and can only be accomplished by the sovereign power of God (Matthew 19:23–26; Mark 10:24–27). He spoke these words right after a wealthy young ruler walked away sorrowful, unwilling to part with his possessions to follow Him (Luke 18:22–23).

In the first-century Jewish world, material prosperity was widely viewed as a visible sign of God's favor, which explains why the disciples were astonished and asked, "Who then can be saved?" (Matthew 19:25). Jesus paired the largest familiar animal in the region with the tiny opening of a literal sewing needle (rather than a small city gate, which is a later legend lacking historical evidence) to paint an unmistakable picture of human inability.

Wealth had become an idol for that young man, exposing how deeply sin binds the human heart to earthly security rather than to God. When Jesus declared, "With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible" (Matthew 19:26), He pointed directly to the necessity of regeneration, the supernatural work of God giving spiritual life to a dead heart, and to justification by grace alone through faith alone (Ephesians 2:8–9). Left to ourselves, every person stands guilty before a holy God and spiritually bankrupt, completely unable to earn eternal life (Romans 3:23). That is why Jesus Christ, the eternal Son of God, lived a sinless life, died on the cross as the substitutionary sacrifice for sinners, and rose bodily from the dead to rescue those who cannot rescue themselves (1 Corinthians 15:3–4; 2 Corinthians 5:21).

For anyone seeking to follow the Lord faithfully, a practical step is to regularly examine what earthly comforts or achievements compete for your trust, and to cultivate intentional generosity so that possessions remain a tool rather than a master (1 Timothy 6:17–19).

If you have never placed your hope in Him, turn from sin and self-reliance, and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. What do you think makes it so tempting for people to rely on their own resources or achievements rather than entrusting themselves completely to God?
How do we decide which books belong in the Bible since the Bible does not say which books belong in the Bible?

While the Bible does not contain an inspired table of contents, Christians did not arbitrarily decide which books belong in it; rather, the church *recognized* the 66 books that God had already inspired and authenticated as His Word. Many people understandably wonder whether church councils centuries after Jesus simply picked their favorite writings, yet the historical record shows a careful process of recognition rather than invention.

The word *canon* comes from an ancient Greek term (*kanon*) meaning a measuring rod or standard, and it refers to the authoritative collection of writings that govern Christian faith and practice. Because God is the ultimate author of Scripture, His Word is *self-authenticating*, meaning its divine authority does not depend on a human committee to grant it power. Just as Jesus said that His sheep hear His voice and follow Him (John 10:27), God's people recognized the books that unmistakably carried His voice.

Historically, this recognition took place across two main eras. For the Old Testament, Second Temple Jewish communities already possessed a settled collection of sacred writings long before the earthly ministry of Jesus. Jesus Himself affirmed the established divisions of the Hebrew Scriptures when He referred to the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms (Luke 24:44), and the Apostle Paul declared that all Scripture is "God-breathed" (2 Timothy 3:16).

For the New Testament, the church is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets (Ephesians 2:20), and believers were already recognizing new apostolic writings as Scripture during the first century. Peter explicitly placed Paul's letters alongside "the rest of the Scriptures" (2 Peter 3:15–16), and Paul quoted a saying from the Gospel of Luke right beside a command from Deuteronomy under the single heading of "Scripture" (1 Timothy 5:18; Deuteronomy 25:4; Luke 10:7). Across the Roman world, early churches carefully received books based on three clear marks:

* **Apostolicity:** The book was written by an apostle or a close companion of an apostle, such as Mark or Luke.
* **Orthodoxy:** Its teaching agreed fully with the gospel message already taught by Christ and the apostles.
* **Widespread reception:** It was consistently read, trusted, and preserved among faithful churches everywhere, rather than emerging from a small, isolated sect.

When church councils met in the fourth century, they did not invent the canon or bestow authority on these books; they formally affirmed what congregations had already recognized and obeyed for generations. As a practical next step, if you would like to examine how these writings speak with one unified voice, try reading the Gospel of John alongside the Book of Romans this week and notice how clearly both point to the person and work of Jesus Christ.
What does it mean to walk by the Spirit (Galatians 5:16)?

To walk by the Spirit means to live each day in active, conscious dependence on the indwelling Holy Spirit, allowing His power and God's Word to shape your desires, choices, and conduct. In Galatians 5:16, the Apostle Paul promises that believers who live this way will not gratify the desires of the flesh.

In the first-century Jewish and Greco-Roman world, the Greek word Paul uses for "walk" (*peripateo*) refers to a person's habitual manner of life, taken one step after another. Paul writes this within his broader argument in Galatians that Christians are set free from both legalistic rule-keeping and lawless self-indulgence (Galatians 5:1; Galatians 5:13–18). In historic Christian theology, this daily reliance on God is known as progressive sanctification, the lifelong work by which the Spirit conforms a justified believer into the likeness of Christ.

Walking by the Spirit begins with an honest awareness that an ongoing conflict remains inside every Christian between the Spirit and the "flesh," which is our remaining sinful nature (Galatians 5:17). Walking by the Spirit does not mean passively waiting for mystical impressions, nor does it mean trying to earn God's favor through sheer willpower. Instead, it means continually submitting your mind and will to the Spirit who speaks through Scripture, putting sinful desires to death by His strength (Romans 8:13), and cultivating the fruit of the Spirit: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23). Because the Spirit has already given believers new life in Christ, we are called to walk in step with Him (Galatians 5:25).

In everyday life, walking by the Spirit looks like pausing in a moment of impatience or temptation to ask God for help before speaking or acting, rather than reacting out of old habits. As a practical step this week, set aside ten minutes each morning to read a portion of Galatians 5, pray specifically for the Spirit to grow one aspect of His fruit in your relationships that day, and stay connected with fellow believers in a local church who can encourage you and stir you up to love and good deeds (Hebrews 10:24–25).
What does the Bible mean when it says "The fool says in his heart, 'There is no God'"?

When the Bible says, "The fool says in his heart, 'There is no God'" (Psalm 14:1; Psalm 53:1), it is describing moral and spiritual rebellion rather than a lack of intelligence. It speaks of a person who wills to live and act as though God is absent, unconcerned, or has no rightful authority over human life.

In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, the word translated "fool" (*nabal*) refers not to a lack of mental capacity, but to someone who is morally senseless, arrogant, and stubbornly resistant to wisdom, while the "heart" represents the center of the will and moral choices. In the world of ancient Israel, where outright philosophical atheism was rare, saying "there is no God" in the heart primarily meant practical atheism, convincing oneself that God will not see or judge evil, which Psalm 14:1 immediately connects to corrupt and vile deeds.

The New Testament deepens this picture. In Romans 3:10–12, the Apostle Paul quotes Psalm 14:1–3 to teach the doctrine of total depravity, showing that apart from God's grace, sin corrupts every human heart and leads us to resist our Creator. Earlier, in Romans 1:18–21, Paul explains that God has made His eternal power and divine nature clearly visible through general revelation in creation, meaning that denying God is ultimately a moral suppression of known truth rather than an innocent lack of evidence.

At the same time, Psalm 14 does not leave humanity in despair, for it closes with a longing for salvation to come out of Zion (Psalm 14:7), a hope fulfilled in Jesus Christ, who died and rose again to forgive our rebellion and give sinners new hearts that know and love God (2 Corinthians 5:17). Even believers can drift into moments of practical atheism when we worry, nurse secret sin, or make daily choices without seeking the Lord. As a concrete step today, take a quiet moment to examine your habits and pray through one area where you have been living as though God were not present, trusting instead in His wisdom and mercy.
What is onanism? Is onanism a sin?
