Onanism is a term taken from the biblical account of Onan in Genesis 38, traditionally referring to coitus interruptus (withdrawal during intercourse to avoid conception), and later broadened in common English usage to mean masturbation.

In the Ancient Near Eastern and Israelite context, Onan was bound by the custom of levirate marriage, later codified in the Mosaic law (Deuteronomy 25:5–10), which required a man to marry his childless brother's widow to raise up an heir for his deceased brother's name and inheritance. When Judah instructed Onan to fulfill this duty with Tamar, Onan knew the child would not legally count as his own, so he deliberately wasted his seed on the ground whenever he was with her (Genesis 38:8–9).

Onan's action was unquestionably a sin, and Scripture states that what he did was evil in the sight of the Lord, who put him to death (Genesis 38:10). His sin was not merely a physical act; it was a greedy, rebellious refusal to fulfill his covenant duty to his brother, combined with selfishly using Tamar for sexual pleasure while denying her an heir and future security.

When the word is used today to refer to masturbation, it is important to recognize that Genesis 38 does not describe solitary self-stimulation, and Scripture never mentions masturbation by that specific name. Even so, the Bible establishes a clear moral standard for all sexual desire and behavior: God created sexual intimacy exclusively for the covenant union of one man and one woman in marriage (Genesis 2:24; Hebrews 13:4). Masturbation is ordinarily driven by lustful thoughts, which Jesus explicitly identifies as sin in the heart (Matthew 5:27–28), and represents a surrender to fleshly desire rather than the holiness and self-control to which God calls His people (1 Thessalonians 4:3–5; Galatians 5:22–23). Seeking sexual gratification outside God's design is sinful and dishonors the body that belongs to Him (1 Corinthians 6:18–20).

While the struggle with sexual sin and selfishness is deeply rooted in our fallen nature, the Gospel offers real hope and mercy. Through His penal substitutionary death on the cross and His bodily resurrection, Jesus Christ secures full forgiveness and justification for all who turn from their sin in repentance and trust in Him alone (Romans 3:23–26; 1 Corinthians 6:9–11). For those united to Christ, the Holy Spirit works progressive sanctification, giving believers both the desire and the strength for the mortification of sinful passions (Romans 8:13; Titus 2:11–12). As a concrete step, anyone battling sexual temptation should flee from lustful triggers (2 Timothy 2:22), bring their struggle honestly to God in prayer, and seek regular accountability and prayer with a trusted, mature believer in a local church (James 5:16).
Is Israel and the church the same thing? Does God still have a plan for Israel?

National Israel and the New Testament church are not identical as covenant institutions, yet all who trust in Christ, both Jew and Gentile, are united as one spiritual family, and God still has a gracious, redemptive purpose for Jewish people (Romans 11:1–5; Galatians 3:28–29). Faithful Christians who hold to dispensationalism emphasize God's unchanging integrity regarding His literal Old Testament land and kingdom promises, arguing that ethnic Israel and the church remain distinct entities and that God will fulfill His specific national promises to Israel in the future. Holding to a Reformed Baptist covenant theology, which is one faithful option within historic Christianity alongside other orthodox views, I believe the church is the New Covenant community where believing Jews and Gentiles share together in the one tree of God's saving promise, distinct from the temporary Mosaic national covenant yet continuous with the faithful remnant of Israel (Romans 11:17–24; 1 Peter 2:9–10).

Writing in the first-century Jewish and Greco-Roman world, the Apostle Paul addressed mixed Jewish and Gentile congregations in Rome who wondered whether widespread Jewish unbelief meant God's word had failed (Romans 9:1–6; Romans 11:1). Using the image of a cultivated olive tree, Paul explained that unbelieving branches were broken off and believing Gentiles were grafted in to share the nourishing root of the Abrahamic promise by faith, not to replace Israel or boast over them (Romans 11:17–20; Galatians 3:7–9). This highlights the foundational truth of justification by faith: God never operates two separate paths of salvation, for both Jew and Gentile are reconciled to Him solely through the penal substitutionary death and bodily resurrection of Jesus Christ (Ephesians 2:14–18).

Regarding God's ongoing plan for Israel, Christians also interpret Paul's promise that "all Israel will be saved" in different ways within historic orthodoxy (Romans 11:25–26). Some understand this phrase to mean the full number of God's elect from every nation, while many others, including historic Reformed Baptists like Charles Spurgeon, anticipate a large-scale future turning of ethnic Jewish people to Jesus as their Messiah before His return (Romans 11:23; Romans 11:28–32). Whichever view one holds on those future details, Scripture makes clear that God's heart toward the Jewish people remains compassionate, and His plan for them is centered in the Gospel of Christ. This truth guards us against any spiritual pride or hostility toward Jewish people (Romans 11:18–21), and as a practical step this week, you can read through Romans 11 and join Paul in praying earnestly for Jewish friends and neighbors (Romans 10:1), rejoicing that God weaves both Jew and Gentile into one tapestry of grace.
Are Catholic beliefs and practices biblical?

Roman Catholicism shares vital, biblical foundations with historic Christianity, yet several of its distinctive doctrines and practices depart from the clear teaching of Scripture. Discerning between the two requires honoring what is held in common while testing every tradition against the written Word of God.

On core truths about God and the person of Christ, Catholic teaching aligns with the Bible. The Catholic Church affirms the Trinity (one God eternally existing in three Persons), the *hypostatic union* (Jesus Christ as truly God and truly man in one person), His virgin birth, His bodily resurrection, and His future return to judge the living and the dead (John 1:1; John 1:14; 1 Corinthians 15:3–4; 2 Timothy 4:1). Many Catholics sincerely love God and seek to honor Christ through these shared biblical convictions.

However, official Roman Catholic dogma diverges from Scripture in several critical areas that affect the heart of the Gospel:

* **The Authority of Scripture:** The Bible teaches that all Scripture is God-breathed and completely equips believers for every good work, and Jesus explicitly warned against elevating human traditions alongside God's commands (2 Timothy 3:16–17; Mark 7:7–8). In contrast, Roman Catholicism treats Sacred Tradition and the Church's teaching office (including papal infallibility) as equal authorities alongside the Bible. It also grants canonical status to the Apocrypha, books that were not part of the Hebrew Scriptures recognized by Jesus and first-century Judaism (Luke 24:44).
* **Justification by Faith Alone:** In the New Testament, Paul uses the Greek legal term for "justify" (*dikaioo*) to describe a courtroom verdict where God pardons guilty sinners and credits Christ's righteousness to them through faith alone, apart from works (Romans 3:28; Romans 4:4–5; Ephesians 2:8–9). Historic Protestantism summarizes this biblical teaching as *justification* by grace alone through faith alone. Official Catholic teaching, however, defines justification as an ongoing process infused through the sacraments and sustained by human merit, explicitly rejecting the claim that believers are justified by faith alone.
* **The Sufficiency of Christ's Sacrifice and Mediation:** Scripture declares that Jesus offered one single, sufficient sacrifice for sins for all time and serves as the sole mediator between God and humanity (Hebrews 10:12–14; 1 Timothy 2:5). Practices such as viewing the Mass as a sacrificial re-presentation of Christ's body and blood, teaching purgatory and indulgences, praying to Mary or the saints, and affirming doctrines about Mary (such as her immaculate conception and bodily assumption) lack biblical support and obscure the finished work of Christ.

Because God's Word is our ultimate authority, every church practice and belief must be examined daily against Scripture, just as the Bereans tested apostolic teaching against the text (Acts 17:11). When discussing these differences with Catholic friends or family, speak with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15), keeping the conversation centered on the finished work and sufficient grace of Jesus Christ.
What should we learn from the tribe of Simeon?

From the tribe of Simeon, we learn both the sobering cost of unchecked anger and sin, and the enduring mercy of God's covenant faithfulness even when His people fail. Descending from Jacob's second son, Simeon was uniquely scattered within the territory of Judah and suffered a dramatic decline, yet the tribe was never utterly cast off by the Lord.

In Hebrew, the name Simeon comes from a root meaning "to hear," reflecting Leah's gratitude that the Lord had heard her affliction (Genesis 29:33). Sadly, Simeon's early history was marked by fierce wrath rather than patient trust. Alongside his brother Levi, Simeon deceitfully slaughtered the men of Shechem in retaliation for the assault on their sister Dinah (Genesis 34:25–30). In the Ancient Near Eastern world, a dying patriarch's words carried authoritative, prophetic weight over his descendants' future, and Jacob foretold that Simeon and Levi would be dispersed and scattered throughout Israel because of their cruel fury (Genesis 49:5–7).

Later chapters show how persistent sin weakens a community. During the wilderness journey, Zimri, a leader from the tribe of Simeon, openly defied God's command through idolatry and sexual immorality at Peor, bringing a deadly plague upon Israel (Numbers 25:6–15). Between the first and second censuses, Simeon's fighting men plummeted from 59,300 to 22,200, the sharpest decline of any tribe (Numbers 1:23; Numbers 26:14). Moses omitted Simeon from his final blessing over Israel (Deuteronomy 33:1–29), and under Joshua, Simeon received no independent border, only towns scattered inside Judah's territory (Joshua 19:1–9).

Yet Simeon's history also displays the remarkable interplay of God's justice and His providence. While the Lord disciplined Simeon's sin, placing this diminished tribe inside Judah's borders sheltered them close to Jerusalem, the worship of God, and the royal line of David. Centuries later, faithful Simeonites still stood among God's people (1 Chronicles 4:24–43), and Simeon is explicitly included among the sealed tribes in the book of Revelation (Revelation 7:7). God's sovereign grace is greater than human failure; through the cross of Christ, He does not merely expose sin, He forgives and restores all who turn to Him in repentance.

In our ongoing sanctification, Simeon reminds us that nursing bitterness, rage, or willful compromise never stays contained; it harms our families and communities. Take time this week to read Psalm 51:1–12 and Ephesians 4:26–32 slowly, praying directly to God to search your heart for any hidden anger or stubborn sin, and share one specific area where you need steady accountability with a trusted believer or elder in your local church.
What is the hypostatic union?

The hypostatic union is the biblical and historic Christian doctrine that Jesus Christ is one divine person who possesses two complete, distinct natures, being at the same time truly God and truly man. The word *hypostatic* comes from the Greek term *hypostasis*, meaning a distinct personal reality or subsistence, and describes how Christ's divine and human natures are united in His single person forever without confusion, change, division, or separation.

Scripture reveals this mystery plainly. In the opening of his Gospel, John writes of the eternal Word who was with God and was God, declaring, "The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us" (John 1:1; John 1:14). In the Jewish context of the Old Testament, God's glorious presence dwelt in the tabernacle among Israel, and John uses that very imagery to show that the eternal Son took on real human flesh to live among His people. Likewise, Paul affirms that in Christ "all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form" (Colossians 2:9), while the author of Hebrews describes the Son both as the exact imprint of God's nature (Hebrews 1:3) and as one who genuinely shared in our flesh and blood (Hebrews 2:14). Early Christian theologians adopted the phrase "hypostatic union" as a careful summary of these passages to guard against any teaching that would either strip Jesus of His deity or treat His humanity as an illusion.

This doctrine is far more than abstract theology, because our salvation rests upon it. As the one Mediator between God and mankind (1 Timothy 2:5), Christ had to be truly human in order to represent us, obey God's law in our place, and suffer real death for our sins (Hebrews 2:17). At the same time, He had to be truly God so that His sacrificial death on the cross, known as penal substitution, would carry infinite worth to satisfy divine justice and triumph over death through His bodily resurrection (2 Corinthians 5:19; Romans 1:4). When you feel weighed down by weakness or temptation today, take heart and bring those struggles directly to Jesus in prayer, trusting that as truly man He deeply sympathizes with your frailty (Hebrews 4:15), and as truly God He holds sovereign power to sustain and keep you.
Doubting God — how can I overcome doubt in my relationship with God?

Experiencing doubt in your relationship with God can feel deeply unsettling and exhausting, yet you are certainly not alone in this struggle. Many faithful believers throughout Scripture wrestled with honest questions during seasons of weakness. In the immediate context of Mark 9:24, a desperate father brought his afflicted son to Jesus and cried out, "I do believe; help my unbelief!" Rather than turning the man away for having imperfect faith, Jesus met his fragile honesty with mercy and power.

Often, doubt grows when we look inward at the strength of our own feelings rather than outward to the finished work of Christ. Because of human sin, none of us can secure peace with God by our own effort or emotional certainty. Yet in love, Jesus Christ lived a sinless life, died on the cross in the place of sinners, and rose bodily from the dead to win our salvation. Through justification by grace alone through faith alone, God declares believers righteous once for all (Romans 5:1). Your standing before God rests on Christ's unchanging righteousness, not on the daily ups and downs of your confidence. As the Holy Spirit carries forward your sanctification, those who truly belong to Christ are kept secure by God's own power (1 Peter 1:5; Philippians 1:6).

To move through this season with steadiness, anchor yourself in the practical means of grace God has provided. Set aside ten quiet minutes each morning to read through a Gospel, such as the Gospel of John, letting the historical testimony of who Jesus is rebuild your confidence, since faith comes by hearing the word of Christ (Romans 10:17). Alongside reading Scripture, bring your exact questions directly to God in prayer rather than pulling away from Him; reading through Psalm 13 or Psalm 42 can help guide your own honest words to a High Priest who truly sympathizes with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15–16). Finally, do not walk through this in isolation, but share what you are experiencing with a pastor, elder, or mature believer in your local church and ask them to pray with you (James 5:16).

Rather than waiting for every question to vanish before drawing near, turn from relying on your own shifting feelings and trust in Jesus Christ, who died and rose again so you can have forgiveness and lasting peace with God. What specific questions or circumstances seem to be stirring up your doubt right now?
Did God create other people in addition to Adam and Eve?

No, Scripture teaches that God created Adam and Eve as the first and only original human beings, and that every person who has ever lived is descended from them (Genesis 1:27; Genesis 2:7; Genesis 2:21–22). The apostle Paul later affirms this plain historical truth when he explains that from one man God made every nation of mankind to live on all the face of the earth (Acts 17:26).

In the Hebrew text of Genesis, Adam named his wife Eve, a name connected to the word for "living," specifically because she would become the mother of all the living (Genesis 3:20). People sometimes wonder about other created humans because of the account of Cain, who feared others would kill him and who had a wife in the land of Nod (Genesis 4:14–17). However, the narrative goes on to state that Adam and Eve lived for centuries and had many other sons and daughters (Genesis 5:4). In those earliest generations of human history, long before God prohibited close-kin marriage in the Mosaic Law (Leviticus 18:6–18), Cain would have married one of his sisters or another close female descendant of Adam and Eve.

This biblical account is foundational to the historic Christian doctrines of federal headship and original sin. Because Adam was not merely one man among several separate human lines, but the biological and covenantal representative of the entire human race, his disobedience brought sin and death to all of his descendants (Romans 5:12–19). That reality also illuminates the beauty of the Gospel, for Jesus Christ entered history as the "last Adam" to stand as a new representative, securing righteousness and eternal life through His death and resurrection for all who trust in Him (1 Corinthians 15:22; 1 Corinthians 15:45).

Recognizing our shared origin in Adam and Eve reminds us that every single person you encounter bears the image of God and is part of one human family, calling you to treat every neighbor with genuine humility, dignity, and love.
What does the Bible say about self-discipline?

The Bible teaches that self-discipline, often called self-control, is a vital Christian virtue produced by the Holy Spirit that enables believers to resist sin and pursue godliness. Far from mere human willpower, true biblical self-discipline flows from God's grace at work in a believer's heart (Galatians 5:22–23; Titus 2:11–12).

In the Old Testament, wisdom literature warns that a person without self-control is as vulnerable as a city with broken-down walls, left wide open to spiritual ruin (Proverbs 25:28). In the New Testament, the Greek word translated as self-control (*enkrateia*) refers to inner mastery and restraint, which the Apostle Paul illustrates through the rigorous training of Greco-Roman athletes competing for a prize (1 Corinthians 9:24–27). While ancient philosophers viewed self-discipline as an achievement of human pride, Scripture teaches that God gives His people a spirit of power, love, and self-control so they can run the race of faith with endurance (2 Timothy 1:7; Hebrews 12:1–2).

Theologically, Christians understand this ongoing training as part of progressive sanctification, the lifelong work of the Holy Spirit conforming believers to the likeness of Christ. God does not call us to earn our salvation through strict habits, for we are saved by grace alone, yet that very grace actively trains us to renounce ungodliness and live self-controlled, upright lives (Titus 2:11–12). Even the Lord's loving correction during trials is meant to train us so that we share in His holiness and reap the peaceful fruit of righteousness (Hebrews 12:10–11).

To grow in self-discipline without falling into exhausting self-reliance, choose one specific area of life to surrender to Christ this week, such as guarding your speech, managing your digital habits, or establishing a consistent morning devotion. Begin each day by praying directly to God for the Spirit's strength, anchoring your mind in a passage like Psalm 119:9–16, and sharing your goal with a mature believer in your local church who can pray with you (James 5:16) and encourage you as you walk in faithfulness.
What is original sin?

Original sin is the state of moral guilt and spiritual corruption that every human being inherits from Adam as a result of the Fall (Genesis 3:1–19; Romans 5:12). Rather than referring only to the first sin committed in the Garden of Eden, the term describes the fallen condition in which all people, except the Lord Jesus Christ, are now conceived and born (Psalm 51:5; Ephesians 2:1–3).

In Romans 5:12–19, writing to a mixed congregation of Jewish and Gentile Christians in first-century Rome, the Apostle Paul explains this condition by drawing a deliberate parallel between Adam and Christ based on the Old Testament creation account. Paul teaches that Adam acted as the legal representative of the entire human race, so that his one act of disobedience brought condemnation and death upon everyone he represented. Historic Christian theology summarizes this biblical teaching with the concepts of *federal headship* (Adam standing as humanity's representative), *imputation* (his guilt being counted to all his descendants), and *total depravity* (the reality that sin affects every part of our minds, wills, and desires, leaving us spiritually dead and unable to save ourselves) (Romans 3:10–12; Romans 5:18–19).

Thankfully, Paul does not explain our ruin in Adam without immediately pointing to our rescue in Christ, the greater representative who brings *justification* and eternal life through His perfect obedience, atoning death on the cross, and bodily resurrection (Romans 5:17–19; 1 Corinthians 15:21–22). Because salvation is a gift of grace received through faith rather than human achievement (Ephesians 2:8–9), understanding original sin frees us from pride and self-righteousness. When you notice stubborn sinful patterns in your own heart this week, bring them honestly to God in prayer and let that awareness deepen your gratitude for a Savior who rescues helpless sinners.
Are intrusive thoughts sin? Are spontaneous violent, sexual, or blasphemous thoughts sin?

Having spontaneous, unwanted violent, sexual, or blasphemous thoughts flash into your mind can feel terrifying and deeply distressing, especially when those thoughts go against everything you love and believe. 

In Scripture, simply experiencing an uninvited, intrusive thought is not in itself a sin. The Bible draws a vital distinction between temptation (an unwanted suggestion or mental assault) and actual transgression (a willful choice of the heart). In James 1:14–15, sin is pictured as a process where desire entices us, conceives, and "gives birth to sin." Sin takes place when the will consents to the thought, welcomes it in, and cherishes it. Similarly, when Jesus warns against lust in Matthew 5:28, the original Greek wording points to looking with the *purpose* or *intent* to lust, rather than merely having an unwanted image cross your awareness. 

Consider our Lord Jesus Himself. In the wilderness, Satan directly suggested blasphemous thoughts to Jesus, tempting Him to doubt God and even worship the devil, yet Jesus was tempted in every way as we are and remained completely without sin (Matthew 4:1–11; Hebrews 4:15). Paul also reminds believers that we face "flaming arrows of the evil one" (Ephesians 6:16). Just as you cannot stop a bird from flying over your head, you cannot always prevent a jarring thought from crossing your mind, though by God's grace you can refuse to let it build a nest there. In fact, the very grief and horror you feel when a blasphemous or violent thought appears is often evidence of the Holy Spirit's work of *sanctification* in you, because a heart at peace with sin does not recoil at it.

Of course, if we stop treating an ungodly thought as an intruder and instead deliberately linger on it, indulge it, or act upon it, that willful consent becomes sin. Yet even when we do fail and sin in our thoughts, the believer's standing before God rests on *justification* by grace alone through faith in Jesus Christ, not on flawless mental control. Because Christ lived a sinless life, died as a substitutionary sacrifice on the cross, and rose bodily from the dead, every sin we confess is completely forgiven (1 John 1:9; Romans 8:1). If you have never yet turned from sin and trusted in Jesus Christ alone, look to Him today for forgiveness, cleansing, and peace with God.

Because relentless intrusive thoughts can sometimes stem from heightened anxiety or medical conditions such as obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), please keep in mind that I cannot provide medical or psychiatric advice. Seeking evaluation from a qualified doctor can be a wise step of stewardship alongside spiritual care. 

For your next step this week, rather than fighting the thoughts by panicking or endlessly analyzing whether you "meant" them, let them pass while you bring your distress directly to God in prayer. Anchor your mind in the promise of Romans 8:1 ("Therefore, there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus"), and share what you are experiencing with a trusted pastor, elder, or certified biblical counselor (such as through the Association of Certified Biblical Counselors) so they can stand with you and pray for you (James 5:16).

If you feel comfortable sharing, how long have you been carrying this burden, and do you have a local pastor or mature believer you can talk with about it?
Book of 1 Corinthians - Bible Survey

First Corinthians is a pastoral and corrective letter written by the Apostle Paul around AD 55 to the church in Corinth, addressing deep divisions, moral compromises, and theological confusion by applying the cross of Christ to everyday life (1 Corinthians 1:2; 1 Corinthians 2:2).

**Historical Context**
Writing from Ephesus during his third missionary journey (1 Corinthians 16:8), Paul addresses a young, largely Gentile congregation living in a wealthy Greco-Roman port city famous for commercial ambition, philosophical pride, and widespread sexual immorality. Because the Corinthians were allowing these surrounding cultural values to shape the church, Paul reminds them of who they are in Christ and calls them to live out their **sanctification** in holiness and unity (1 Corinthians 1:2; 1 Corinthians 6:11).

**Key Themes and Structure**
* **Unity and the Wisdom of the Cross (1 Corinthians 1:10–4:21):** Paul confronts rival factions rallying behind human teachers by pointing the church back to the message of Christ crucified, which overturns human pride and displays the true power and wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:18–24; 1 Corinthians 3:5–11).
* **Moral Purity and Church Discipline (1 Corinthians 5:1–7:40):** Paul rebukes the church for tolerating incest, taking fellow believers to secular courts, and misusing their bodies. He grounds sexual purity in the believer's **union with Christ**, reminding them that their bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit bought at the price of Christ's **substitutionary atonement** as our Passover Lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7; 1 Corinthians 6:15–20). He also offers wise counsel on marriage, singleness, and godly contentment (1 Corinthians 7:1–17).
* **Christian Liberty and Worship (1 Corinthians 8:1–14:40):** Addressing disputes over meat offered to idols, Paul teaches that knowledge must be governed by self-giving love for weaker brothers and sisters (1 Corinthians 8:1–13; 1 Corinthians 10:23–33). He corrects abuses at the Lord's Supper (1 Corinthians 11:17–34) and explains how spiritual gifts are meant to build up the whole body under the supreme rule of love and order (1 Corinthians 12:4–7; 1 Corinthians 13:1–13; 1 Corinthians 14:40).
* **The Bodily Resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:1–16:24):** Paul concludes with a triumphant defense of the Gospel, centering on Christ's historical death for our sins, burial, and **bodily resurrection** on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). Without the resurrection, faith is futile; because Christ is risen, believers have the unshakeable promise of future resurrection and eternal victory over death (1 Corinthians 15:17–22; 1 Corinthians 15:54–58).

**Doctrinal Significance and Application**
Theologically, First Corinthians demonstrates that sound doctrine and godly living can never be separated, because the Gospel of Christ's cross and resurrection transforms how believers think, worship, and treat one another. As a concrete step today, follow Paul's call to seek the good of others over your own preferences (1 Corinthians 10:24; 1 Corinthians 14:26) the next time you face a disagreement in your local church, trusting that the risen Lord sees and strengthens every act of humble love.
How do I identify my spiritual gift?

You identify your spiritual gift primarily by actively serving within a local church, observing where God produces spiritual fruit through your efforts, and listening to the affirmation of mature believers and church leaders. Scripture never instructs us to take a personality test to discover a hidden label; instead, it calls us to love and serve others faithfully, trusting the Holy Spirit to equip us as we step out in obedience (1 Peter 4:10–11; Romans 12:6–8).

In the New Testament, the Greek term often translated as "spiritual gifts" (*charismata*) literally means "gifts of grace." Writing to the early churches, the apostle Paul emphasized that these abilities are not badges of personal status, as some in Corinth mistakenly believed, but unmerited endowments given by the Spirit for the common good (1 Corinthians 12:7). As part of our ongoing sanctification and stewardship before God, every gift is intended to build up the body of Christ and glorify the Lord, never to draw attention to ourselves (Ephesians 4:11–12; 1 Corinthians 14:12).

To discern how God has gifted you, consider these four practical principles:

*   **Start serving a present need.** It is far easier to steer a ship that is already moving than one tied to the dock. Rather than waiting to feel uniquely qualified, look for practical ways to care for people around you, such as helping with hospitality, assisting with youth or children, visiting the sick, or supporting administrative tasks. Clarity almost always comes in the midst of faithful service.
*   **Examine your burdens and your joy.** Reflect on the biblical descriptions of ongoing gifts of grace, such as teaching, showing mercy, encouraging, giving, leading, and hospitality (Romans 12:6–8; 1 Peter 4:9–11). Pay attention to what needs in the church burden your heart, and notice when serving brings you a quiet, Spirit-given sense of joy and effectiveness rather than mere exhaustion.
*   **Seek the confirmation of your church family.** Because spiritual gifts are designed for community, you should not try to discern them in isolation. Ask your pastors, elders, or trusted mature Christians where they see God's grace visibly at work in your life and how they see others being built up through your service (Proverbs 15:22).
*   **Pray directly for wisdom and humility.** Ask the Lord to give you a willing heart like Christ's, who came not to be served but to serve, and trust Him to guide your steps and use even your weaknesses for His glory (Mark 10:45; James 1:5; 2 Corinthians 12:9).

For a concrete next step this week, reach out to a pastor, elder, or ministry leader at your church and ask, "Where is a real need in our congregation right now where I can step in and help?" Commit to serving in that area for a season, and after a month or two, invite a mature believer serving alongside you to share honest encouragement and feedback on where they see God using you most.
What is lacking in Christ’s afflictions (Colossians 1:24)?

Nothing is lacking in the saving value or sufficiency of Christ’s death on the cross; rather, what remains "lacking" in Colossians 1:24 is the ongoing, appointed suffering of Christ’s body, the church, as the completed gospel is carried to the nations. Paul is speaking of his own missionary hardships, which serve to bring the message of Christ’s finished work to the Colossians.

In the immediate literary context, Paul leaves no room to doubt the completeness of Christ’s atonement. Just verses earlier, he declares that God made peace through the blood of Christ’s cross to reconcile believers completely (Colossians 1:20–22), and he soon adds that God forgave all our trespasses and canceled our debt by nailing it to the cross (Colossians 2:13–14). Christ’s penal substitution for sinners is finished and needs no human merit added to it.

The original language and setting clarify what Paul means. Writing from Roman custody for preaching the gospel (Colossians 4:3; Colossians 4:18), Paul uses the Greek word *thlipsis* ("afflictions" or "tribulations"), a term the New Testament uses for missionary distress and persecution rather than for Jesus’ atoning sacrifice. Because of our union with Christ, Jesus so closely identifies with His people that to persecute the church is to persecute Him directly (Acts 9:4). While Christ’s redemptive work is finished, His ongoing suffering *with* and *in* His people continues until the full number of believers is gathered and He returns (2 Corinthians 1:5; Philippians 3:10). Paul’s trials were "lacking" only in the sense that the church’s witness-bearing suffering must still be lived out so that others might hear and see the gospel.

In your own walk with the Lord, this means that when you face hardship, rejection, or quiet perseverance for the sake of Jesus, you are never trying to pay off a debt to God; instead, you can patiently endure with joy, trusting that God uses your faithfulness to display the already-sufficient grace of Christ to a watching world.
How can I get my prayers answered by God?

God answers the prayers of His children not because we use a secret formula, but because we come to Him through a living relationship with Jesus Christ, praying in faith according to His will (1 John 5:14–15). While God always hears and responds to His people, His answers flow from His infinite wisdom and love rather than our demands.

In the ancient world of the New Testament, people often treated prayer like a transaction, using repeated formulas to persuade distant deities. Jesus broke completely with that mindset by teaching His disciples to address the Almighty as "Father" (Matthew 6:9) and to pray in His name (John 14:13–14). To pray in Jesus' name is not a magical phrase tacked onto the end of a request; it is a recognition of Christ's mediation, coming before a holy God on the merit of Jesus, our great High Priest, and aligning our desires with His character (1 Timothy 2:5; Hebrews 4:14–16).

Scripture highlights several ways we align our hearts with God when we pray:

* **Pray according to God's will:** Our requests are guided by what Scripture reveals about God's glory and goodness (1 John 5:14–15). Trusting God's sovereignty means bringing our deepest desires honestly, while echoing Jesus' posture in Gethsemane: "not as I will, but as You will" (Matthew 26:39).
* **Pray with a repentant, humble heart:** Cherishing unconfessed sin or holding onto bitterness hinders our fellowship with God (Psalm 66:18; 1 Peter 3:7). Turning quickly from sin keeps our relationship with Him clear.
* **Pray in faith and persistence:** God invites us to ask boldly without giving up, even when His loving answer is "wait" or "no" for the sake of our sanctification and deeper growth in Christ (Luke 18:1–8; 2 Corinthians 12:7–9; Romans 8:28–29).

Because our sin separates us from a holy God, true access to Him in prayer begins with the Gospel. Jesus Christ, fully God and fully man, died on the cross for our sins and rose bodily from the dead to reconcile us to the Father and grant us adoption into His family (Romans 5:1–2; Galatians 4:4–6). If you have not yet placed your faith in Him, turn from your sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone for forgiveness and new life so that you may come boldly to God as your Father.

As a practical step this week, set aside ten minutes each morning to open your Bible to Psalm 23:1–6 or Matthew 6:9–13, and pray directly to God in your own words using those truths to guide your requests and thanksgiving. Remember also to share your burdens with a mature believer or pastor in a local church and ask them to pray with you, for Scripture reminds us that the prayer of a righteous person has great power to prevail (James 5:16).

Is there a particular burden or unanswered prayer you have been carrying lately that prompted your question?
What is the more excellent way (1 Corinthians 12:31)?

The "more excellent way" that the Apostle Paul introduces in 1 Corinthians 12:31 is the way of self-giving Christian love, which he immediately unfolds in 1 Corinthians 13. While spiritual gifts are valuable for serving God's people, love is the indispensable motive and standard that gives those gifts true worth (1 Corinthians 13:1–3).

In the first-century church at Corinth, believers were divided by pride and rivalry, treating visible spiritual gifts like tongues and prophecy as badges of personal status rather than tools to build up the body of Christ (1 Corinthians 12:12–26; 1 Corinthians 14:12). Against that backdrop, Paul uses the Greek word *agape* to describe love not as a passing emotion, but as a deliberate, sacrificial commitment to another's good, patterned after God's own redemptive love in Christ (1 John 4:8–10; Ephesians 5:2). Without this love, Paul explains, even extraordinary faith, deep biblical knowledge, or outward generosity amounts to nothing spiritually (1 Corinthians 13:2–3).

Theologically, walking in this love is the clearest evidence of genuine sanctification and the supreme fruit of the Holy Spirit at work in a believer's heart (Galatians 5:22). Practically, you pursue this more excellent way not by comparing your gifts with others, but by intentionally using the abilities God has given you to patiently serve, forgive, and encourage the fellow believers in your local church (1 Corinthians 13:4–7; 1 Corinthians 14:1). Love is what turns spiritual gifting into true Christlikeness.
What is the open heaven concept?

In the Bible, the concept of an "open heaven" refers to decisive moments when God parts the veil between His dwelling and the earth to reveal His glory, speak His word, pour out blessing, or act in redemptive history. In modern Christian conversation, the phrase is also often used to describe a heightened sense of God's presence, unusual answers to prayer, or a season of spiritual revival.

Throughout the Old Testament, the prophets used this imagery to describe divine revelation and covenant faithfulness. While living among the exiles in Babylon, Ezekiel saw that "the heavens were opened" and received visions of God's sovereign throne (Ezekiel 1:1). Later, Isaiah pleaded with God to "rend the heavens and come down" to rescue His people (Isaiah 64:1), and Malachi promised that God would open "the floodgates of heaven" to pour out abundance on a faithful Israel (Malachi 3:10).

In the first-century Jewish world, many longed for God to break centuries of prophetic silence and visit His people again, and the New Testament reveals that this longing is fulfilled in Jesus Christ. At His baptism, the heavens opened, the Spirit descended like a dove, and the Father spoke in approval of His Son (Matthew 3:16–17). Soon after, Jesus promised Nathanael that he would see "heaven open and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man" (John 1:51). By echoing Jacob's dream of a stairway between earth and heaven (Genesis 28:12), Jesus declared that He Himself is the true bridge between God and humanity. Later, as Stephen faced martyrdom, he saw the heavens opened and the exalted Christ standing at God's right hand (Acts 7:56), and Revelation portrays heaven opening at the end of the age when Christ returns in victory (Revelation 19:11).

Theologically, this biblical theme points directly to Christ's mediation and our reconciliation to God. Because Jesus accomplished penal substitution on the cross, bearing the penalty of sin in our place, and now serves as our one mediator before the Father (1 Timothy 2:5), the barrier of sin separating us from God has been removed. While some modern teachings speak of trying to "open the heavens" through special spiritual techniques or by clearing spiritual atmospheres over a city, Scripture teaches that believers already have open, uninterrupted access to the Father through Christ by one Spirit (Ephesians 2:18).

Rather than waiting for an extraordinary spiritual atmosphere or chasing special experiences, you can draw near to God's throne of grace with confidence (Hebrews 4:14–16), stepping into daily prayer and Scripture reading today with the quiet assurance that, in Jesus Christ, heaven is already open to you.
What is the origin of baptism?

Christian baptism originates directly in the command and example of Jesus Christ, who instituted it as a permanent ordinance for the church after first submitting to the ministry of John the Baptist. Historically, this practice drew its outward form from Old Testament ceremonial washings and first-century Jewish purification rituals, while receiving a distinct redemptive meaning in Christ.

In the New Testament, the Greek verb *baptizo* means to dip, plunge, or immerse. Long before the first century, God prescribed ritual washings with water in the Old Testament for priestly consecration and cleansing from ceremonial impurity (Exodus 29:4; Leviticus 14:8). By the time of Jesus, Jewish communities widely practiced ritual immersion in baths called *mikva'ot* for ceremonial purity. While historians debate whether Jewish baptism for Gentile converts predated John's ministry, the imagery of washing with water as a sign of cleansing was already deeply rooted in Jewish life.

John the Baptist took this familiar imagery and administered a unique, one-time baptism of repentance in the Jordan River to prepare Israel for the coming Messiah (Mark 1:4–5; Acts 19:4). Jesus came to be baptized by John not because He had any sin to confess, but to identify with sinners and fulfill all righteousness as He stepped into His public ministry, affirmed by the voice of the Father and the descent of the Holy Spirit (Matthew 3:13–17).

After His death and bodily resurrection, Jesus established Christian baptism for all nations in the Great Commission, commanding His apostles to make disciples and baptize them in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19–20). Under the New Covenant, water baptism serves as a visible sign of a believer's spiritual union with Christ in His death, burial, and resurrection (Romans 6:3–4; Colossians 2:12), pointing to the inward washing away of sin through faith in His saving work (Acts 22:16; 1 Peter 3:21). As Paul explains in Romans 6:4, remembering what baptism signifies calls believers to walk daily in a new way of life, resting in the grace that Christ has secured.
What is historical criticism?

Historical criticism, often called the historical-critical method or higher criticism, is an approach to studying ancient texts that investigates their origins, authorship, sources, and historical development using the tools of secular historical research. When applied to the Bible, it typically evaluates Scripture in the same way scholars examine any other ancient human writing, often separating the text from traditional beliefs about its divine origin.

While studying the genuine historical background of the Bible (such as Ancient Near Eastern customs or first-century Greco-Roman culture) greatly enriches our understanding, historical criticism frequently begins with naturalistic assumptions. For example, many practitioners rule out miracles or predictive prophecy before even reading the text, or they divide biblical books into speculative later sources rather than accepting the plain testimony of the text itself.

In contrast, historic Christianity affirms the inspiration and inerrancy of Scripture, meaning that God breathed out His Word through human authors so that the Bible is completely true and trustworthy in everything it affirms (2 Timothy 3:16; 2 Peter 1:20-21). Under the principle of *sola Scriptura* (Scripture alone as our ultimate authority), believers do not sit in judgment over the Bible. Instead, we receive its historical accounts, including the miracles and bodily resurrection of Jesus Christ, as real events that occurred in space and time (Luke 1:1-4; 1 Corinthians 15:3-8). Faithful biblical study uses a historical-grammatical approach, which carefully examines original languages, literary genres, and historical contexts in humble submission to the Bible's own authority.

As a practical step in your own study, consider using a trustworthy study Bible or historical commentary to learn about the background of a biblical book while continuing to read Scripture directly and prayerfully as God's faithful Word.
What does the Bible say about paying taxes?

The Bible clearly teaches that believers are to pay their taxes honestly and faithfully as a matter of obedience to God. Both Jesus and the Apostles affirmed that civil governments operate under God's sovereign authority, meaning citizens owe them due revenue while reserving ultimate allegiance for God alone.

In first-century Judea, Roman taxation was deeply resented by many Jews as a mark of pagan occupation. When religious leaders tried to trap Jesus on this controversial issue, He asked for a Roman denarius bearing Caesar's portrait and inscription, and replied, "Give to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's" (Matthew 22:15–21; Mark 12:13–17). Because the coin carried Caesar's stamp, it belonged to the civic sphere, whereas human beings bear the *imago Dei* (the image of God) and therefore owe their whole selves to their Creator. Elsewhere, even after affirming His unique freedom as the Son of God, Jesus willingly paid the temple tax so as not to cause unnecessary offense (Matthew 17:24–27).

The Apostle Paul further grounds this duty in God's providence and common grace, explaining that governing authorities are instituted by God as His servants to maintain order and restrain evil (Romans 13:1–4). Consequently, believers are to pay taxes not merely to avoid punishment, but "also because of conscience," giving everyone what is owed, including taxes and revenue (Romans 13:5–7). Peter echoes this call, urging Christians to submit to earthly authorities for the Lord's sake so that upright living honors Christ before a watching world (1 Peter 2:13–17).

Submitting to taxation does not mean Christians approve of everything a government does, and if a state ever commands believers to sin, they must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). Still, Scripture gives no license to withhold lawful taxes out of political frustration. Practically, you can honor the Lord by reporting your income with complete integrity and setting aside time this week to pray for your local and national leaders (1 Timothy 2:1–2).
Should Christian women wear pants?

Whether a Christian woman wears pants is a tertiary matter of Christian liberty (historically called *adiaphora*, or things neither commanded nor forbidden by God) where faithful believers may respectfully disagree. Scripture sets timeless principles for modesty and upholding God-given gender distinctions, yet it leaves room for varied application because specific styles of clothing differ across cultures and centuries.

Among Bible-believing Christians, there are two main convictions on this question. First, some believers hold that women should wear only skirts or dresses, appealing to Deuteronomy 22:5, which forbids a woman from wearing a man's garment and a man from wearing a woman's garment. From this perspective, wearing skirts or dresses maintains a clear, visible distinction between men and women in a culture that frequently blurs those lines. Second, many other Christians believe that pants tailored for women are entirely permissible. In the Ancient Near Eastern context of Deuteronomy 22:5, both men and women wore tunics and outer robes, meaning the command prohibited deceptive cross-dressing or rejecting one's created sex rather than outlawing a specific modern garment. Because women's trousers are widely recognized today as distinctly female attire, these believers conclude that wearing pants can fully honor the biblical call to dress respectably, with modesty and self-control (1 Timothy 2:9).

In matters where God's Word does not give a direct command, the Apostle Paul calls the church to practice Christian liberty with love (Romans 14:1-13). Each woman should be fully convinced in her own mind before the Lord, acting from a clear conscience and genuine faith (Romans 14:5; Romans 14:23). At the same time, those who feel free to wear pants must not look down on sisters who wear only skirts, and those who hold a stricter personal standard must not judge or bind the consciences of others where Scripture has left them free (Romans 14:3-4; Romans 14:13).

As a practical next step, evaluate your own wardrobe in prayer, asking God for wisdom so that your clothing reflects modesty, honors your God-given womanhood, and keeps the focus on the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit (1 Peter 3:3-4). Above all, pursue warm unity with the women in your local church, remembering that our standing before God rests entirely on the righteousness of Christ, not on the cut of our clothes.
Why wasn't Jesus named Immanuel?

In Scripture, "Immanuel" is a prophetic title describing Jesus' divine identity and mission as "God with us," rather than a requirement for His given legal name (Isaiah 7:14; Matthew 1:23). The angel specifically instructed Joseph to name the child Jesus, which comes from the Hebrew *Yeshua* and means "the LORD saves," because He would save His people from their sins (Matthew 1:21).

In the Ancient Near Eastern and Jewish context of the prophets, a promised "name" often functioned as a description of a person's character or what God would accomplish through them, rather than a personal name used in everyday speech. We see this same pattern when Isaiah prophesies that the coming king would be called "Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace" (Isaiah 9:6). Matthew highlights this fulfillment by translating *Immanuel* ("with us is God") for his readers, showing that Jesus Himself is the promised presence of God arriving to dwell among His people (Matthew 1:22–23; John 1:14).

Together, the name Jesus and the title Immanuel point directly to the incarnation and the hypostatic union, the foundational truth that Jesus Christ is one person who is truly God and truly man. Because He is truly God with us, His sinless life and sacrificial death on the cross are sufficient to reconcile sinners to a holy God, and His bodily resurrection secures forgiveness and eternal life for all who trust in Him (Romans 4:25; 2 Corinthians 5:19). 

Whenever you feel distant from God or weighed down by guilt, bring those burdens directly to Him in prayer, remembering that in Jesus, the Savior who died for you is also God personally present with you (Hebrews 4:14–16).
How is choosing a good name better than choosing riches (Proverbs 22:1)?

Choosing a good name is better than choosing riches because godly character and an honorable reputation endure long after material wealth fades or fails. In Proverbs 22:1, Scripture places higher value on moral integrity and genuine esteem than on silver and gold.

In the Ancient Near Eastern context of Israel's wisdom writings, the Hebrew word for "name" (*shem*) meant far more than a personal label; it signified a person's proven character, trustworthiness, and lasting legacy. Riches are fragile and can disappear quickly through crisis, theft, or foolishness (Proverbs 23:4–5), whereas a steady reputation builds trust within a community and outlives a person's earthly years (Ecclesiastes 7:1).

Theologically, a truly good name is not mere social polish, but the outward fruit of sanctification, as the Holy Spirit reshapes a believer's heart and habits after the righteousness of Christ (1 Thessalonians 4:3; Titus 2:7–8). Money can buy influence and temporary comfort, yet it cannot purchase a clear conscience or favor before God, who weighs faithfulness above outward wealth (Proverbs 16:2; Proverbs 11:4). Because Christians carry the name of Jesus into their homes and workplaces, living with quiet honesty and grace commends the truth of the Gospel to a watching world (1 Peter 2:12).

In daily life, choosing a good name means refusing to trade honesty, kindness, or a kept promise for a quicker profit or an easier path. For a practical step this week, pick one ordinary area of your routine, such as how you report your work hours, speak about someone who frustrates you, or follow through on a small promise at home, and deliberately choose complete truthfulness even if it costs you convenience or gain.
What is the lust of the eyes?

The "lust of the eyes" (translated "the desires of the eyes" in the Berean Standard Bible) is a sinful, disordered craving sparked by what we see, leading the heart to covet possessions, status, or sexual gratification rather than resting contentedly in God (1 John 2:16). Rather than simply appreciating the beauty God has made, it turns created things into idols that compete with our love for the Father.

In 1 John 2:15–17, the Apostle John warns believers living in a Greco-Roman world saturated with materialism and visual idolatry not to love the passing world. The Greek word behind "lust" or "desires" (*epithumia*) describes a strong, consuming longing or coveting, echoing the very first temptation in Eden when Eve saw that the forbidden fruit was "pleasing to the eyes" before she took it (Genesis 3:6). Jesus likewise exposed this inward root when He taught that looking at someone with lustful intent is already committing adultery in the heart (Matthew 5:28).

Historic Christian theology describes this internal pull toward forbidden or withheld things as *concupiscence* or covetousness, recognizing that outward sin begins in the desires of the heart (James 1:14–15). While every person falls short and struggles with wandering eyes and dissatisfied hearts, our hope rests in Jesus Christ, who faced every temptation without sinning and gave His life as a substitutionary sacrifice on the cross, rising bodily to secure forgiveness and new life for all who trust in Him (Hebrews 4:15; 1 John 2:1–2). Through justification by faith alone in Christ, our guilt is removed, and through the Holy Spirit's ongoing work of sanctification, God renews our affections so we prize Him above fleeting pleasures (1 John 2:17; Colossians 3:1–2).

As a practical step today, pray Psalm 119:37 directly to God, asking Him to turn your eyes away from worthless things, and pair that prayer with one clear boundary on the images, shopping, or media you place before your eyes this week.
What does the Bible say about Voodoo? How should a Christian view Voodoo?

While the Bible does not mention Voodoo by name because the practice developed centuries after Scripture was completed, God's Word clearly condemns all forms of spiritism, divination, sorcery, and the worship of any spirit besides the living God. A Christian must view Voodoo as a spiritually dangerous form of idolatry that stands in direct opposition to the Gospel of Jesus Christ, while still treating people involved in it with humility, patience, and genuine love.

Historically, Voodoo (or Vodou) emerged from West African spirit traditions blended with Roman Catholic imagery, a religious mixing known theologically as syncretism. In the ancient world, Israel was surrounded by nations that practiced similar rituals to appease spirits, seek hidden knowledge, or manipulate circumstances. God strictly forbade His people from imitating those ways, declaring that anyone who practices divination, sorcery, casts spells, or consults the dead is detestable to the Lord (Deuteronomy 18:10–12). In the Greco-Roman context of the New Testament, the Apostle Paul likewise listed "idolatry" and "sorcery" (from the Greek word *pharmakeia*, referring to magic potions, spells, and occult practices) as sins that keep people from inheriting God's kingdom (Galatians 5:19–21). Scripture warns that spirit invocation is never a harmless cultural tradition, because behind false gods stand real demonic forces, and a believer cannot partake of both the Lord's table and the table of demons (1 Corinthians 10:20–21).

With that biblical foundation, a Christian should respond to Voodoo with both clarity and compassion:

*   **Recognize the practice as sin:** Voodoo violates the foundational command to worship God alone (Exodus 20:3). Christians must never participate in it, wear protective charms, or seek spiritual guidance through mediums or rituals, even out of curiosity.
*   **Rest in the supremacy of Christ:** Believers do not need to live in terror of curses or evil spirits. Through His substitutionary atonement on the cross and His bodily resurrection, Jesus Christ disarmed and triumphed over every spiritual ruler and authority (Colossians 2:15). He rescues His people from the dominion of darkness and brings them into His kingdom (Colossians 1:13).
*   **Show love and share the Gospel:** Many people turn to Voodoo out of fear, desperation, or a longing for protection and healing in a broken world. Rather than mocking or fearing them, Christians should pray for them and point them to the one true Mediator between God and humanity, the Lord Jesus Christ (1 Timothy 2:5). Anyone caught in occult practices can find complete forgiveness and freedom by repenting of sin and trusting in Christ alone, whose blood cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7).

As a practical step, if you or someone you know has ever dabbled in Voodoo or kept items tied to occult practices, follow the example of the early believers in Ephesus who openly renounced their past and destroyed their magic scrolls when they turned to Jesus (Acts 19:18–19). Remove any objects associated with those rituals, pray directly to God asking for His cleansing and protection, and seek steady discipleship and support from pastors and mature believers in a faithful local church.
What is the meaning of Lent?

Lent is a historic forty-day season (excluding Sundays) observed by many Christians leading up to Easter, set aside for prayer, fasting, and repentance in preparation for remembering the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ. The word "Lent" derives from an old English term meaning "spring," pointing to the season of lengthening days in which it occurs.

In the early centuries of the church, this forty-day period developed as a time of instruction and fasting for those preparing to be baptized at Easter, intentionally echoing Israel's forty years in the wilderness and Jesus' forty days of fasting before His public ministry (Matthew 4:1–11). While Scripture encourages fasting and humble repentance as genuine expressions of devotion to God (Joel 2:12–13; Matthew 6:16–18), the New Testament nowhere commands an annual forty-day liturgical fast.

Because the observance of Lent rests on church tradition rather than an explicit biblical command, it is a non-essential matter in which faithful Christians hold different practices. Many believers in liturgical traditions, such as Anglicans and Lutherans, observe Lent through structured fasting, confession, and setting aside certain comforts to remind themselves of their daily dependence on God. Conversely, many Reformed and Baptist Christians do not observe Lent as a formal church season, preferring to emphasize that every Sunday already celebrates Christ's resurrection and wishing to guard against turning voluntary traditions into binding spiritual duties (Colossians 2:16–17).

In matters of calendar and custom, Scripture upholds the principle of Christian liberty: one believer may set aside a specific season to honor the Lord, while another treats every day alike, and neither should judge or look down on the other (Romans 14:5–6). Whatever practice a believer follows, the true purpose of any spiritual discipline is to serve our ongoing sanctification, turning our hearts away from self-reliance and fixing our hope on the finished work of Christ.

Whether you formally observe Lent or simply cultivate steady rhythms of devotion throughout the year, a helpful concrete step is to spend fifteen minutes a day reading slowly through the Gospel accounts of Jesus' final week, letting His sacrificial love lead you into fresh gratitude and repentance.
What doth every sin deserve?

Every sin deserves God's righteous wrath and curse, both in this present life and in the life to come (Ephesians 5:6; Galatians 3:10). Because God is infinitely holy and just, any rebellion against Him, no matter how small it may seem to human eyes, earns spiritual and eternal death (Romans 6:23).

In the New Testament, the primary word for sin (*hamartia*) means missing the mark of God's perfect standard, while sin is also described as crossing the boundary of His revealed law (Romans 5:14). Within the Old Testament covenant framework, breaking God's law brought the covenant curses of judgment and separation from His blessed presence (Deuteronomy 27:26; Galatians 3:10). Historic Christian theology summarizes this sobering reality under God's *retributive justice*, meaning a holy Judge cannot simply ignore guilt without denying His own righteousness.

Yet the astonishing good news of Scripture is that God Himself provided the rescue we could never earn. Jesus Christ, the eternal Son of God who took on human flesh and lived a sinless life, stood in the place of sinners through *penal substitution*. On the cross, He bore the full weight of the wrath and curse our sins deserved as a *propitiation* (a wrath-absorbing sacrifice), and He was buried and raised bodily on the third day in victory over sin and death (Galatians 3:13; Romans 3:25; 1 Corinthians 15:3–4). All who belong to Him receive *justification*, being declared righteous by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, rather than by their own works (Ephesians 2:8–9; Romans 5:1).

Practically, remembering what every sin deserves keeps us from making light of daily temptations, such as bitterness or pride, and moves us to confess our sins honestly to God rather than hiding in shame (1 John 1:9). Turn from your sin today and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose again for you, to receive full forgiveness and new life. As you reflect on this truth, how does knowing that Christ bore the curse of sin shape the way you view your standing before God right now?
What does the Bible say about diligence?

The Bible teaches that diligence is steady, purposeful, and wholehearted faithfulness in both our daily work and our spiritual walk, carried out ultimately to honor God rather than to impress people. Throughout Scripture, diligence is praised as the path of wisdom and fruitful stewardship, while laziness and carelessness are warned against as destructive (Proverbs 10:4; Colossians 3:23).

In Old Testament wisdom literature, especially Proverbs, diligence is tied closely to the created order of cause and effect in God's world. The Hebrew word frequently used for "diligent" (*charuts*) carries the sense of being sharp, decisive, and industrious, describing someone who plans thoughtfully and works steadily rather than rushing blindly or idling away opportunity (Proverbs 12:24; Proverbs 21:5). This effort applies not only to physical labor and provision, where "the soul of the diligent is fully satisfied" (Proverbs 13:4), but also to our inner spiritual life, as Scripture commands us to "guard your heart with all diligence, for from it flow springs of life" (Proverbs 4:23).

In the New Testament, the Greek word often translated as diligence or earnestness (*spoude*) highlights an eager, attentive devotion to Christ. Paul reminds believers not to let their zeal subside, but to maintain spiritual fervor in serving the Lord (Romans 12:11), working at every earthly task with their whole being as service to Christ Himself (Colossians 3:23). Similarly, Peter urges Christians to "make every effort" to grow in virtue, knowledge, self-control, and love, confirming their calling in Christ (2 Peter 1:5–7; 2 Peter 1:10), and the author of Hebrews calls believers to show diligence to the very end so that their hope remains sure (Hebrews 6:11).

Theologically, biblical diligence belongs to sanctification and Christian vocation, never justification. We are saved and declared righteous by grace alone through faith alone in Christ, not by our own hard work (Ephesians 2:8–9). Yet because God has rescued us and called us His own, diligence becomes the joyful fruit of a transformed heart, expressing faithful stewardship of the time, gifts, and responsibilities He entrusts to us.

To put this into practice this week, choose one neglected responsibility in your home, work, or church life, and commit to completing it steadily each day with prayerful focus, offering that ordinary labor to the Lord as an act of worship.
What is agnosticism?

Agnosticism is the view that the existence of God, or the ultimate truth about the divine, is either currently unknown or inherently unknowable. The word comes from the Greek term *agnostos*, meaning "unknown," and was coined in 1869 by English biologist Thomas Henry Huxley to describe suspending judgment on claims that cannot be verified through physical observation.

Historically, this posture of uncertainty regarding the divine is not new. When the Apostle Paul visited Athens in the first century, he walked through a city filled with idols and noticed an altar bearing the inscription, "TO AN UNKNOWN GOD" (Acts 17:23), which uses that same Greek root. Rather than dismissing their curiosity, Paul addressed their uncertainty by proclaiming that the Creator is near and desires to be found by those who seek Him (Acts 17:27).

From a biblical perspective, while finite human minds can never exhaustively comprehend an infinite God through unaided wisdom (Job 11:7; Romans 11:33), God has deliberately made Himself known. Theologians describe this in two categories: *general revelation* and *special revelation*. Through general revelation, God clearly displays His eternal power and divine nature in the created world so that humanity is without excuse (Psalm 19:1–2; Romans 1:19–20). Through special revelation, God speaks clearly in the Scriptures and ultimately through the incarnation of His Son, Jesus Christ, who visibly reveals the Father (John 1:18; Hebrews 1:1–3).

In practice, rather than settling into permanent uncertainty, someone exploring agnosticism can take the concrete step of reading the Gospel of John to examine the historical life, teaching, and claims of Jesus firsthand.
What does it mean to “be angry and do not sin” (Psalm 4:4)?

To "be angry and do not sin" (Psalm 4:4) means that feeling deep agitation or moral outrage over sin and injustice is not automatically sinful, so long as you restrain that emotion before it turns into bitterness, malice, or vengeance. Rather than lashing out in fleshly wrath, believers are called to bring their troubled hearts quietly before God and entrust justice to Him.

In the historical setting of Psalm 4, King David is praying amid slander and distress, addressing people whose honor was being turned into shame (Psalm 4:2). The Hebrew verb translated "be angry" (*ragaz*) literally means to tremble or be deeply agitated, and the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament rendered it as "be angry," which the Apostle Paul later quotes directly in Ephesians 4:26.

Scripture draws a vital line between righteous anger, which echoes God's own holiness and hatred of evil, and sinful human anger, which does not produce the righteousness God desires (James 1:19–20). Because our fallen hearts easily turn even a legitimate grievance into pride or self-centered retaliation, Paul warns us not to let the sun go down on our anger, lest we give the devil a foothold (Ephesians 4:26–27). In the lifelong work of sanctification, the Holy Spirit reshapes our emotions after the pattern of Jesus Christ, who felt righteous indignation at hardness of heart without ever committing a single sin (Mark 3:5). David provides the steady antidote right in the surrounding verses: instead of nursing wrath, we are to search our hearts silently on our beds, offer righteous sacrifices, and trust in the Lord (Psalm 4:4–5).

Practically, the next time you feel a surge of anger over a genuine wrong, pause before speaking or sending a sharp reply, examine your own motives privately before God in prayer, and deliberately surrender any desire to get even.
How will the covenant with death be annulled (Isaiah 28:18)?

In Isaiah 28:18, God Himself annuls (or dissolves) the covenant with death by sending His righteous judgment through the overwhelming scourge of an invading army, which sweeps away Judah's false refuge and tramples their defenses (Isaiah 28:17–18). Because no human scheme can bargain with death or outmaneuver the sovereign Lord, He uses justice as a measuring line and righteousness as a plumb line to expose and shatter every false source of security (Isaiah 28:17).

In the historical setting of the late eighth century BC, the scoffing rulers of Jerusalem boasted that their political scheming, particularly a hoped-for alliance with Egypt against the Assyrian Empire, had bought them immunity from disaster (Isaiah 28:14–15; Isaiah 30:1–3). They arrogantly called this deceptive strategy a covenant with death and an agreement with Sheol, the grave, believing the coming catastrophe would pass them by (Isaiah 28:15). God declared that their refuge of lies would offer no shelter when the floodwaters of His judgment swept through the land (Isaiah 28:17–19).

Yet right before pronouncing this judgment, the Lord pointed to the only true shelter by promising to lay a tested, precious cornerstone in Zion, declaring that the one who believes will never be shaken (Isaiah 28:16). The New Testament identifies that cornerstone as Jesus Christ (Romans 9:33; 1 Peter 2:6). While human bargains with death collapse under divine wrath, death itself is finally conquered through Christ's penal substitutionary atonement on the cross and His bodily resurrection, which disarm death's power for all who are united to Him by faith (1 Corinthians 15:54–57; Hebrews 2:14–15). Instead of placing your confidence in earthly stability, human wisdom, or personal morality, rest your hope daily in Jesus Christ, the unshakable Cornerstone, who alone delivers sinners from sin and eternal death.
What is the Hindu caste system?

The Hindu caste system is a traditional social hierarchy in South Asia that divides people into hereditary groups based on birth, occupation, and concepts of ritual purity. Rooted in ancient Hindu texts and linked to beliefs about *karma* (actions and their consequences) and *dharma* (religious and social duty), it broadly organizes society into four main categories called *varnas*: Brahmins (priests and teachers), Kshatriyas (rulers and warriors), Vaishyas (merchants and farmers), and Shudras (laborers and servants). Outside and beneath these four tiers are the Dalits, historically referred to as "untouchables," while in everyday life the system functions through thousands of localized sub-castes known as *jatis*. Although India's constitution outlawed caste-based discrimination in 1950, the cultural and social effects of the system still influence areas such as marriage, status, and community life.

From a biblical perspective, while Christians are called to treat our Hindu neighbors with genuine respect and kindness, Scripture presents a fundamentally different foundation for human worth through the doctrine of the *imago Dei* (the image of God). The Bible teaches that every human being, regardless of family line, occupation, or social standing, is created in the image of God and carries equal, inherent dignity (Genesis 1:27). God does not show favoritism based on earthly rank, and through Jesus Christ, social and ethnic divisions are broken down so that all who belong to Him stand on equal footing by grace (Acts 10:34–35; Galatians 3:28). In daily life, this truth calls believers to actively reject social partiality (James 2:1–4) and to honor and serve every person with humility and love.
What does the Bible say about rest and relaxation?

Scripture presents rest and relaxation not as laziness or a selfish luxury, but as a gracious gift woven into the very fabric of God's creation. Because we are finite creatures rather than the Creator, pausing from our labor reflects our trust in God's providence and points us toward the deeper spiritual rest found in Jesus Christ.

From the beginning, God built a rhythm of work and cessation into human life. After six days of creation, God rested on the seventh day and blessed it (Genesis 2:2–3). The Hebrew word for this rest (*shabbat*) simply means to cease or stop. God did not stop because He was exhausted, since He never grows weary (Isaiah 40:28), but to set a pattern for humanity and to invite us to delight in His finished work. Later, the Psalms remind us that anxious overwork is futile because God provides for His people even while they sleep (Psalm 127:2) and grants peaceful rest under His watchful care (Psalm 4:8). Choosing to step back and relax is a quiet confession that God is sovereign and that the world does not depend on our constant striving.

Jesus Himself modeled intentional withdrawal and refreshment during His earthly ministry. When His disciples returned worn out from teaching and serving, He did not rebuke them for their limits, but invited them to go privately to a solitary place and rest for a while (Mark 6:31). Jesus also regularly stepped away from the crowds to pray in quiet places (Luke 5:16), reminding us that rest for the body and renewal for the soul belong together. While New Covenant believers enjoy Christian liberty regarding which specific day they set apart for rest and worship (Romans 14:5–6; Colossians 2:16–17), Jesus affirmed the lasting principle that God designed rest as a blessing for our good, not a burden (Mark 2:27).

Ultimately, every physical nap, quiet afternoon, and day off serves as a small signpost pointing to the gospel. Jesus calls out to those who are weighed down by life and guilt, promising to give them true rest for their souls (Matthew 11:28–30). Through justification by faith alone, believers cease from the exhausting effort of trying to earn God's approval by their own works and enter into the lasting spiritual rest secured by Christ's death and resurrection (Hebrews 4:9–10). 

As a practical next step this week, try setting aside one deliberate, unhurried block of time where you turn off notifications and step away from chores or work. Use that quiet space to enjoy something simple God has made, share an unhurried meal with loved ones, and read through Psalm 23 in prayer to remind your heart that the Lord is your Shepherd who leads you beside quiet waters.
What is deism? What do deists believe?

Deism is the belief that a supreme God created the universe and set its natural laws in motion, then withdrew from active involvement in the world. Deists hold that human reason and observation of nature are sufficient to recognize a Creator, while rejecting miracles, answered prayer, and supernatural revelation such as the Bible.

Often illustrated by a watchmaker who builds and winds a clock before leaving it to run on its own, deism gained influence during the 17th and 18th century Enlightenment. Core deist beliefs generally include:

* **A distant Creator:** God designed an orderly cosmos, yet He does not intervene in human history or personal affairs.
* **Reason over Scripture:** Knowledge of God and morality come strictly from human reason and the natural world rather than from prophetic writings or inspired texts.
* **Denial of miracles and Christ's deity:** Deists reject supernatural events, the virgin birth, the bodily resurrection, and the biblical truth that Jesus Christ is truly God and truly man, viewing Him at most as a moral teacher.

Scripture presents a strikingly different picture of the living God. While the Bible affirms that creation clearly displays God's eternal power and divine nature, a truth theologians call general revelation (Psalm 19:1; Romans 1:19–20), it teaches that God is intimately near rather than detached. He actively governs all creation through His sovereign providence, sustaining the universe moment by moment by His powerful word (Psalm 103:19; Colossians 1:17; Hebrews 1:3).

Even more wonderfully, God did not leave humanity to guess about Him through fallen reason alone. Through special revelation, He has spoken infallibly in Scripture (2 Timothy 3:16) and stepped directly into human history in the incarnation, when the eternal Son took on human flesh to die for sin and rise again so that sinners might be reconciled to God (John 1:14; Hebrews 1:1–2; Romans 5:8). Practically, remembering this guards believers against living as "functional deists," encouraging us to pray with confidence and cast every daily anxiety on a Heavenly Father who genuinely hears and cares for His people (Matthew 6:26–30; 1 Peter 5:7) in every ordinary moment.
Is the distinction between clergy and laity biblical?

A rigid, two-tiered divide between a sacred "clergy" and an ordinary "laity" is not biblical, though Scripture clearly establishes distinct leadership offices alongside the equal spiritual standing of all believers. Historic Christian traditions that maintain a sharper clergy and laity distinction do so out of reverence for Christ's delegated authority, believing that formally ordained ministers are uniquely set apart to guard sound doctrine and faithfully administer the Word and sacraments for the protection of the church. 

Within historic Christianity, a Reformed Baptist understanding offers one faithful approach by affirming the priesthood of all believers alongside the functional offices of elders and deacons, rather than a spiritual caste system. In the New Testament, the Greek word *laos* simply refers to the entire people of God (1 Peter 2:9–10), while *kleros* (from which the English word "clergy" derives) refers to an allotted inheritance and is used by Peter to describe the whole flock entrusted to leaders, not a separate priestly class (1 Peter 5:3). Because Christ has become our sole Great High Priest under the New Covenant, every believer has direct access to God and shares the sacred privilege of offering spiritual sacrifices to Him (Hebrews 4:14–16; 1 Peter 2:5; 1 Peter 2:9).

At the same time, equality of standing in Christ does not erase order or distinct calling in the local church. Christ gives biblically qualified elders (also called overseers) and deacons to shepherd, teach, and serve the congregation, equipping all the saints for works of service (Ephesians 4:11–12; 1 Timothy 3:1–13; Titus 1:5–9).
