In daily life, this means you can approach your everyday work, hospitality, and gospel witness as genuine ministry before God, while joyfully honoring and submitting to the spiritual oversight of faithful elders in your local church (Hebrews 13:17).
What does it mean to have a wilderness experience?

A "wilderness experience" refers to a season of spiritual dryness, testing, or hardship through which God leads His people to strip away self-reliance and deepen their trust in Him. Far from indicating divine abandonment, Scripture presents the wilderness as a purposeful instrument of God's providence and sanctification.

In the Ancient Near East, the Hebrew word for wilderness (*midbar*) described arid, uninhabited regions where survival was impossible without constant provision. When God led Israel through the desert for forty years, He humbled and tested them to reveal what was in their hearts and to teach them that people do not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of the Lord (Deuteronomy 8:2–3). Later, the prophet Hosea portrayed the wilderness as a place of tender mercy where God draws His people away from earthly distractions to speak gently to their hearts (Hosea 2:14).

The New Testament brings this pattern to its fulfillment in Jesus Christ, who was led by the Spirit into the wilderness for forty days to be tempted by the devil (Matthew 4:1–11). Where Israel faltered in unbelief, Christ obeyed perfectly, demonstrating His sinless righteousness and becoming a sympathetic High Priest who understands our weakness when we face trial (Hebrews 4:15). Through union with Christ, believers can recognize difficult seasons not as meaningless suffering, but as part of progressive sanctification, the Spirit's refining work that proves our faith and shapes us into the image of Christ (1 Peter 1:6–7; Romans 8:28–29).

In everyday Christian life, a wilderness season might look like prolonged grief, unanswered prayer, or feeling spiritually numb during ordinary routines. If you are walking through such a season, resist the urge to measure God's love by your fluctuating emotions; instead, anchor your days by reading one Psalm each morning (such as Psalm 63) to guide your own prayers, and share what you are facing with a pastor or mature believer in your local church so they can stand with you in prayer (James 5:16).
What does Malachi 2:16 mean when God says, ‘I hate divorce’?

In Malachi 2:16, God declares His strong opposition to the treacherous breaking of the marriage covenant, condemning men in Judah who were abandoning their wives for selfish and idolatrous reasons. Because marriage is a sacred covenant witnessed by God Himself (Malachi 2:14), tearing it apart through unfaithfulness and cruelty strikes against God's own faithful character.

Writing to post-exilic Judah, Malachi addresses a widespread sin in which Israelite men were divorcing the wives of their youth in order to marry women who worshipped foreign gods (Malachi 2:11; Malachi 2:14–15). In this same verse, God rebukes the man who "covers his garment with violence" (Malachi 2:16), drawing on the Ancient Near Eastern custom in which a man's garment symbolized marital shelter and protection (Ruth 3:9), so to cover it with violence meant turning a promise of care into an act of betrayal. (Some Hebrew scholars note that the opening clause can also be translated as a warning against the husband who "hates and divorces" his wife, though either translation affirms the same truth: God fiercely opposes treacherous divorce.)

This passage underscores the biblical teaching that marriage is a creation ordinance established by God as a lifelong covenant (Genesis 2:24; Matthew 19:4–6). Far from being a temporary human contract, marriage is meant to reflect God's own covenant faithfulness and, as the New Testament reveals, Christ's sacrificial love for His Church (Ephesians 5:25–32). Because God hates the sin of covenant-breaking and the harm it brings, Scripture treats divorce as a serious moral tragedy, permitting it only in specific, painful situations such as sexual immorality or desertion by an unbelieving spouse (Matthew 19:9; 1 Corinthians 7:15).

At the same time, God's hatred of divorce does not mean He lacks compassion for those who have suffered through it or who carry regret over past failures. If you are facing strain in your marriage or carrying the weight of a past divorce, take the concrete step of meeting with a trusted pastor or mature believer in your local church for prayerful counsel and support. Above all, remember that no sin or broken relationship is beyond the reach of Jesus Christ, whose substitutionary death on the cross and bodily resurrection provide complete forgiveness, healing, and strength for all who turn to Him in repentance and faith (1 John 1:9; Romans 8:1).
How transparent should church finances be?

Church finances should be thoroughly transparent, accountable, and open to the congregation, reflecting the biblical call to faithful stewardship. While Scripture does not prescribe a specific accounting software or spreadsheet format, it clearly requires church leaders to manage God's resources in a manner that is above reproach before both the Lord and the watching world.

In the first-century Greco-Roman world, suspicions of financial self-dealing among religious teachers and fund collectors were widespread. When the Apostle Paul organized a major relief collection for struggling believers in Jerusalem, he refused to handle the funds alone, instead arranging for trusted representatives chosen by the churches to travel alongside him (2 Corinthians 8:18–21). Paul explained that he took these precautions so that no one could criticize their administration of the gift, seeking to do what was honorable not only in the eyes of the Lord, but also in the eyes of men (2 Corinthians 8:20–21). Earlier in Jerusalem, the apostles likewise instituted shared financial oversight by appointing seven men of proven character to manage daily benevolence distributions (Acts 6:1–6).

From a theological standpoint, this practice flows directly from the biblical doctrine of stewardship and the qualifications for church leadership. Because every tithe and offering belongs to the Lord and not to the pastor or board, stewards are required to be found trustworthy (1 Corinthians 4:2). Elders and deacons must be above reproach and free from the love of money (1 Timothy 3:2–3; 1 Timothy 3:8). Healthy transparency protects both the flock from abuse and the shepherds from unfair accusation. In practical terms, this means a church should maintain clear internal controls (such as dual-signature checks and independent counting teams), conduct regular external audits or financial reviews, and provide members with understandable financial reports.

At the same time, faithful churches with different approaches to church polity sometimes apply transparency in slightly different ways. Many congregational churches distribute detailed, line-item budgets and monthly reports for the entire membership to review and vote upon, while some elder-led churches present broader spending categories to the congregation and entrust sensitive details, such as individual staff salaries, to an elected finance committee or diaconate to protect personal privacy. Regardless of the exact structure, no healthy church should keep secret accounts, withhold budgets from members who ask, or concentrate financial authority in the hands of one person.

As a practical next step, if you are a church member wondering about your congregation's finances, gently ask an elder, deacon, or church treasurer if you may review the current annual budget and learn what safeguards are in place. If you serve in church leadership, consider scheduling an annual independent financial review and inviting a member of the finance team to walk the congregation through a clear, unhurried financial update each year so everyone can rejoice together in God's provision.
Is intinction the correct way to do communion?

Intinction, the practice of dipping the bread into the wine rather than taking them separately, is one historic way Christians observe Communion, though it is not the only or most biblically direct method. Many faithful believers, such as Anglicans and Eastern Orthodox Christians, practice intinction out of deep reverence to prevent spilling the wine, promote hygiene, and symbolize the unity of Christ's body and blood in a single act.

From a Reformed Baptist perspective, taking the bread and the cup separately is a more faithful way to observe this ordinance, though it stands as one conscientious approach among other valid traditions within historic Christianity. In the original Second Temple Jewish context of the Passover meal, Jesus distributed the unleavened bread and the cup as two distinct acts, with the cup explicitly given "after supper" (Luke 22:20; 1 Corinthians 11:25). When Christ commanded His disciples to "Take and eat" the bread and then to "Drink from it, all of you" regarding the cup, He established two separate visible signs that proclaim His broken body and shed blood until He returns (Matthew 26:26–27; 1 Corinthians 11:26).

Ultimately, the Lord's Supper is a spiritual means of grace in which believers commune with Christ by faith, rather than a ritual whose power depends on one specific technique of distribution. Because Scripture emphasizes heartfelt faith and discerning the Lord's body rather than binding every logistical detail of how the elements are handed out (1 Corinthians 11:27–29; Romans 14:5–6), you can receive Communion by intinction with a clear conscience if your church practices it, or speak kindly with your pastor if you wish to understand your congregation's practice more fully.
What is the church suffering?

The church's suffering takes two primary forms: external persecution from a world opposed to Christ, and internal trials such as false teaching, division, and spiritual compromise. Because Scripture describes the church as the body of Christ on earth, believers inevitably share in the rejection that Jesus Himself experienced (`2 Timothy 3:12`; `John 15:18-20`).

In the first-century Greco-Roman world, early Christians suffered social ostracism, economic loss, imprisonment, and even death because their confession of Jesus as Lord clashed with pagan idolatry and loyalty to the emperor (`1 Peter 4:12-14`). Theologically, this hardship is rooted in our union with Christ, and God uses it for our sanctification, refining our faith like gold in a furnace so that we cling to Him rather than this passing world (`Romans 8:17`; `1 Peter 1:6-7`). Today, many brothers and sisters around the globe still face violent persecution, while churches in more comfortable settings often suffer spiritually from worldliness, doctrinal drift, and neglect of the Gospel (`Revelation 2:4-5`; `2 Timothy 4:3-4`).

As a faithful response, we can make it a regular habit to pray by name for persecuted Christians worldwide and to stay deeply rooted in a local, Bible-teaching church where believers bear one another's burdens (`Hebrews 13:3`; `Galatians 6:2`).

What does it mean that a person will not inherit the kingdom of God (1 Corinthians 6:9-11)?

To "not inherit the kingdom of God" in 1 Corinthians 6:9–11 means that people whose lives are characterized by unrepentant, habitual sin do not belong to God's saving rule now and will be excluded from eternal life in His coming kingdom. It is a solemn warning that unrighteousness cannot enter God's holy presence, paired with a glorious promise of transformation for those who trust in Christ.

In the Greco-Roman city of Corinth, idolatry and sexual immorality were woven into daily culture, and some professing believers were tempted to excuse sinful lifestyles or treat them lightly. Drawing on the Old Testament image of Israel receiving the promised land, the New Testament uses the phrase "inherit the kingdom" to describe God's children receiving eternal salvation, while the wording in 1 Corinthians 6:9–10 points to an ongoing, defining pattern of life rather than a believer's occasional stumble.

Paul explicitly names sins such as sexual immorality, idolatry, adultery, homosexual acts, theft, greed, drunkenness, verbal abuse, and swindling (1 Corinthians 6:9–10). Scripture does not soften these behaviors; they are rebellion against a holy God whose wrath against sin is real (Ephesians 5:5–6; Galatians 5:19–21). Anyone who persists in these practices without repentance shows that they have not experienced *regeneration* (being born again by the Holy Spirit) and remain outside the saving reign of Christ.

Yet Paul immediately follows this warning with the breathtaking hope of the Gospel: "And that is what some of you were. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God" (1 Corinthians 6:11). Historic Christian theology summarizes these two distinct blessings as *justification* (God's legal declaration that a sinner is righteous through Christ's substitutionary death and bodily resurrection) and *sanctification* (the Spirit's ongoing work of setting believers apart and renewing their desires and habits). True Christians still battle temptation and grieve when they stumble, yet they are no longer enslaved to or defined by their former sins because Christ has made them new (Romans 6:17–18; 2 Corinthians 5:17).

Practically, this passage calls us to examine our hearts honestly rather than presuming on God's grace while harboring unrepentant sin; if you recognize ongoing patterns of sin in your life, bring them into the light through confession to God and accountability within a faithful local church. No matter your past or present struggle, Jesus Christ died on the cross for sinners and rose bodily from the dead so that the unrighteous can be forgiven, cleansed, and welcomed as His children. Turn from your sin in repentance and trust in Jesus Christ alone for forgiveness and new life in His kingdom.

Is it wise for Christian teens to be dating?

Scripture does not lay down a strict rule either forbidding or requiring teenage dating, which makes this an area of Christian wisdom and liberty where faithful families can reach different conclusions. Whether dating is wise for a Christian teen depends largely on their spiritual maturity, their readiness to pursue marriage in the foreseeable future, and their commitment to honoring God in purity.

Within Christianity, believers generally take one of two thoughtful approaches to this question. Many parents and pastors encourage teens to wait until young adulthood to date, noting that romance naturally awakens deep emotional and physical desires best reserved for a season when marriage is a realistic goal (Song of Solomon 8:4; Proverbs 4:23). Other faithful Christians allow supervised, intentional dating during the teen years, viewing it as a helpful way to practice godly communication, discernment, and relational maturity under the guidance of parents (Proverbs 1:8–9; Ephesians 6:1–3). Because the Bible does not prescribe one specific timeline or courtship method, believers should exercise charity toward different family convictions rather than turning a matter of wisdom into a test of faithfulness (Romans 14:1–5).

At the same time, God's moral standards for relationships are clear and unchanging. Every believer is called to progressive sanctification, which means growing by the Spirit in self-control and holiness in how we treat one another (1 Thessalonians 4:3–5). Writing to a young pastor about life inside the church family, Paul urges believers to flee youthful passions and to treat one another as brothers and sisters in Christ with absolute purity (2 Timothy 2:22; 1 Timothy 5:1–2). A concrete way to apply this is to prioritize group activities and public settings rather than isolated one-on-one time, keeping accountability natural and guarding against emotional or physical compromises that belong only in marriage.

As a practical next step, sit down with your parents or a mature believer in your local church to pray together, seek wise counsel, and establish clear biblical boundaries before entering any romantic relationship (Proverbs 15:22). Why does God allow us to go through trials and tribulations?

Trials and tribulations are genuinely painful realities in a fallen world, yet God allows them in His wise providence to refine our faith, conform us to the image of Christ, and display His sustaining grace in our weakness.

Scripture reveals several clear purposes behind the hardships we endure:

* **Spiritual maturity and sanctification:** God uses difficulty to strip away spiritual complacency and deepen our trust in Him. Writing to early Jewish Christians scattered by persecution and poverty, James uses a Greek word (*peirasmos*) for trials that refers to a testing process meant to prove genuineness, much like gold being purified by fire (James 1:2–4; 1 Peter 1:6–7). In Christian theology, this reflects the ongoing work of **sanctification**, through which the Holy Spirit transforms believers into the likeness of Christ (Romans 8:28–29).
* **Deeper dependence on God:** Hardship exposes how fragile our self-sufficiency really is, teaching us to rely on the Lord's strength rather than our own (2 Corinthians 1:8–9; 2 Corinthians 12:9).
* **Compassion for others:** When God sustains us through dark seasons, He equips us to comfort other hurting people with the same grace we have received from Him (2 Corinthians 1:3–4).

It is equally important to remember that God's **sovereignty** over trials never means He is cold or distant toward our pain. The cross of Christ proves that God steps directly into human suffering. Jesus, the sinless Son of God, endured betrayal, agony, and death on the cross for our sins, and rose bodily from the grave so that all who repent and trust in Him receive forgiveness and eternal life (Isaiah 53:3–5; 1 Corinthians 15:3–4). Because He Himself suffered, He stands as our compassionate High Priest who truly understands our frailty and invites us to draw near for mercy (Hebrews 4:15–16).

As a concrete next step today, bring your honest questions and burdens directly to God rather than carrying them in silence. Set aside ten minutes to read Psalm 23 or Psalm 42 slowly, turning each line into your own personal prayer for strength, and reach out to a mature believer or pastor in your local church who can walk with you and pray for you (James 5:16) during this season.

What does Deuteronomy 10:12 tell us God requires of us?

Deuteronomy 10:12 teaches that God requires His people to fear Him, walk in all His ways, love Him, and serve Him with all their heart and soul (Deuteronomy 10:12). The following verse completes the sentence by adding that they are to keep His commandments and statutes for their own good (Deuteronomy 10:13).

Moses spoke these words on the plains of Moab as Israel prepared to enter the Promised Land, using the pattern of Ancient Near Eastern covenant treaties in which a sovereign king called his people to loyal devotion. In this covenant context, "fearing" the Lord does not mean cowering in hopeless terror, but holding Him in deep, reverent awe that expresses itself in affectionate loyalty and wholehearted obedience.

Crucially, Moses places this call immediately after reminding Israel of God's unmerited grace in choosing them and forgiving their idolatry with the golden calf (Deuteronomy 10:1–11; Deuteronomy 10:14–15). This order highlights the vital theological distinction between justification and sanctification: sinners are never declared righteous before God by keeping the law, for justification is by grace alone through faith alone in Jesus Christ (Romans 3:28; Galatians 2:16). Rather, those whom Christ has redeemed by His atoning death and resurrection grow in sanctification, learning to love and obey God because He first loved us (1 John 4:19). Jesus Himself affirmed the enduring heart of this passage when He taught that loving God with all our heart, soul, and mind is the first and greatest commandment (Deuteronomy 6:5; Matthew 22:37–38).

In daily life, this means your faithfulness in ordinary responsibilities, whether speaking truthfully at work, showing patience at home, or turning away from sin, is meant to be an act of grateful worship rather than a burden to earn God's favor. As a simple next step, read Deuteronomy 10:12–22 slowly today and pray directly to God, asking Him to deepen your reverence for His holiness and your gratitude for His mercy in Christ.
Is it okay to get tattoos if they are of a Christian nature?

Whether a Christian may get a tattoo, even one of a Christian nature, is a non-essential matter of Christian liberty on which faithful believers hold different convictions. Scripture does not give a direct New Testament command either forbidding or endorsing modern tattoos, so Christians arrive at different conclusions depending on how they apply Old Testament context and New Testament principles of stewardship and conscience.

Many Christians believe that getting a tasteful, Christ-honoring tattoo is permissible. In its original Ancient Near Eastern setting, the command in Leviticus 19:28 against cutting the flesh or making tattoo marks was specifically tied to pagan mourning rituals for the dead, warning Israel not to imitate the idolatrous practices of surrounding nations. Viewing that restriction as bound to Israel's distinct ceremonial separation, these believers see a Christian tattoo under the New Covenant as a lawful personal expression of faith or a natural bridge for Gospel conversations, provided it is done thoughtfully and respects the body as the temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19–20).

At the same time, other faithful Christians believe it is wiser to abstain from tattoos. They emphasize that our bodies belong to the Lord and should be stewarded with care, noting that permanent markings may draw unnecessary attention to ourselves rather than cultivating quiet godliness (1 Timothy 2:9). They also point out that in certain cultures, families, or churches, tattoos can become an unnecessary stumbling block to others when believers are called to do everything for the glory of God without causing offense (1 Corinthians 8:9; 1 Corinthians 10:31–32).

Because this falls within the realm of Christian liberty, Paul reminds believers not to judge or look down on one another over disputable matters, for each person stands before the Lord (Romans 14:1–13). True sanctification grows through walking in love and obedience to Christ, not through outward marks or the lack of them. Still, Scripture teaches that everything not done from faith is sin (Romans 14:23), which means you should never move ahead with a permanent decision while your conscience remains uneasy or divided.

As a practical next step, spend time praying directly to God about your motives, asking whether your desire is simply to follow a trend or genuinely to honor Christ, and seek wise counsel from a mature believer or an elder in your local church who knows both your walk and your community context.
What day is the Sabbath, Saturday or Sunday?

In the Bible, the seventh-day Sabbath is Saturday, while Sunday is the Lord's Day. Under the Old Covenant, God commanded Israel to observe the Sabbath (from the Hebrew *shabbat*, meaning "to cease" or "to rest") on the seventh day of the week, running from Friday at sundown to Saturday at sundown, to commemorate both His rest after creation and Israel's deliverance from Egypt (Genesis 2:2–3; Exodus 20:8–11; Deuteronomy 5:15). In the New Testament, because Jesus rose bodily from the dead on the first day of the week (Matthew 28:1; Luke 24:1), the early church began gathering for worship, preaching, and the Lord's Supper on Sunday, which the Apostle John calls "the Lord's Day," from the Greek *kyriake hemera*, meaning a day belonging to the Lord (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2; Revelation 1:10).

Because the New Testament explains how Christ fulfills the Old Covenant, faithful Christians hold different views on how the Sabbath applies today, making this a matter of Christian liberty where believers are called to walk in charity rather than judgment (Romans 14:5–6). Many in the Reformed tradition see continuity in the creation pattern of one day in seven for worship and rest, viewing Sunday as the Christian Sabbath under the New Covenant. Another widely held historic view teaches that the Old Covenant Sabbath was a shadow pointing to our spiritual rest in Christ, meaning believers are not bound to a weekly Sabbath law (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 4:9–10), yet gladly gather on Sunday to celebrate the resurrection. A smaller number of faithful Christians, such as Seventh Day Baptists, continue to observe Saturday while trusting in Christ alone for salvation.

Following the pattern of the apostles and historic Reformed Christianity, I view Sunday as the Lord's Day, a weekly gift set apart for corporate worship, spiritual renewal, and rest in celebration of the risen Christ, while warmly respecting fellow believers who hold another conviction in good conscience. Regardless of how you understand the Sabbath command itself, a faithful next step is to prioritize gathering with a local church each Sunday to hear God's Word, enjoy fellowship, and let your soul rest in the finished work of Jesus.
Why did God punish Pharaoh for Abram’s lie (Genesis 12:17)?

At first glance, it can seem unfair that Pharaoh suffered plagues when Abram was the one who lied. Yet Scripture shows that God afflicted Pharaoh both to protect the promised covenant line from compromise and to restrain Pharaoh from committing a grave sin against Abram's marriage (Genesis 12:17).

First, God acted out of covenant faithfulness and providence. Just before Abram entered Egypt, God had pledged to make Abram a great nation and to bless all families of the earth through his offspring, promising to curse those who opposed him (Genesis 12:1–3). In the Ancient Near East, once a monarch took a woman into his royal harem, she could not leave unless a higher power intervened (Genesis 12:15). Had Sarai remained in Pharaoh's palace, the lineage through which God planned to bring the promised Savior, Jesus Christ, would have been threatened (Galatians 3:16). The plagues forced Pharaoh to recognize that something was wrong and to release Sarai before her marriage was violated.

Second, Pharaoh was not entirely blameless in the matter. Although Abram acted sinfully out of fear and unbelief, seizing a woman for a royal harem based solely on her beauty reflected the unchecked entitlement of an ancient king (Genesis 12:14–15). In a similar account later in Genesis, God warns King Abimelech that taking another man's wife, even unknowingly, brings the penalty of death, and God intervenes directly to keep the king from sinning against Him (Genesis 20:3–7). In this way, the plagues also served as a severe mercy that halted Pharaoh before he incurred deeper guilt.

Finally, the Bible never excuses Abram's dishonesty. God permitted a pagan ruler to rebuke Abram openly for his deception and send him away in embarrassment (Genesis 12:18–19). Abram's deliverance displays God's sovereign grace: the Lord does not endorse the lies of His people, yet His redemptive purposes remain unshaken by human weakness.

When fear tempts you to bend the truth to protect yourself, remember that God does not need dishonest shortcuts to fulfill His word; bring that fear to Him in prayer and choose integrity, trusting His providence to guard your steps.
Christmas Story — Day 4 — Do Christians worship Mary?

No, Christians do not worship Mary, because Scripture reserves all worship for the triune God alone. While believers rightly honor Mary as the mother of Jesus and a cherished example of faithful obedience, she is a fellow human being saved by grace rather than a divine figure or a mediator between God and humanity.

In the first-century Jewish world, faithful Israelites longed for the promised Messiah, and Mary understood her unique calling strictly in light of God's mercy toward her. In her song of praise, she calls God "my Savior" (Luke 1:47), openly acknowledging her own need for redemption. When she adds that future generations will call her "blessed" (Luke 1:48), the Greek term (*makaria*) points to the joy of receiving God's unmerited favor, not to any divine status or sinless perfection of her own (Luke 1:46–49). Later in Jesus' ministry, when a woman in the crowd praised the womb that bore Him, Jesus gently redirected her focus from Mary's biological motherhood to the greater blessing of hearing and obeying God's Word (Luke 11:27–28).

Confusion often arises because Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox traditions make a formal distinction between worship due to God alone (*latria*) and veneration or high honor given to Mary (*hyperdulia*), which includes asking for her intercession. However, historic biblical Christianity upholds *solus Christus* (Christ alone), recognizing that Jesus is the one and only Mediator between God and humanity (1 Timothy 2:5) and the merciful High Priest through whom believers approach God's throne directly (Hebrews 4:14–16). Throughout Scripture, religious worship and prayer belong exclusively to the Lord (Matthew 4:10; Revelation 22:8–9), because only Christ's incarnation, atoning death, and resurrection reconcile sinners to the Father.

As you reflect on the Christmas story, you can honor Mary rightly by imitating her humble trust when she told the angel, "May it happen to me according to your word" (Luke 1:38), while directing all of your prayers, worship, and hope exclusively to the Savior she bore.
What is Kemetic spirituality / Kemetism?

Kemetic spirituality, often called Kemetism, is a modern neopagan movement that seeks to revive and reconstruct the ancient polytheistic religion of Egypt, whose native name was *Kemet* (meaning "the black land"). Followers worship ancient Egyptian deities, such as Ra, Isis, Osiris, and Anubis, and generally organize their ethics and rituals around *Ma'at*, the ancient Egyptian concept of cosmic order, truth, and balance.

Emerging primarily in the late twentieth century, Kemetism takes different forms, ranging from strict historical reconstructionist groups to eclectic individual practices involving home altars, prayers, and offerings. Many people drawn to this path are searching for historical rootedness, moral harmony, and a deeper connection to the spiritual realm.

From a biblical perspective, Scripture teaches strict monotheism, affirming that there is only one eternal, living God who created all things (Deuteronomy 6:4; Isaiah 45:5). Upholding what theologians call the Creator-creature distinction, the Bible identifies the worship of other gods or created things as idolatry (Exodus 20:3; Romans 1:25). Indeed, during the Exodus, God sent plagues upon Egypt specifically to execute judgment against all the gods of Egypt and demonstrate His unmatched sovereignty (Exodus 12:12).

While Christians are called to treat neighbors who explore Kemetic spirituality with patience, gentleness, and respect (1 Peter 3:15), Scripture teaches that true spiritual order and peace with God are not found through ancient pantheons or striving after cosmic balance. Rather, reconciliation with the living Creator comes exclusively through Jesus Christ, the one mediator between God and humanity (1 Timothy 2:5), through His cross and resurrection. When discussing these beliefs with someone drawn to Kemetism, a helpful practical step is to listen kindly to their desire for meaning and order, and then gently point them to the goodness and truth of the one God revealed in Scripture.
Should Christians be concerned about the idea of Sharia Law?

Christians have valid reasons to be thoughtfully concerned about the civil implementation of Sharia law, particularly regarding religious liberty and moral authority, yet they should respond with steady discernment and love rather than fear.

Understanding the issue requires a brief distinction. For many Muslims around the world, the word "Sharia" primarily refers to personal religious duties such as prayer, charity, and diet. When Christians express concern, it is usually regarding Sharia as a formal legal and political system imposed by the state. 

From a biblical perspective, there are two primary reasons for thoughtful vigilance. First, while Christians recognize that non-Christian legal systems may still reflect certain moral standards through God's common grace (His general preservation of moral order among all people), Sharia as a comprehensive worldview denies core truths of the Christian faith. It rejects the deity of Christ, His substitutionary atonement on the cross, and the supreme authority of Scripture. Scripture teaches that sinners are justified by grace alone through faith in Jesus Christ, not by adherence to any religious law code (Galatians 2:16; Ephesians 2:8–9).

Second, where strict Sharia is enforced as civil law, freedom of conscience is routinely curtailed. Laws against apostasy and evangelism directly hinder believers from openly worshipping Christ and obeying the Great Commission. Scripture instructs Christians to pray for civil authorities precisely so that society may remain peaceful and orderly, allowing the Gospel to be freely proclaimed (1 Timothy 2:1–4). Civil government is instituted by God to uphold justice and restrain evil (Romans 13:1–4), not to coerce religious allegiance or silence the witness of the church.

At the same time, concern should never harden into panic or hostility toward Muslims. The sovereignty of God stands unshaken over every nation and legal system, for He removes kings and establishes them according to His wisdom (Daniel 2:21; Psalm 115:3), and Jesus Christ already holds all authority in heaven and on earth (Matthew 28:18). While faithful Christians may differ on specific political strategies for preserving religious liberty in a pluralistic society (Romans 14:19), we are united in our duty to live peaceably with all people as far as it depends on us (Romans 12:18) and to love our Muslim neighbors as fellow image-bearers of God (Genesis 1:27).

As a practical next step, commit this week to praying regularly by name for your local civil leaders, asking God to preserve religious freedom in your community, and intentionally look for an opportunity to show hospitality to a Muslim neighbor or coworker so you can bear witness to Christ with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15).
What is the meaning of the foxes in Song of Solomon 2:15?

In Song of Solomon 2:15, the "little foxes" represent small, seemingly minor threats, distractions, or compromises that can quietly damage a blossoming relationship if they are not addressed early. Because the couple's "vineyards are in bloom," symbolizing their tender and growing love, these subtle intrusions pose a real danger to future fruitfulness.

In the Ancient Near Eastern agricultural world, foxes (from the Hebrew *shu'alim*, which can refer to foxes or jackals) were known for burrowing under vineyard walls, disturbing roots, and gnawing on young, tender shoots before grapes could mature. Within the poetry of the book, the vineyard is a recurring image for the couple's romantic affection and devotion (Song of Solomon 1:6; Song of Solomon 8:12). Calling to "catch the foxes" is therefore a plea to protect their covenant bond from unresolved friction, selfishness, or neglect before small troubles cause lasting ruin.

While the immediate context celebrates marital love and fidelity, the wisdom of this passage also speaks directly to our progressive sanctification in Christ. Just as a harvest can be ruined by small pests rather than only major storms, our walk with God and our relationships with others are often hindered by small, tolerated sins such as bitterness, pride, or careless words (Hebrews 12:1; Ephesians 4:26–27). Rather than excusing minor compromises as harmless, we guard both our homes and our fellowship with the Lord by confronting them promptly through honest communication, confession, and humble repentance.
What is the false cause fallacy?

The false cause fallacy is an error in reasoning where someone concludes that one event caused another simply because the two events happened together or one occurred before the other. In other words, it mistakes mere sequence or correlation for genuine causation.

This fallacy commonly appears in two forms:

*   **Sequential (*post hoc ergo propter hoc*, "after this, therefore because of this"):** Assuming that because Event B happened after Event A, Event A must have caused Event B. For example, if you wear a particular pair of socks and your favorite team wins a game, concluding that the socks caused the victory commits this error.
*   **Correlational (*cum hoc ergo propter hoc*, "with this, therefore because of this"):** Assuming that because two things happen at the same time, one must cause the other, while overlooking coincidence or a hidden third factor. For instance, noticing that ice cream sales and sunburns both rise in July does not mean eating ice cream causes sunburns; both are caused by warm summer weather.

To avoid the false cause fallacy in everyday decisions, ask whether there is a real, demonstrable connection between two events or if a separate factor explains them both. Slowing down to test assumptions protects us from gullibility and helps us discern what is actually true (Proverbs 14:15).
Is it a sin to share copyrighted material on the internet?

Sharing copyrighted material on the internet without the owner's permission or a valid legal exception (such as fair use) is a sin, because it violates God's command against theft and disregards rightful civil authority. On the other hand, sharing copyrighted material when you have the creator's authorization, an open license, or a lawful fair-use purpose is entirely permissible.

In the context of ancient Israel, the Eighth Commandment, "You shall not steal" (Exodus 20:15), protected a neighbor's property and livelihood so the community could live in justice and trust. Writing later to Christians living under Roman rule, the Apostle Paul reminded believers to submit to governing authorities and to "pay everyone what you owe him" (Romans 13:1–7). Together, these passages reflect God's enduring **moral law**, which remains the objective standard for human conduct and shapes our **sanctification** as followers of Christ. Even though copying a digital file does not remove a physical item from someone's shelf, distributing a creator's book, music, film, or software without permission still deprives them of the rightful fruit of their labor (Ephesians 4:28; 1 Timothy 5:18).

Because the internet makes copying and forwarding files effortless, it is easy to treat digital piracy as harmless. Yet true Christian **stewardship** calls us to be just as honest behind a screen as we would be in a local shop. Sharing a direct link to a creator's official website or quoting a brief passage within fair-use guidelines honors their work, whereas uploading or downloading pirated copies takes what does not belong to us. 

If you realize you have crossed this line, remember that the Gospel meets our failure with grace, because Jesus Christ paid the penalty for all our sins on the cross and calls us into a new life of integrity. As a concrete next step, review the digital files or links you share, delete any pirated copies from your devices, and purchase or use legitimate sources going forward, asking the Lord in prayer for a tender conscience in your everyday online habits.
What does the Bible say about Christian fathers?

Scripture calls Christian fathers to lead, provide for, and spiritually instruct their children with sacrificial love, firm discipline, and tender patience. Rather than ruling with harshness, a godly father reflects the character of God the Father and nurtures his household in the truth of the Gospel.

In the first-century Greco-Roman world, fathers held sweeping legal authority over their households, which makes the Apostle Paul's command in Ephesians 6:4 striking: "Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger; instead, bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord." Within Scripture, biblical headship is not domineering control, but humble, covenantal stewardship modeled after Christ's self-giving love for the church (Ephesians 5:25).

Across both Testaments, the Bible highlights four core duties for fathers:

*   **Spiritual instruction:** Fathers bear primary responsibility for passing down the faith. God commanded Israelite families to impress His words diligently upon their children throughout everyday life (Deuteronomy 6:6–7), and the book of Proverbs repeatedly portrays a father urging his children to embrace wisdom and the fear of the Lord (Proverbs 4:1–4).
*   **Loving discipline:** Godly fathers correct sin faithfully without exasperating or crushing their children's spirit (Proverbs 13:24; Colossians 3:21). Just as God disciplines His children for their sanctification and good (Hebrews 12:9–10), a father's correction aims at repentance and restoration rather than venting personal anger.
*   **Provision and integrity:** Scripture calls fathers to work diligently to care for their household's material needs (1 Timothy 5:8) and to walk in righteousness, leaving a legacy of integrity for the next generation (Proverbs 20:7).
*   **Tender compassion:** Far from being emotionally distant, a Christian father mirrors the mercy of God, who shows compassion to His children because He understands their weakness (Psalm 103:13–14).

Because every earthly father falls short of this standard, faithful fatherhood depends daily on the forgiveness and strength found in Jesus Christ. As a concrete step, a father can establish a simple daily rhythm of family worship, taking five minutes after dinner or before bed to read a short passage of Scripture and pray aloud with his children.
What was the process of deciding on the Old Testament canon?

The Old Testament canon was not invented or voted on by a later human council; rather, it was progressively received and recognized by God's people as prophets wrote under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. Rather than creating Scripture's authority, the covenant community acknowledged the books that already carried God's inherent authority, and the collection was effectively settled well before the earthly ministry of Jesus Christ.

In keeping with Ancient Near Eastern practice for binding covenant treaties, Moses placed the Book of the Law beside the ark of the covenant to preserve it as Israel's authoritative standard (Deuteronomy 31:24–26). Subsequent prophetic writings were added to this sacred collection as they were given (Joshua 24:26), and later prophets treated earlier prophetic books as established Scripture, such as Daniel studying the written prophecies of Jeremiah (Daniel 9:2). By the Second Temple period, Jewish communities consistently recognized this fixed collection in a threefold structure: the Law, the Prophets, and the Writings.

The Lord Jesus Christ Himself confirmed the boundaries of the Old Testament canon. He referred to the entire span of Old Testament history from Abel in Genesis to Zechariah in 2 Chronicles (the first and last books in the traditional Hebrew arrangement) in Luke 11:51, and He affirmed the threefold division as the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms in Luke 24:44. While Jesus and the Jewish leaders disagreed deeply over how to interpret the Scriptures, they never disagreed over which books belonged in them. Although later Jewish scholars discussed certain books and Greek translations eventually circulated additional writings known as the Apocrypha, neither Jesus nor the apostles ever cited the Apocrypha as authoritative Scripture.

Theologically, this history highlights the doctrines of divine inspiration and providence. The word *canon* comes from the Greek *kanon*, meaning a "measuring rod" or "standard," because Scripture serves as the rule of faith for God's people. Because all Scripture is "God-breathed" and its authors spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit (2 Timothy 3:16; 2 Peter 1:21), these writings possessed divine authority the moment they were written, and God's providence ensured His people recognized and preserved them.

Because Christ Himself trusted these Scriptures as the unbreakable Word of God, you can read the Old Testament today with complete confidence. Make it a regular habit to include an Old Testament chapter alongside a New Testament passage in your daily Bible reading plan, praying that God would help you see how every promise points forward to Jesus Christ.
Is cyber-sex / phone sex a sin?

Yes, outside the covenant of marriage, cyber-sex and phone sex are sins against God. Scripture teaches that God designed sexual intimacy exclusively for one man and one woman united in marriage (Genesis 2:24; Hebrews 13:4).

In the New Testament, believers are repeatedly commanded to flee from sexual immorality (1 Corinthians 6:18; Ephesians 5:3). The Greek word translated as "sexual immorality" is *porneia*, which in the first-century Jewish and Greco-Roman world encompassed every form of sexual expression and gratification outside of lawful marriage. Furthermore, Jesus made clear that sin is not merely physical, warning that anyone who looks with lust has already committed adultery in his heart (Matthew 5:27–28). Engaging in sexual conversation, imagery, or gratification with someone who is not your spouse (even over a phone or through a screen) is both lust and sexual immorality, and it dishonors the body, which God claims as His own temple (1 Corinthians 6:18–20). (If your question is about a married couple separated by travel or deployment, sexual intimacy belongs exclusively to spouses, though husbands and wives should still exercise wisdom and caution regarding digital privacy so that nothing compromises their purity.)

At the same time, God knows the fierce pull of loneliness, temptation, and the desires of the flesh. The great hope of the Gospel is that Jesus Christ came specifically to rescue sinners. Because all of us have broken God's holy law (Romans 3:23), Christ, who is truly God and truly man, lived a sinless life, suffered our penalty on the cross through His penal substitutionary death, and rose bodily from the dead on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4; 2 Corinthians 5:21). Through His finished work, sinners receive justification, being declared righteous by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone (Romans 5:1). If this is an area of guilt or struggle for you, turn from this sin in repentance and trust in Jesus Christ alone for complete forgiveness and new life (1 John 1:9).

As you grow in sanctification, the ongoing work of the Holy Spirit making you holy, take a practical step today: cut off the digital pathways that feed this temptation by deleting the apps, accounts, or contacts involved (Matthew 5:29–30). Share your struggle with a trusted, mature believer or pastor in your local church so they can walk alongside you and pray for you, for the prayer of a righteous person has great power (James 5:16). Bring this honestly before God in prayer yourself, asking Him to guard your mind and satisfy your heart in Christ.

Do unbelievers immediately go to hell when they die?

Scripture teaches that the souls of unbelievers enter a conscious state of torment immediately upon death, while awaiting the final bodily resurrection and judgment when they will be cast into the eternal lake of fire.

In the New Testament, this progression is clarified by the original Greek terms used within their Second Temple Jewish context. In Jesus' account of the rich man and Lazarus, the rich man dies and his soul immediately enters *Hades*, the temporary realm of the dead, where he experiences conscious agony (Luke 16:22–24). Likewise, the Bible affirms that after death comes judgment (Hebrews 9:27) and that the Lord knows how to hold the unrighteous for punishment on the day of judgment (2 Peter 2:9). In historic Christian theology, this period between physical death and Christ's return is called the intermediate state.

When Jesus Christ returns, the final judgment will take place. Both the righteous and the unrighteous will be raised bodily, and everyone whose name is not found written in the Book of Life will be thrown into *Gehenna*, also called the lake of fire, which is the final and eternal hell (Matthew 10:28; Revelation 20:11–15).

Speaking of eternal judgment is never meant to be cold or harsh, for God Himself declares that He takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but desires that they turn and live (Ezekiel 33:11). Still, this sobering truth reminds us of our great need for mercy. Every human being has sinned against a holy God and stands justly under His wrath (Romans 3:23; Romans 6:23). Yet in boundless love, God sent His Son, Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, to live a sinless life and die on the cross in the place of sinners. Through His penal substitution, Christ bore the punishment our sins deserved, was buried, and rose bodily from the dead on the third day to conquer sin and death (1 Corinthians 15:3–4; 2 Corinthians 5:21). Because of His saving work, justification and eternal life are given by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, never by our own good deeds (Ephesians 2:8–9).

Because none of us knows how many days we have left, the wisest step to take in light of eternity is to examine your standing before God today rather than putting it off (2 Corinthians 6:2). Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose again, for forgiveness and eternal life (Acts 16:31).

How should Christians react to persecution against the LGBTQ community?

Christians must firmly oppose persecution, violence, hatred, and unjust treatment directed at the LGBTQ community, because every human being possesses inherent dignity as an image-bearer of God. At the same time, faithful Christian love never compromises biblical truth, calling us to uphold God's design for human sexuality while extending the grace of the Gospel to all people.

The foundation for how we treat every neighbor is the doctrine of the *imago Dei*, the truth that God created all humanity in His own image (Genesis 1:27). Because every person bears God's image, cruelty, harassment, mockery, or physical harm against anyone is a grievous sin against the Creator. Scripture commands believers to live at peace with everyone as far as it depends on them and to do good to all people (Romans 12:18; Galatians 6:10). When Jesus taught the Parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:25-37), He spoke into a first-century Jewish context marked by bitter religious and ethnic hostility between Jews and Samaritans. By making a despised Samaritan the model of neighborly mercy, Jesus showed that Christian compassion must cross social and moral boundaries to protect and care for those who are hurting or mistreated.

Protecting someone from persecution, however, does not mean affirming sinful behavior or identities. God's Word establishes as an objective moral standard that marriage is the lifelong covenant between one man and one woman (Genesis 2:24; Matthew 19:4-6), and Scripture clearly identifies homosexual practice as sin (Romans 1:26-27; 1 Corinthians 6:9-10). Yet the Bible leaves no room for self-righteousness, because all people stand equally guilty before a holy God and in need of mercy (Romans 3:23). Writing to Christians in Corinth, a Greco-Roman city infamous for sexual license, the Apostle Paul reminded them that though some had once lived in homosexual practice and other sins, they experienced genuine transformation through justification and sanctification in Christ (1 Corinthians 6:11). True love warns of the danger of sin while holding out the hope that Jesus Christ died on the cross for sinners and rose bodily from the dead to offer forgiveness and new life to all who repent and trust in Him (2 Corinthians 5:17).

In daily life, you can practice this balance of truth and love in concrete ways. First, refuse to participate in demeaning jokes, harsh rhetoric, or unfair treatment toward LGBTQ individuals in your workplace, family, or community, and speak up gently to defend their basic human dignity when you witness mistreatment (Ephesians 4:29). Second, cultivate genuine, hospitable relationships with neighbors who identify as LGBTQ, listening to them with patience and respect while remaining ready to share the reason for your hope in Christ with gentleness (1 Peter 3:15). Let both your defense of their dignity and your faithfulness to Scripture serve as a clear window into the grace of God.
How did Satan and other angels sin if heaven is sinless?

Heaven is sinless because God Himself is perfectly holy, and no sin can remain in His presence (1 John 1:5). However, before their rebellion, angels were created as good, finite beings who possessed moral agency and creaturely mutability, meaning they were capable of choosing disobedience even in a sinless environment. Satan and the fallen angels sinned not because heaven or God was flawed, but because they freely chose pride and rebellion against their Creator.

Scripture speaks with sober restraint about this event rather than answering every philosophical question. Jesus says that the devil "was a murderer from the beginning, refusing to uphold the truth" (John 8:44), and the Apostle Paul warns church leaders against pride so they will not fall into the same condemnation as the devil (1 Timothy 3:6). Similarly, Jude writes of "the angels who did not stay within their own domain but abandoned their proper dwelling" (Jude 1:6), and 2 Peter 2:4 confirms that God did not spare these angels when they sinned. In the original Greek of Jude 1:6, the word translated "domain" (*arche*) refers to their assigned sphere of authority or original position, underscoring that their sin was a willful rejection of their God-given place.

In historic Christian theology, this points to the vital distinction between God's immutability (His unchanging perfection) and the mutability of His creatures. Only God is incapable of sinning by His very nature; He never tempts anyone to sin and is never the author of evil (James 1:13). Once those angels rebelled, God swiftly judged them and removed them from His blessed presence, while preserving the "elect angels" in confirmed holiness (2 Peter 2:4; 1 Timothy 5:21).

While Scripture leaves the exact inner spark of how a pure creature first conceived pride as a mystery, it offers clear guidance for us today. First, it warns us to watch against pride and self-exaltation, calling us to cultivate a daily habit of humble prayer and submission to God's rightful rule in every area of life. Second, it gives believers deep assurance: unlike the angels before their fall, those who belong to Christ will be brought into a renewed creation where nothing unclean will ever enter again (Revelation 21:27), kept forever by the grace of our unchanging Savior.
What is the greatest sin?

While Scripture teaches that every sin is serious rebellion against a holy God and worthy of judgment (Romans 6:23; James 2:10), the Bible highlights unbelief, specifically the rejection of God and His Son Jesus Christ, along with failing to love God supremely, as the root and greatest of sins (Matthew 22:36–38; John 16:8–9). In its ultimate, hardened form, this is what Jesus warned against as blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, the willful and final refusal to receive the Spirit's witness to Christ (Matthew 12:31–32).

In the New Testament, the primary Greek word for sin (*hamartia*) carries the sense of missing the mark or falling short of God's righteous standard (Romans 3:23). Speaking within a first-century Jewish context where teachers often debated which commands were weightiest, Jesus grounded the entire moral law in Deuteronomy 6:4–5, declaring that the first and greatest commandment is to love the Lord with all your heart, soul, and mind (Matthew 22:37–38). If loving God supremely is the highest command, then refusing to honor Him as God lies at the heart of all pride and idolatry (Romans 1:21–23). In historic Christian theology, this inward rebellion flows from *original sin*, the fallen condition all people inherit from Adam, and it reaches its sharpest expression when someone rejects the Holy Spirit's clear testimony about Jesus (John 3:18; John 16:9).

Practically, this means we should examine our hearts daily for subtle idols, such as trusting in our own morality, comfort, or reputation rather than resting in God. It also offers real comfort if you are anxious about having committed an unforgivable sin, because genuine grief over sin and a desire for God's mercy show that your heart is not permanently hardened against Him.

The glorious hope of the Gospel is that Jesus Christ, who is truly God and truly man, lived a sinless life and died on the cross in the place of sinners (a truth known as *penal substitution*) to bear God's righteous wrath against sin, and He rose bodily on the third day in victory over death (1 Corinthians 15:3–4; 2 Corinthians 5:21). Through Him, sinners receive *justification*, being declared righteous before God by grace alone through faith alone, not by works (Ephesians 2:8–9). Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

Is there a specific Bible passage or personal concern that led you to ask about this today?
What does the Bible say about sedition?

The Bible consistently condemns sedition, treating both rebellion against lawful civil authority and the stirring up of divisive factions within a community as sinful disorder. Scripture teaches that God establishes governing authorities to restrain evil and preserve peace, meaning that willful insurrection opposes God's own appointed order (Romans 13:1–2; Proverbs 24:21–22).

In the Greco-Roman world of the New Testament, political stability was fragile, and the biblical writers warn against both civil insurrection (the Greek term *stasis*, used of the violent uprising involving Barabbas in Mark 15:7 and the false charges brought against Paul in Acts 24:5) and factious division within the church (the Greek term *dichostasia*, listed among the works of the flesh in Galatians 5:19–21 and condemned in Romans 16:17). This aligns with the Old Testament record, where God judged severe rebellions against His appointed leaders, such as Korah's uprising against Moses and Aaron (Numbers 16:1–35) and Absalom's conspiracy against King David (2 Samuel 15:1–12). 

Historically, Christian theology summarizes this biblical teaching under the doctrines of **providence** and the **civil magistrate**. Out of **common grace**, God ordains earthly rulers as His servants to promote justice and curb lawlessness, even when those rulers are imperfect or pagan, as the Roman emperors were when Paul and Peter urged believers to submit to governing authorities (Romans 13:3–4; 1 Peter 2:13–17). 

At the same time, Scripture carefully distinguishes sinful sedition from faithful obedience to God when human laws cross divine commands. Because earthly authority is delegated and limited, believers must refuse to comply if a ruler commands what God forbids or forbids what God commands, standing with the apostles who declared, "We must obey God rather than men" (Acts 5:29; Daniel 3:16–18). Even in those moments, faithful Christians accept the consequences peacefully and pray for their rulers rather than resorting to violent revolt or lawless anarchy (1 Timothy 2:1–2; Matthew 5:44).

In practical terms, this calls believers to obey the laws of their nation, pay taxes honestly, speak respectfully of those in office, and guard the local church against gossip and partisan quarrels (Titus 3:1–2; Romans 13:6–7). Rather than giving way to outrage or factiousness when cultural or political conditions are difficult, we rest in Christ's sovereign rule and pursue the peace and good of our communities with steady integrity.
What is the International Christian Church (ICC), and what do they believe?

The International Christian Church (ICC), also known as the SoldOut Discipling Movement, is a restorationist religious movement founded in 2006 by Kip McKean in Los Angeles, California, following his departure from the International Churches of Christ (ICOC). While the ICC affirms several traditional Christian doctrines, such as the Trinity, the deity of Jesus Christ, and the inspiration of the Bible, its teachings on salvation, church authority, and discipleship depart significantly from historic orthodox Christianity.

First, regarding salvation, the ICC teaches a form of baptismal regeneration rather than justification by faith alone. They hold that a person's sins are not forgiven and salvation is not received until the individual is immersed in water while consciously committing to live as a "disciple" within their movement, which regularly leads them to require re-baptism for Christians coming from other churches. By contrast, Scripture clearly teaches that sinners are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, apart from any human work or ritual (Romans 3:28; Ephesians 2:8-9). In the New Testament, forgiveness and the gift of the Holy Spirit are given the moment a person believes in Jesus (Acts 10:43-47), and water baptism follows as an act of obedience and an outward sign of the inward grace already received.

Second, in its ecclesiology (doctrine of the church), the ICC claims to be the exclusive restored remnant of the first-century church, teaching that Christianity fell into widespread apostasy until their movement emerged. Alongside this exclusivity, they practice a top-down, hierarchical model of "discipling," in which leaders and assigned "disciplers" frequently exercise heavy authority over members' personal decisions, relationships, schedules, and finances. Scripture, however, teaches that Jesus builds His universal church out of all believers who genuinely trust in Him rather than one exclusive modern organization (Matthew 16:18; Ephesians 4:4-6), and it instructs pastors to shepherd God's flock gently rather than lording authority over those entrusted to their care (1 Peter 5:2-3).

While a sincere desire for committed discipleship and evangelism is admirable, love and faithfulness to God require testing every movement's teaching against His Word. If you are looking into the ICC or caring for someone involved in it, take time to compare their requirements directly with the gospel of free grace in Scripture, and seek fellowship in a local Bible-teaching church where Christ's finished work on the cross, rather than institutional loyalty, is your assurance before God.
Do some Christmas traditions have pagan origins?

Yes, some cultural customs associated with the Christmas season, such as winter feasting, exchanging gifts, and decorating with evergreens, have parallels to or roots in pre-Christian winter festivals. At the same time, historians note that many popular claims about direct pagan origins, including the date of December 25 and the sixteenth-century German Christmas tree, are historically debated and often trace back to early Christian calculations or medieval practices rather than straightforward pagan borrowing.

How believers engage with these traditions is a non-essential matter of **Christian liberty** (sometimes called *adiaphora*, meaning things neither commanded nor forbidden by Scripture), because the Bible does not mandate or prohibit the annual celebration of Christ's birth. Because Scripture leaves room for conscience here, faithful Christians hold different perspectives on the matter.

Many Christians joyfully participate in Christmas traditions, understanding that cultural forms like lights, music, and evergreens have lost any pagan religious meaning and have been redeemed to celebrate the **Incarnation** of the Son of God. From this perspective, believers can receive good gifts and cultural customs with thanksgiving to the Creator, recognizing that the earth is the Lord's and everything in it (1 Corinthians 10:25–26; 1 Timothy 4:4–5). On the other hand, some sincere Christians, following the convictions of earlier Reformed and Puritan believers, choose to abstain from Christmas traditions out of reverence for God's Word, wishing to avoid extra-biblical holy days or any cultural association with ancient idolatry.

Scripture directly guides us on how to handle these differing convictions with humility and love. In Romans 14:5–6, the Apostle Paul writes that one person regards a certain day above others while another considers every day alike, and he urges that each believer "should be fully convinced in his own mind." Both the Christian who observes the day in honor of the Lord and the Christian who abstains in honor of the Lord can glorify God, provided they refuse to judge or look down on one another (Romans 14:10; Romans 14:13).

Practically, whether you choose to put up a Christmas tree or treat December 25 as an ordinary day, act with a clear conscience before God and use the season to remind your family and neighbors of the Gospel truth that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14).
Where does the Old Testament predict the coming of Christ?

The Old Testament predicts the coming of Christ from its opening chapters to its final prophets, gradually revealing a Savior who would be both a sovereign King and a suffering Redeemer. After His resurrection, Jesus confirmed that everything written about Him in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms had to be fulfilled (Luke 24:44).

The title "Christ" comes from the Greek translation of the Hebrew word *Mashiach* ("anointed one"). In ancient Israel, oil was poured on prophets, priests, and kings to set them apart for God's service, and the Old Testament builds an expectation that one ultimate Anointed One would unite all three roles in Himself.

Here are the major threads of Old Testament prophecy that point directly to Jesus:

**The Promised Offspring**
Immediately after humanity fell into sin, God promised that an offspring of the woman would crush the serpent's head, even as His own heel was struck (Genesis 3:15). God later narrowed this promise to Abraham, declaring that all nations on earth would be blessed through his line (Genesis 12:3), and to King David, promising that one of his descendants would rule on an everlasting throne (2 Samuel 7:12–16).

**His Birth and Divine Nature**
Centuries before Jesus' birth, the prophet Micah foretold that this eternal ruler would be born in the small town of Bethlehem (Micah 5:2). Isaiah revealed that He would be born of a virgin and called Immanuel, meaning "God with us" (Isaiah 7:14), and explicitly identified this promised child as "Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace" (Isaiah 9:6). These prophecies establish the foundation for the **incarnation**, the truth that the eternal Son of God took on genuine human nature.

**His Suffering, Death, and Resurrection**
Long before crucifixion was practiced in Judea, Isaiah described a Suffering Servant who would be "pierced for our transgressions" and "crushed for our iniquities" so that sinners might have peace with God (Isaiah 53:5). Similarly, David wrote prophetically of hands and feet being pierced and garments divided by casting lots (Psalm 22:16–18), while also expressing confidence that God would not abandon His soul to the grave or let His Holy One see decay (Psalm 16:10). Together, these passages reveal **penal substitution**, showing that Christ bore the just penalty of our sins in our place before rising bodily from the dead.

**His Eternal Kingdom**
During Israel's exile in Babylon, Daniel received a vision of "one like a son of man" approaching the Ancient of Days to receive an everlasting dominion over all peoples and nations (Daniel 7:13–14). Jesus frequently used "Son of Man" as His favorite self-designation to claim this very authority.

Seeing how God wove these promises across more than a thousand years gives us deep confidence in the trustworthiness of Scripture and the faithfulness of God. A practical way to strengthen your faith this week is to read Isaiah 53 alongside Matthew 27, noting how precisely Jesus fulfilled the words written centuries before His birth. That same Savior who came as promised now offers full forgiveness and eternal life to everyone who turns from sin and trusts in Him.
What is spiritual adultery?

Spiritual adultery is covenant unfaithfulness toward God, occurring when His people give their supreme love, trust, or worship to anything or anyone other than Him. Throughout Scripture, the Lord portrays His relationship with His people as a sacred marriage, making idolatry and divided allegiance a personal betrayal rather than merely a broken rule.

In the Ancient Near East, royal covenants demanded exclusive loyalty from a people to their sovereign king, and the Old Testament prophets deepened this picture by portraying the Lord as Israel's faithful Husband. When Israel chased after pagan deities like Baal or trusted in foreign military alliances instead of God, prophets like Jeremiah and Hosea confronted the nation as an unfaithful spouse (Jeremiah 3:8–9; Hosea 2:2–5).

The New Testament carries this same marriage imagery forward, describing the church as betrothed exclusively to Christ (2 Corinthians 11:2). James warns believers bluntly that "friendship with the world is hostility toward God," calling such divided loyalty spiritual adultery (James 4:4). Theologically, this exposes the true nature of **idolatry**: it is not limited to bowing before carved statues, but includes any affection, security, or ambition that rivals God for the throne of the human heart.

Yet the wonder of the Gospel is that Jesus Christ, the faithful Bridegroom, loved an unfaithful people and secured our **justification** by giving Himself up for the church on the cross (Ephesians 5:25–27). By His Spirit, He now works **sanctification** in believers, gently drawing wandering hearts back into single-minded devotion. Practically, guarding against spiritual adultery means regularly examining what you run to for comfort, identity, or security, and turning from any rival love in honest repentance so that Christ remains your first affection.
How can we rely on the power of God?

We rely on God's power not by straining harder in our own strength, but by acknowledging our helplessness and daily depending on His grace through our union with Christ. Jesus told His disciples plainly that apart from Him we can do nothing (John 15:5). 

Consider how the Apostle Paul learned this lesson in 2 Corinthians 12:9–10. Writing into a Greco-Roman culture that prized self-sufficiency, status, and visible strength, Paul embraced his limitations so that Christ's strength would rest upon him, holding fast to the Lord's promise: "My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness" (2 Corinthians 12:9). The Greek word used here for power (*dynamis*) points to an active, enabling might supplied from outside ourselves. In historic Christian theology, this ongoing reliance on the indwelling Holy Spirit to empower obedience and endurance is part of progressive sanctification, and God faithfully delivers that strength through ordinary practices known as the means of grace (Ephesians 3:16).

Practically, leaning on God's power takes shape in three steady rhythms:

*   **Anchor your mind in Scripture.** God's Word is the primary instrument the Spirit uses to steady our hearts, correct our fears, and equip us for every good work (2 Timothy 3:16–17; Psalm 119:28). When we are weak, Scripture reminds us of who God is rather than leaving us trapped in how we feel.
*   **Bring your weakness directly to God in prayer.** Dependence grows when we stop pretending we have it all together and instead approach the throne of grace with confidence to receive mercy and timely help (Hebrews 4:16). You can pray directly to God by opening a passage like Psalm 23 or Ephesians 3:14–19 and turning those verses into your own honest words to Him.
*   **Lean on the fellowship of your local church.** God does not design His people to walk alone; He strengthens our faith through the shared worship, encouragement, and accountability of fellow believers (Hebrews 10:24–25). Asking a mature Christian to pray with and for you is a powerful expression of humility (James 5:16).

As a concrete step this week, identify one specific responsibility or temptation where you feel worn thin, and begin each morning by reading Ephesians 3:14–21 before starting your daily routine. Pray directly to the Father, naming that exact struggle and asking Him to strengthen you in your inner being by His Spirit, and share that need with a trusted believer or pastor at your church so they can stand with you in prayer.
What does it mean that Jesus fulfilled the law, but did not abolish it?

When Jesus declared that He came not to abolish the Law or the Prophets but to fulfill them (Matthew 5:17), He meant that His mission was not to discard God's revealed Word, but to bring all of Old Testament Scripture to its intended goal and completion. Rather than tearing down God's law, Jesus lived out its righteous demands perfectly, bore its penalty in His death, and realized every promise and shadow pointing to Him.

In the Second Temple Jewish world of Jesus' day, the phrase "the Law and the Prophets" was a standard way of referring to the entire Hebrew Scriptures. The Greek verb translated "fulfill" (*plēroō*) carries the sense of filling something to full measure or bringing it to its intended purpose, much as a blooming oak tree fulfills an acorn rather than destroying it.

Scripture unfolds this fulfillment in three vital ways:

First, Jesus fulfilled the prophetic patterns and ceremonies of the Old Testament. Every sacrifice, priesthood, and temple shadow pointed forward to Him (Luke 24:44; Colossians 2:16–17). Once the promised reality arrived in Christ, those ceremonial shadows had completed their God-given work.

Second, Jesus fulfilled the law's righteous demands and penalty on behalf of sinners. Through His sinless life, He rendered *active obedience*, keeping God's law completely in thought, word, and deed (Hebrews 4:15; 1 Peter 2:22). Through His sacrificial death on the cross, He rendered *passive obedience* in *penal substitution*, taking the curse of a broken law upon Himself (Galatians 3:13; Romans 8:3–4). In this way, Christ became the culmination of the law so that everyone who believes in Him receives *justification* by faith, clothed in His perfect righteousness rather than their own flawed efforts (Romans 10:4; 2 Corinthians 5:21).

Third, Jesus upheld the enduring authority of God's *moral law*. Far from relaxing God's standards, He immediately went on in the Sermon on the Mount to expose the heart-level depth of God's commands concerning anger, lust, truthfulness, and love for enemies (Matthew 5:21–48). While believers are no longer under the Mosaic law as a system to earn eternal life, God's moral law remains the unchanging reflection of His holy character, and the Holy Spirit writes it on our hearts to guide our love for God and neighbor (Romans 13:8–10; Galatians 5:14).

In daily life, this truth frees you from both anxious legalism and careless living. Because Christ has already fulfilled the law for you, you do not have to strive to earn God's favor through your own performance; instead, you can rest in His finished work and ask the Holy Spirit each morning to align your words, habits, and affections with His good commands.
What are the Major Prophets and Minor Prophets?

The Major Prophets and Minor Prophets are the two groupings of the seventeen prophetic books at the end of the Old Testament, distinguished solely by the length of the books rather than the importance of their messages. The Major Prophets consist of five longer books (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel, and Daniel), while the Minor Prophets consist of twelve shorter books (Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi).

Historically, the twelve Minor Prophets were brief enough to be copied together onto a single scroll in Jewish tradition, whereas longer works like Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel each required a scroll of their own. In the Christian ordering of the Old Testament, Lamentations is placed alongside Jeremiah as his lament over the fall of Jerusalem, and Daniel is grouped with the Major Prophets because of its length and sweeping prophetic visions.

All seventeen books carry equal divine authority within God's progressive revelation, because the Holy Spirit carried along these prophets to speak the very Word of God (Hebrews 1:1–2; 2 Peter 1:20–21). Through their ministries, the Lord confronted Israel's covenant unfaithfulness, warned the nations of righteous judgment, and pointed forward to the promised salvation accomplished in Jesus Christ (Luke 24:27; Luke 24:44).

As you read the Old Testament, do not overlook the Minor Prophets because of their size; try reading a shorter book like Habakkuk or Micah in a single sitting this week to see how clearly God's holiness and mercy shine through even a few chapters.
Why believe in Jesus?

It is understandable to wonder why anyone should believe in Jesus, especially if He seems like just one wise moral teacher among many, or if trusting in a figure from two thousand years ago feels distant from modern life.

The Bible teaches that Christians believe in Jesus because of who He uniquely is and what He actually accomplished in history to reconcile sinners to God. In the first-century Jewish world that longed for God's promised Messiah, Jesus of Nazareth fulfilled the Old Testament Scriptures through His authoritative teaching and miracles, revealing Himself as the eternal Son of God who took on human flesh (John 1:1–14). Through this miracle of the incarnation, being truly God and truly man, He alone is able to stand as the one mediator between a holy God and humanity (1 Timothy 2:5).

Our deepest need begins with the reality that God is completely holy and just, whereas every human being has sinned and fallen short of His glory, leaving us separated from Him and under His righteous judgment (Romans 3:23; Romans 6:23). We cannot bridge that gap through our own good deeds or moral improvement. Yet in His mercy, Jesus lived the perfectly obedient life we could never live (Hebrews 4:15) and willingly gave Himself on the cross in our place, a saving work known as penal substitutionary atonement, bearing the punishment our sins deserved (2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 Peter 2:24). He truly died, was buried, and rose bodily from the grave on the third day, proving His victory over sin and death (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). Exalted now as Lord at the right hand of the Father (Acts 2:32–36), Christ freely offers justification, meaning God declares forgiven sinners righteous, by grace alone through faith alone in Him, and not by works (Ephesians 2:8–9; Romans 5:1). Because He alone paid the debt of sin and conquered the grave, salvation is found in no one else (John 14:6; Acts 4:12).

A practical step you can take this week is to read through the Gospel of John slowly, noticing how Jesus speaks to ordinary people who had questions and doubts.
